sections.title: PD-M04-L02: Pre-mortems, choice overload and regret
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can run a pre-mortem on a plan, cut down options when choices overwhelm you, and handle regret in a useful way. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Imagining that your plan has already failed reveals risks you would otherwise miss; too many options rarely matter as much as claimed, but when they do, limit them; regret is information, not a sentence.

## The science

**Pre-mortems.** Psychologist Gary Klein described the **pre-mortem** in the Harvard Business Review in 2007. Before starting a project, the team imagines it is the future and the project has failed badly, then each person writes down every reason why. Klein based it on research by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington (1989), who found that imagining an event *has already happened* ("prospective hindsight") increased people's ability to identify reasons for an outcome by about 30%. A pre-mortem also makes it safe to voice doubts that people would otherwise keep quiet ([Klein, 2007](https://comprobo24.github.io/assignments/performing_a_project_premortem.pdf)).

**Choice overload.** In a famous study, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a jam-tasting stall in a supermarket. When 24 jams were on display, more people stopped, but only about 3% bought; with 6 jams, about 30% of those who stopped bought. This "paradox of choice" became a business and self-help favourite. But when Benjamin Scheibehenne and colleagues pooled 50 experiments with over 5,000 people in 2010, the **average effect was virtually zero**, with large differences between studies. Choice overload seems to happen only in some conditions: when you have no clear preference, no option clearly stands out, the options are hard to compare and you are short of time ([Scheibehenne et al., 2010](https://abcwest.cogs.indiana.edu/pmwiki/pdf/scheibehenne.options.2010.pdf)). So the honest rule is: more choice is not always bad, but when you are stuck, reduce the options deliberately.

**Regret.** Research by Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec suggests that in the short term people regret actions that went wrong, but over the long term they regret **inactions** more: the things they did not try. Regret can be useful when it points to something you can still change. It becomes harmful when it turns into rumination (going over the same loss again and again, PD-M11-L01).

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prospective hindsight improves identifying risks | **Moderate** | Supported by the 1989 study and practical use; few large trials of pre-mortems themselves. |
| Choice overload as a general rule | **Mixed or weak** | The famous jam study was striking, but a meta-analysis found an average effect near zero. |
| Choice overload in specific conditions | **Moderate** | More likely with no clear preference, hard-to-compare options and time pressure. |
| Long-term regret is more about inaction | **Moderate** | Found in several studies by Gilovich and colleagues; depends on how regret is asked about. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Joseph sir is helping five aspirants in Thottilpalam plan a 12-week study group before the Degree Level prelims. Before starting, he runs a pre-mortem: "It's twelve weeks from now. The group fell apart and nobody's scores improved. Write down why."

In five minutes, they write: "Meetings at 7 pm clashed with family duties," "Two people dominated," "We chatted instead of testing," "Monsoon power cuts killed online mocks," "Nobody knew what to study each week." They fix each before starting: meetings move to Sunday 3 pm, a timer gives each person a turn, every meeting starts with a 20-question test, mocks are downloaded in advance, and a shared plan lists each week's topics.

One member, Shamna, is overwhelmed by choosing among nine YouTube channels and four apps. Joseph sir asks her to pick one source per subject using two criteria (covers the syllabus, has practice questions) and to ignore the rest for 12 weeks.

## How to use it

**Pre-mortem in 10 minutes (alone or with others):**

1. Describe the plan in two lines.
2. Say: "It is [date]. The plan has failed badly."
3. Each person writes, silently, every reason it failed (5 minutes).
4. Go round, one reason each, until all are listed.
5. For the three most likely or most damaging, write one change to the plan now.

**When choices overwhelm you:**
- Set two or three **must-have criteria** before looking at options.
- **Cut to three** options that meet them, then compare only those.
- For small choices, take the first good-enough option (satisfice).
- Set a decision deadline.

**Using regret well:** write the regret in one line, ask "Is there anything I can still do?", and if yes, schedule one small step. If no, write what you learned and close it. If you keep replaying the same regret for weeks, use a thought record (PD-M11-L02).

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gary Klein (2007), "Performing a Project Premortem", Harvard Business Review (PDF copy)](https://comprobo24.github.io/assignments/performing_a_project_premortem.pdf) | Read the whole short article on the premortem method | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd (2010), "Can There Ever Be Too Many Options?" choice-overload meta-analysis (PDF)](https://abcwest.cogs.indiana.edu/pmwiki/pdf/scheibehenne.options.2010.pdf) | Read the abstract and the discussion section (when does choice overload happen?) | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Wikipedia: Overchoice (choice overload)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overchoice) | Read the conditions for choice overload | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Run a pre-mortem on one real plan (your study plan for the next month, a purchase, a family event). Write at least eight failure reasons and three fixes.
2. Make one of the fixes this week.
3. Find one place where choice overwhelms you (apps, books, courses, clothes, phone plans). Write two or three must-have criteria, cut to three options and choose.
4. Write one regret from the last year: action or inaction? Is there one small step you can still take? Schedule it or write the lesson and close it.

**Proof to record:** Your pre-mortem list with three fixes (one done), a criteria-and-three-options note with your choice, and a regret note.

## Template: Pre-mortem and choice-cutting

```
PRE-MORTEM                 Plan: ______________________________
"It is ______ (date). The plan has failed badly. Why?"
1. ________________ 2. ________________ 3. ________________
4. ________________ 5. ________________ 6. ________________
7. ________________ 8. ________________
Top 3 (most likely or most damaging) -> fix now:
A. ______________ -> ______________
B. ______________ -> ______________
C. ______________ -> ______________

CHOICE CUTTING        Choosing: ______________   Deadline: ______
Must-haves: 1. ________ 2. ________ 3. ________
Three options that meet them: A ______ B ______ C ______
Choice: ______  (good enough? Y)  Stop looking until: ______
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Turning the pre-mortem into general worry.** It is a 10-minute exercise with fixes at the end, not permission to imagine disaster all week.
- **Quoting the jam study as proof that choice is bad.** The average effect across studies is close to zero. Say "sometimes too many options can stall us".
- **Comparing every option forever.** Set criteria first, cut to three, set a deadline.
- **Letting regret become rumination.** One step or one lesson, then close it. Seek help if it persists.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What makes a pre-mortem different from ordinary risk thinking?
    - A) You ask one expert to predict the result
    - B) You wait until after the project fails
    - C) You only list the good outcomes
    - D) You imagine the plan has already failed and explain why
2. What did the 2010 meta-analysis of 50 choice-overload experiments find?
    - A) Choice overload always reduces buying
    - B) Only jam is affected
    - C) More choice always increases happiness
    - D) An average effect of virtually zero, with large differences between studies
3. When is choice overload most likely?
    - A) When you know exactly what you want
    - B) When there are only two options
    - C) When you have no clear preference and options are hard to compare
    - D) When one option is clearly best
4. According to Gilovich and Medvec's work, what do people regret most in the long run?
    - A) Nothing
    - B) Things they did not do
    - C) Small purchases
    - D) Things they did that went well

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and Klein's premortem article
- **Action:** run a pre-mortem on a real plan and make one fix, cut one overwhelming choice to three options and write one regret note. It is done when your proof is saved: your pre-mortem list with three fixes (one done), a criteria-and-three-options note with your choice, and a regret note.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Prospective hindsight ("it has failed; why?") surfaces more reasons.
2. **D.** The effect depends on conditions and is not a general rule.
3. **C.** These are the conditions identified in the research.
4. **B.** Over time, regrets of inaction tend to dominate.

sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

Part B, Master yourself, starts with knowing yourself. Not in a vague "find yourself" way, but with tested tools: a values exercise, a life wheel, a research-grade personality measure and a strengths survey. Each gives you a specific design decision: which goals fit you (Module 7), which habits need support (Module 8), where stress hits hardest (Module 11).

You already have your baseline scores from week 0. This module teaches you to read them sensibly and to avoid both over-trusting and dismissing them.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Name, rank and explain your top five values.
- Read your life wheel and pick one area to improve.
- Interpret your Big Five scores and turn each into a design sentence.
- Explain three reasons MBTI-style type tests are unreliable.
- Use your VIA top strengths deliberately.

## Time

About 3 hours in total: 2 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: week 4, with the module project due in week 4.

## Lessons

1. PD-M05-L01: Values and the life wheel (about 1 hour)
2. PD-M05-L02: Big Five personality, VIA strengths, and the limits of type tests (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The values worksheet (PD-M05-L01).
- The self-awareness profile with trait sentences and a strengths log (PD-M05-L02).

## Module project: your one-page self-awareness profile

1. Combine your values, life-wheel scores, Big Five design sentences and strengths into one page.
2. Add one line: "The area I most want to change in the next six months is ______, because it serves my value ______."
3. Show the page to one trusted person and ask: "What did I miss?" Add their answer.
4. Copy the key lines into your Personal Playbook.

**Proof to record:** Your one-page profile with the trusted person's comment.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- My top five values: ______. I check one value-based action every Sunday.
- My VIA top strengths: ______. Because I score ______ on ______, I rely on ______.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Values | Generic list | Five values with some meaning | Five ranked values, each with a behaviour sentence |
| Personality | Scores only | Scores with some interpretation | A design sentence for each trait |
| Strengths | VIA list only | Strengths used on some days | Seven-day log and outside view compared |
| Honesty about tests | Treats type tests as truth | Knows they are weak | Explains reliability and dichotomy problems |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Write your top three values and your lowest life-wheel area.
- Write one "Because I score…, I will rely on…" sentence for conscientiousness.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Values versus goals | Values are directions; goals are completable points on the way. |
| The Big Five | Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism (emotional stability). |
| Best Big Five predictor of performance | Conscientiousness. |
| Maturity principle | Most adults slowly become more conscientious, agreeable and emotionally stable. |
| MBTI retest problem | 39–76% got a different type after five weeks. |
| Why types mislead | Trait scores cluster in the middle; either/or cut-offs split near-identical people. |
| VIA survey | Free survey ranking 24 character strengths. |
| Life wheel status | Coaching tool for reflection, not a validated test. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Doing the tests but not the design sentences.** Self-knowledge matters only when it changes how you set up your days.
- **Copying values from parents or posters without checking.** Keep inherited values you truly hold; check each against your behaviour.
- **Labelling others by type.** Ask what people enjoy and how they work best instead.

sections.title: PD-M05-L01: Values and the life wheel
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can name your top five values in your own words, score your life wheel, and pick one value-based action for your lowest area. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 40 minutes of exercises).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Knowing what matters to you gives direction when motivation is low; values are chosen directions, not goals you finish, and they are best seen in what you do, not what you say.

## The science

**What values are.** Psychologists describe values as broad, lasting beliefs about what is important: family, honesty, freedom, security, achievement, helping others, tradition. Shalom Schwartz's research across more than 80 countries found a similar set of basic human values everywhere, arranged in a circle where some sit naturally together (achievement and power) and some pull against each other (tradition versus stimulation, self-interest versus caring for others). Cultures and people differ mainly in how they **rank** these values, not in having different ones.

**Values versus goals.** In **Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)**, a form of CBT with good evidence for anxiety, depression and chronic pain, values are described as directions, like "west", while goals are places on the way, like "Kozhikode". You never finish "being a caring son"; you can complete "take my father to his eye check-up on Saturday". Values help when goals fail: if you miss a rank list, the value of "learning" or "serving people" is still there to act on.

**Does writing about values help?** Short "values affirmation" exercises, in which people write about a value that matters to them, were found in early studies to reduce stress and improve the performance of students under threat. Later, larger replications found smaller and less consistent effects. So treat values writing as a useful reflection tool, not a magic intervention.

**The life wheel.** The life wheel (or wheel of life) is a coaching tool, not a psychological test. You rate satisfaction in about eight areas of life from 1 to 10. Its value is practical: it shows imbalance at a glance (a "flat" spoke) and gives a baseline to compare later. Your baseline scores from week 0 are on your Baseline A note.

**A Kerala note.** In family-centred cultures, people sometimes list values they were taught (duty, respect for elders, religion) without asking whether they also hold them personally. Both can be true: many people deeply hold inherited values. The exercise is to *choose* consciously, not to reject tradition.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A common set of basic values across cultures (Schwartz) | **Strong** | Supported by surveys in more than 80 countries. |
| Values-based action as part of ACT | **Moderate** | ACT has good trial evidence; the specific contribution of values work is harder to isolate. |
| Brief values-affirmation writing improves performance | **Mixed or weak** | Early studies were promising; large replications found small or inconsistent effects. |
| Life wheel | **Practical tool** | A coaching tool for reflection and tracking; not a validated test. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Ashiq lists his values quickly: "success, family, money". When he does the exercise properly, he finds that the stories he is proudest of are teaching his nephew maths, standing by a friend in a dispute, and organising flood relief in 2018. His top five, in his own words: "helping people learn", "loyalty to friends and family", "being fair", "financial independence", "steady improvement".

His life wheel shows Health 3, Friends 4, Learning 7, Money 4, Family 6, Fun 2, Purpose 5, Mind 4. His lowest areas are Fun and Health. He picks a value-based action for Health that also fits "loyalty to friends": a 6 am walk with his cousin three times a week. It is small, but it serves two values at once.

## How to use it

**Find your values in four steps (about 30 minutes):**

1. **Peak moments:** write three times you felt proud, alive or "this is me". What values were you living?
2. **Anger and envy:** what makes you angry (injustice? laziness? cruelty?) and whom do you envy? Both point to values being blocked or wanted.
3. **The funeral or retirement speech:** what would you like people to say about you at 70? (Not your job title: how you treated people, what you stood for.)
4. **Choose five,** in your own words, and rank them. For each, write one sentence: "This means I ______."

**Use them weekly:** in the Sunday reflection, ask "Which value did I act on this week? Which did I neglect?"

**With others:** values explain many family arguments. Your father may rank **security** highly and you may rank **freedom**: you are not enemies, you weigh things differently. Naming this ("I think you want me to be safe; I also want to try this") lowers the heat.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley: free articles, quizzes and podcasts](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/) | Search the site for "values" and read one article about living by your values | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Greater Good in Action (UC Berkeley): free, research-based practices](https://ggia.berkeley.edu/) | Search for a values-affirmation or "Best Possible Self" practice and read it | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Noba Project: free psychology modules and textbooks (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://nobaproject.com/) | Search for the module "Self and Identity" and read the introduction and the part on the self-concept | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Do the four-step values exercise in your Playbook notebook.
2. Write your top five values, ranked, each with a "This means I…" sentence.
3. Look at your Baseline A life wheel. Choose the lowest area and write one action for the next week that serves one of your values.
4. Do the action and write two lines about how it went.

**Proof to record:** Your ranked top five values with meanings, your life-wheel scores, one value-based action for your lowest area, and two lines on doing it.

## Template: Values worksheet

```
VALUES WORKSHEET                         Date ______
Peak moments (3): what was I doing, what value was I living?
1. ______________________ -> ______________
2. ______________________ -> ______________
3. ______________________ -> ______________
What makes me angry? ____________  Whom do I envy, and for what? ____________
At 70, I want people to say I was: ____________________________________
MY TOP FIVE (ranked, in my words)     This means I...
1. ________________                   ______________________________
2. ________________                   ______________________________
3. ________________                   ______________________________
4. ________________                   ______________________________
5. ________________                   ______________________________
Lowest life-wheel area: ________  Value-based action this week: ______________
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Listing what sounds good.** Check each value against your behaviour. If you never act on it, it is a wish, not a value (or a value you want to grow into: say so).
- **Treating values as goals.** Values are directions. Turn them into weekly actions.
- **Trying to raise every life-wheel area at once.** Pick one low area at a time.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the difference between a value and a goal, in ACT terms?
    - A) Goals matter and values do not
    - B) They are the same thing
    - C) Values are only religious
    - D) A value is a direction you never finish; a goal is a point you can complete
2. What did large replications find about brief values-affirmation writing?
    - A) Large effects for everyone
    - B) That it harms students
    - C) That it was never studied
    - D) Smaller and less consistent effects than early studies
3. What kind of tool is the life wheel?
    - A) A personality test
    - B) A medical scale
    - C) A diagnostic test
    - D) A coaching tool for reflection and tracking, not a validated test
4. Your father values security and you value freedom. What is the most helpful view?
    - A) You weigh shared values differently; naming this can reduce conflict
    - B) Values cannot be discussed
    - C) One of you is wrong
    - D) You should drop your values

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and one Greater Good article on values
- **Action:** find your top five values, act on one in your lowest life-wheel area, and write about it. It is done when your proof is saved: your ranked top five values with meanings, your life-wheel scores, one value-based action for your lowest area, and two lines on doing it.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Values are like "west"; goals are destinations on the way.
2. **D.** The early promise did not fully hold up in larger studies.
3. **D.** It is useful for seeing balance, not for measuring traits.
4. **A.** Most value conflicts are about ranking, not having opposite values.

sections.title: PD-M05-L02: Big Five personality, VIA strengths, and the limits of type tests
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can interpret your Big Five and VIA results sensibly, explain why MBTI-style type tests are unreliable, and use your strengths deliberately. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (25 minutes reading, 30 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Personality is best described as five broad traits on a scale, not as types; traits are fairly stable but can change, and knowing your strengths is useful only if you use them.

## The science

**The Big Five.** Decades of research, starting from the words people in many languages use to describe each other, converged on five broad traits (OpenStax Psychology 2e chapter 11 and Noba cover them):

- **Openness to experience:** curiosity, imagination, liking new ideas.
- **Conscientiousness:** organisation, self-discipline, reliability.
- **Extraversion:** sociability, energy, seeking stimulation.
- **Agreeableness:** warmth, cooperation, trust.
- **Neuroticism** (or its opposite, **emotional stability**): tendency to feel anxiety, worry and low mood.

Each trait is a **continuum**; most people score near the middle. The Big Five predicts real outcomes modestly but reliably: conscientiousness predicts job and academic performance and even health and longevity; neuroticism predicts risk of anxiety and depression. Effects are real but moderate; your traits do not decide your life.

**Do traits change?** Traits are fairly stable in adulthood, but they shift slowly, with most people becoming more conscientious, agreeable and emotionally stable from their twenties to middle age (the "maturity principle"). Some studies suggest people who want to change a trait and act differently for weeks can shift a little, though results vary. Expect small changes over this course, if any.

**Your test.** The [IPIP Big Five Factor Markers](https://openpsychometrics.org/tests/IPIP-BFFM/) test you took uses public-domain items from the [International Personality Item Pool](https://ipip.ori.org/). It is a good research-style measure for self-understanding, but it is not a clinical or hiring test.

**Why not MBTI?** The Myers–Briggs Type Indicator sorts people into 16 types using four either/or choices (for example, introvert or extravert). Its problems, documented in the research ([summary on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myers%E2%80%93Briggs_Type_Indicator)):
- **Unreliable:** between 39% and 76% of people get a different type when they retake it after only five weeks.
- **False either/or:** scores on each scale cluster in the middle (like height), not in two groups, so people with nearly identical scores get opposite labels.
- **Weak prediction:** its own manual advises against using it to predict job success.
- **Overlap:** its scales roughly match four of the Big Five, minus neuroticism.

Free online "type" quizzes (including ones based on the Enneagram, colours or animals) are entertainment at best.

**Character strengths (VIA).** Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman catalogued 24 character strengths (such as kindness, curiosity, perseverance, humour, fairness), grouped under six virtues, and the free [VIA survey](https://www.viacharacter.org/) ranks yours. Studies of "use your top strengths in a new way each day" exercises found small boosts in wellbeing in some trials; evidence is moderate and effects are modest. The useful idea: build on what you are already good at, rather than only fixing weaknesses.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Big Five traits describe personality across cultures | **Strong** | Found in many languages and countries, though some traits appear less clearly in some cultures. |
| Conscientiousness predicts work, study and health outcomes | **Strong** | Consistent, moderate effects in large studies and reviews. |
| Traits change slowly with age (maturity principle) | **Strong** | Large long-term studies show average increases in conscientiousness, agreeableness and stability. |
| Deliberately changing a trait in weeks | **Mixed or weak** | Some studies find small changes; others do not. |
| MBTI types are reliable and predictive | **Failed to replicate or myth** | Poor retest reliability and weak prediction; scores are not two separate groups. |
| Using top strengths in new ways boosts wellbeing | **Moderate** | Small positive effects in several trials. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Sreeja's results: Openness 82nd percentile, Conscientiousness 35th, Extraversion 28th, Agreeableness 70th, Emotional stability 30th. Her VIA top five: love of learning, kindness, fairness, curiosity, appreciation of beauty.

She first reads them as a verdict ("I'm lazy and anxious"). Then she reframes. Low-ish conscientiousness means she will rely more on **systems** than on discipline (environment design and if-then plans in Module 8). Lower emotional stability means stress tools matter for her (Module 11), and that her worry is a trait, not a personal failure. High openness and love of learning are strengths she can use: she turns dull topics into curiosity questions ("Why did this river become the boundary?"). Her friend took a free "16 personalities" quiz and was told he is "an introvert who should avoid sales". She shows him the retest numbers and suggests he judge himself by what he has actually done.

## How to use it

**Using your Big Five:**

- **Not a label, a map.** Write: "Because I score ______ on ______, I will rely on ______ (a system or support)." For example: "Because my conscientiousness is low, I will set fixed study times and keep my phone out of the room."
- **Know your traps:** high agreeableness may make saying no hard (PD-M26-L02); low extraversion may make networking tiring (plan shorter events and recovery time, PD-M31-L03); high openness may scatter your focus across too many interests.
- **Remember the middle:** if you are near the 50th percentile, the trait barely describes you either way.

**Using your strengths (one week):** each day, use one of your top five strengths in a new way: "kindness" by helping a younger aspirant with a doubt, "curiosity" by asking a shopkeeper how their business started, "perseverance" by doing one extra past paper.

**With others:** never judge people by a type. Ask about what they enjoy and how they work best instead.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Open-Source Psychometrics: IPIP Big Five Factor Markers test (50 items, educational use)](https://openpsychometrics.org/tests/IPIP-BFFM/) | If you skipped the baseline, take the 50-item test now; read the explanation of each trait on the results page | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [VIA Institute on Character: free character strengths survey (24 strengths, about 12 minutes)](https://www.viacharacter.org/) | Read the descriptions of your top five strengths on the site | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Wikipedia: Myers–Briggs Type Indicator (criticism section)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myers%E2%80%93Briggs_Type_Indicator) | Read the criticism section (reliability, dichotomies, validity) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Noba Project: free psychology modules and textbooks (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://nobaproject.com/) | Search for the module "Personality Traits" and read the Big Five section | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write your five Big Five percentiles and your VIA top five in your Playbook notebook.
2. For each Big Five trait, write one "Because I score…, I will rely on…" sentence.
3. For seven days, use one top strength in a new way each day and log it in one line.
4. Ask one person who knows you well which three strengths they see in you. Compare with your VIA results.

**Proof to record:** Your trait sentences, a seven-day strengths log and the other person's three strengths compared with your VIA top five.

## Template: Self-awareness profile

```
SELF-AWARENESS PROFILE                 Date ______
Big Five (percentiles):  O ___  C ___  E ___  A ___  Emotional stability ___
Because I score ______ on ______, I will rely on ______.
Because I score ______ on ______, I will watch out for ______.
VIA top five: 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______ 4 ______ 5 ______
Strengths others see in me (ask 1-2 people): ______ ______ ______
Strengths-in-a-new-way log (7 days):
Day | Strength | New way I used it | How it felt (1-5)
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Treating scores as fixed destiny.** Traits shift slowly and do not decide outcomes. Use them to design systems, not excuses.
- **Comparing your percentiles with friends as "better" or "worse".** Each trait has advantages and costs. High agreeableness helps teamwork but can make you easy to pressure.
- **Taking type quizzes seriously.** Retest reliability is poor. Prefer the Big Five, and judge people by behaviour.
- **Ignoring strengths and only fixing weaknesses.** Use your strengths to work around weaknesses.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which Big Five trait most consistently predicts work and study performance?
    - A) Extraversion
    - B) Conscientiousness
    - C) Agreeableness
    - D) Openness
2. What is the main reliability problem with MBTI?
    - A) Many people get a different type when retested after a few weeks
    - B) It is too expensive
    - C) It has too many questions
    - D) It measures only intelligence
3. Scores on personality scales usually:
    - A) Split into two clear groups
    - B) Are all extreme
    - C) Cluster around the middle, like height
    - D) Change every day
4. How should you use a low conscientiousness score?
    - A) Retake the test until it is higher
    - B) Accept you can never be disciplined
    - C) Rely more on systems such as fixed times and environment design
    - D) Ignore it

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson, your trait descriptions and the MBTI criticism section
- **Action:** write a trait sentence for each Big Five trait and use a top strength in a new way for seven days. It is done when your proof is saved: your trait sentences, a seven-day strengths log and the other person's three strengths compared with your VIA top five.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Conscientiousness shows consistent, moderate links with performance.
2. **A.** Between 39% and 76% got a different type after five weeks in studies.
3. **C.** Traits are continuous, so either/or types mislabel many people.
4. **C.** Traits guide which supports you need; they are not destiny.

sections.title: Module 6: Motivation
sections.summary: What really drives lasting motivation: self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness), intrinsic and "owned" extrinsic motivation, goal-setting theory, and the progress principle. You redesign one goal so motivation comes from the design, not from willpower.
sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

Motivation is not a feeling you wait for; it is something you can design. This module gives you the two best-supported ideas: meet your three basic needs, and set specific, challenging goals with visible progress. Together they explain why some study plans keep you going for months and others die in a week.

If procrastination is your main problem, Module 8 and the [Learning Capabilities procrastination module](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/learning-capabilities/lrn-m06) (in the Practical Learning Capabilities course) go deeper. Here the focus is on the *engine* of motivation.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain SDT and the difference between controlled and owned motivation.
- Redesign a task to support autonomy, competence and relatedness.
- Use rewards wisely (to start dull tasks, not to bribe interest).
- Write three-layer goals with feedback, and keep a daily progress note.

## Time

About 2 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 4–5, with the module project due in week 5.

## Lessons

1. PD-M06-L01: Self-determination theory: intrinsic and extrinsic motivation (about 1 hour)
2. PD-M06-L02: Goal-setting theory and the progress principle (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The SDT redesign sheet (PD-M06-L01).
- The three-layer goal sheet with daily progress note (PD-M06-L02).

## Module project: a motivation redesign of one real goal

1. Pick your most important goal for the next three months.
2. Write it as a three-layer goal sheet (PD-M06-L02).
3. Run the SDT redesign (PD-M06-L01) on its hardest daily task.
4. Track for two weeks: process-goal completion, your weekly feedback number and daily progress notes. Write a five-line review.

**Proof to record:** The goal sheet, the SDT redesign, two weeks of tracking and the five-line review.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- When I lose motivation I check: Do I have choice? Can I see progress? Who is in this with me?
- My goals have three layers: outcome, learning, process; I check one feedback number every Sunday.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Goal quality | Vague goal | Specific outcome goal only | Outcome, learning and process layers with feedback |
| Needs support | No changes made | One need addressed | All three needs addressed with real changes |
| Tracking | No tracking | Some days tracked | Two weeks of daily progress notes and weekly feedback |
| Reflection | No review | Review describes what happened | Review adjusts the plan based on data |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Write one outcome goal with a number and date, and one process goal.
- Keep a one-line daily progress note for a week.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Three SDT needs | Autonomy, competence, relatedness. |
| Owned (identified) motivation | Doing something for an outside goal you have made your own; nearly as strong as intrinsic. |
| When can rewards backfire? | Expected tangible rewards for already-interesting tasks can reduce interest. |
| Goal-setting theory | Specific, challenging goals with commitment and feedback beat "do your best". |
| Learning goal | "Find and practise methods for X": better than a score target for new complex skills. |
| Process goal | A goal fully in your control: sessions, times, actions. |
| Progress principle | Small progress in meaningful work is the top feature of good workdays (diary study). |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Relying on motivational videos.** They lift mood briefly; design (needs, goals, feedback) lasts.
- **Setting goals others chose for you without making them yours.** Write your own reason, or negotiate the goal.
- **Changing goals every week.** Commit for at least a month before judging.

sections.title: PD-M06-L01: Self-determination theory: intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain self-determination theory, tell intrinsic from extrinsic motivation, and redesign one task so it meets your needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

People are most motivated, and stay motivated longest, when they feel choice (autonomy), growing skill (competence) and connection (relatedness); rewards help some tasks but can crowd out interest in others.

## The science

**Self-determination theory (SDT)** was developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan from the 1970s onwards and is one of the most researched theories of motivation ([Center for Self-Determination Theory](https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/theory/)). It says people have three basic psychological needs:

- **Autonomy:** feeling that what you do is your own choice, in line with your values (not necessarily doing it alone).
- **Competence:** feeling effective and able to grow.
- **Relatedness:** feeling connected to and cared for by others.

When these needs are supported, people show more lasting motivation, better performance on complex tasks and better wellbeing. When they are thwarted (constant control, repeated failure without help, isolation), motivation drops or becomes grudging.

**Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation.** Intrinsic motivation means doing something because it is interesting or enjoyable in itself. Extrinsic motivation means doing it for an outcome outside the activity: money, marks, praise, avoiding punishment. SDT adds an important idea: extrinsic motivation comes in **degrees**. At one end is doing something only because you are forced or to avoid guilt (controlled). At the other end is doing something because you have made its purpose your own: you may not enjoy revising Indian history, but you value the job it can lead to and the family security it brings (identified or integrated). This "owned" extrinsic motivation works almost as well as intrinsic motivation for persistence.

**Can rewards backfire?** In Deci's early experiments, people paid to solve interesting puzzles later spent less free time on them than unpaid people. A large 1999 review by Deci, Koestner and Ryan concluded that expected, tangible rewards for an interesting task tend to reduce intrinsic motivation. Other researchers (Cameron and Pierce) argued the effect is smaller and limited to specific conditions. A balanced reading: rewards work well for dull tasks and for getting started; for tasks you already enjoy, heavy controlling rewards can make them feel like work. Positive, informative feedback ("your answers on Polity improved") tends to increase motivation.

**Motivation in India and Kerala.** SDT research has been done in many cultures, including collectivist ones. Autonomy does not mean ignoring family: you can feel autonomous when you willingly accept a family goal because you share its value. Feeling *forced* into a goal is what drains motivation.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supporting autonomy, competence and relatedness increases lasting motivation | **Strong** | Many studies in schools, workplaces, health and sport, in many countries. |
| "Owned" (identified) extrinsic motivation predicts persistence | **Strong** | Consistent across SDT studies. |
| Expected tangible rewards reduce intrinsic motivation for interesting tasks | **Moderate** | Supported by a large review; debated in size and conditions. |
| Informative positive feedback increases motivation | **Moderate** | Supported in many studies. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Anu finds PSC study a grind. She does it because her mother keeps asking about it and because she feels guilty when cousins get jobs. Using SDT, she redesigns her week:

- **Autonomy:** instead of following a coaching centre's timetable, she chooses her own order of topics within the syllabus and writes down *her* reason: "A government job gives me independence and lets me support Amma." The study did not change; the ownership did.
- **Competence:** she starts each session with five questions she can answer and ends with a quick score. Seeing her Polity score rise from 11/20 to 15/20 in three weeks makes her want to continue.
- **Relatedness:** she joins two friends on a Sunday call where each explains one topic.

She also stops promising herself a new dress for every mock above 60%, since the rewards were making the mocks feel like bribed work, and keeps a simple progress graph instead.

## How to use it

**The SDT redesign (for any task you avoid):**

| Need | Ask | Changes to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Autonomy | "Where do I have choice? What is my own reason?" | Choose the order, time or method; write your own "why" in one line. |
| Competence | "Can I see myself improving?" | Start with a win; track a simple score; make tasks the right difficulty. |
| Relatedness | "Who is in this with me?" | A study partner, a weekly call, telling someone your progress. |

**On rewards:** use small rewards to start dull tasks (tea after the first 25 minutes), but for things you want to love, rely on progress and meaning instead of bribes.

**With others:** if you lead, teach or parent, support others' needs: give choices ("Would you rather start with maths or GK?"), give informative feedback rather than only praise or criticism, and show you care about the person, not just the result. Controlling pressure ("You must, or else") works short-term and backfires long-term.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Center for Self-Determination Theory: the theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness)](https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/theory/) | Read the overview of the theory: the three needs and the types of motivation | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, chapter 10: Motivation and Emotion (10.1 and 10.4)](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/10-introduction) | Read 10.1 Motivation (intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, theories of motivation) | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Noba Project: free psychology modules and textbooks (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://nobaproject.com/) | Search for the module "Motives and Goals" and read the introduction | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Pick the one task you most avoid (a PSC subject, exercise, a household duty).
2. Rate it 1–5 on autonomy, competence and relatedness right now.
3. Write one change for each need, using the table, and do all three this week.
4. At the end of the week, rate the three needs again and write how many times you did the task compared with the week before.

**Proof to record:** Before and after ratings for the three needs, your three changes, and the task count for both weeks.

## Template: SDT redesign sheet

```
SDT REDESIGN                Task I avoid: ________________________
                   Before (1-5)   Change I'll make                    After (1-5)
Autonomy           ___            ______________________________      ___
Competence         ___            ______________________________      ___
Relatedness        ___            ______________________________      ___
My own reason for doing this (one line): ______________________________
Times I did the task: last week ___  this week ___
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Waiting to "feel motivated".** Motivation often follows action and visible progress. Start small and let competence grow.
- **Thinking autonomy means doing everything alone.** You can choose to accept help or a family goal; what matters is that it is your choice.
- **Bribing yourself for everything.** Use rewards to start dull tasks; use progress and meaning for lasting interest.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What are the three basic needs in self-determination theory?
    - A) Autonomy, competence and relatedness
    - B) Discipline, rewards and punishment
    - C) Food, money and status
    - D) Intelligence, effort and luck
2. You study history because you value the job it leads to, though you don't enjoy it. What kind of motivation is this?
    - A) Controlled motivation
    - B) Owned (identified) extrinsic motivation
    - C) Pure intrinsic motivation
    - D) No motivation
3. According to the 1999 review, when can rewards reduce motivation?
    - A) When expected, tangible rewards are given for an already interesting task
    - B) Only for children
    - C) Always
    - D) Never
4. Which is the most motivating feedback?
    - A) "Good job"
    - B) "Your Polity score went from 11 to 15; your errors are now mostly about dates"
    - C) "You must do better"
    - D) "Others are doing better than you"

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the SDT overview
- **Action:** redesign your most-avoided task for autonomy, competence and relatedness and compare one week before and after. It is done when your proof is saved: before and after ratings for the three needs, your three changes, and the task count for both weeks.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Deci and Ryan's three basic psychological needs.
2. **B.** The outcome is external, but you have made its purpose your own.
3. **A.** Rewards can crowd out interest in tasks people already enjoy; the size is debated.
4. **B.** Informative feedback supports competence.

sections.title: PD-M06-L02: Goal-setting theory and the progress principle
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can set specific, challenging goals with feedback, break them into progress steps, and use a daily progress note. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Specific, challenging goals with feedback beat "do your best"; and on ordinary days, seeing small progress in meaningful work is one of the strongest boosts to motivation.

## The science

**Goal-setting theory.** Edwin Locke and Gary Latham summarised about 35 years of research (more than 400 studies) in 2002: **specific, difficult goals** lead to better performance than easy goals or vague "do your best" goals, as long as the person is committed, has the ability and gets **feedback** on progress. Goals work by directing attention, increasing effort, increasing persistence and prompting people to find strategies.

Important limits from the same research:
- For **complex tasks you are still learning**, a performance goal ("score 80") can backfire; a **learning goal** ("find and practise three strategies for percentage problems") works better at first.
- Very hard goals with no feedback, or goals imposed without commitment, can cause stress, cheating or giving up.
- Too many goals compete for attention.

**SMART goals** (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) is a popular management acronym that roughly matches this research, but it was not itself tested as a package. "Achievable" also undersells the finding that *challenging* goals work best.

**The progress principle.** Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer studied nearly 12,000 daily diary entries from 238 professionals in seven companies. On days when people felt most positive and motivated, the most common event was **making progress in meaningful work**, even small progress. Setbacks had an even bigger negative effect than progress had a positive one (a sign of negativity bias, PD-M10-L01). Their study is observational (diaries), so it shows a strong link rather than proof of cause, but it fits much other research on feedback and competence.

**Putting it together:** a good goal system has one or two challenging, specific outcome goals, broken into learning or process goals you control, with frequent feedback and a way to see daily progress.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specific, challenging goals with feedback improve performance | **Strong** | Hundreds of studies summarised by Locke and Latham. |
| Learning goals beat performance goals for new, complex tasks | **Moderate** | Supported in several studies; matters most early in learning. |
| SMART as a tested package | **Practical tool** | A popular acronym consistent with parts of the research, not tested as a whole. |
| Progress in meaningful work drives daily motivation | **Moderate** | Large diary study; observational, but consistent with feedback research. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Vinod's goal was "prepare well for LDC". It changed nothing. He rewrites it.

**Outcome goal (challenging, specific):** "Score 70 or more out of 100 on a full PSC-pattern mock by 15 March." His current mock average is 52.

**Learning goals (for weak areas):** "Learn and practise three methods for percentage and ratio questions by 31 January."

**Process goals (fully in his control):** "Five study sessions a week of 90 minutes; one mock every Sunday; every error logged."

**Feedback:** a graph of Sunday mock scores on his shop wall.

**Progress:** every night, a one-line note: "Today's progress: finished 20 ratio questions; 16 right." On bad days he writes even tiny progress ("read one page of the Constitution"). After a month his mocks are at 58, below plan but rising, and he adjusts his plan instead of giving up.

## How to use it

**Write goals in three layers:**

1. **One or two outcome goals** for the next three months: specific number, date, and challenging (a stretch, not a fantasy).
2. **Learning goals** for skills you don't yet have: "Find and practise…".
3. **Process goals** you control completely: how many sessions, when, how long.

Then add **feedback** (a weekly number you can see) and a **daily progress note** (one line each evening: "Today's progress: ______").

**When you miss a goal:** check commitment (do I still want it?), ability (do I need a learning goal first?) and feedback (did I see the problem early enough?). Adjust the plan, not your self-worth.

**With others:** when you help others set goals, ask them to set their own, make them specific, and agree on how they will see progress. Celebrate small progress you notice; it matters more than big speeches.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, chapter 10: Motivation and Emotion (10.1 and 10.4)](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/10-introduction) | Re-read the part of 10.1 on theories of motivation and goals | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley: free articles, quizzes and podcasts](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/) | Search the site for "progress principle" or "small wins" and read one article | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/20203) | Read the part of Franklin's Autobiography about his plan for "moral perfection" and his weekly chart of 13 virtues (search the text for "thirteen") | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write one outcome goal for the next three months with a number and a date.
2. Break it into one learning goal and two or three process goals.
3. Choose the feedback number you will check every Sunday and put it somewhere visible.
4. Write a one-line daily progress note every evening for seven days.

**Proof to record:** Your three-layer goal sheet, the feedback number and seven daily progress notes.

## Template: Three-layer goal sheet

```
THREE-LAYER GOAL SHEET                         Written: ______
OUTCOME GOAL (specific, challenging, dated):
  ______________________________________ by ______  (now: ______)
LEARNING GOAL(S) (skills I need first):
  Find and practise ______________________ by ______
PROCESS GOALS (fully in my control):
  ___ sessions a week, ___ minutes, at ______ ; ______________________
FEEDBACK I check every Sunday: ______________  Where it's visible: ______
DAILY PROGRESS NOTE (one line each evening):
  Date | Today's progress (however small) | Setback?
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Setting ten goals.** One or two outcome goals at a time; the rest is distraction.
- **Only outcome goals.** You cannot fully control results. Process goals are where daily effort goes.
- **Using a performance goal for a skill you have not learned.** Start with a learning goal; set the score target once you know the methods.
- **Ignoring small progress.** Write it down. It is what keeps motivation alive on ordinary days.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which kind of goal led to the best performance in Locke and Latham's research?
    - A) "Do your best"
    - B) Secret goals with no feedback
    - C) Specific and challenging, with feedback
    - D) Easy and vague
2. For a complex skill you are still learning, which goal tends to work better at first?
    - A) No goal
    - B) A learning goal, such as "find and practise three methods"
    - C) A high score target
    - D) Many goals at once
3. What did Amabile and Kramer find in about 12,000 diary entries?
    - A) Long holidays drove motivation
    - B) Progress in meaningful work was the most common feature of the best days
    - C) Criticism improved motivation
    - D) Pay rises made the best days
4. What is the main limit of the progress-principle study?
    - A) It was never published
    - B) It was done on animals
    - C) It had only ten people
    - D) It is observational, so it shows a strong link rather than proof of cause

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and Franklin's virtues chart passage
- **Action:** write a three-layer goal sheet and keep a daily progress note for seven days. It is done when your proof is saved: your three-layer goal sheet, the feedback number and seven daily progress notes.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Specific, difficult goals with commitment and feedback outperform the others.
2. **B.** Performance pressure before you know the methods can hurt.
3. **B.** Small wins in meaningful work were strongly linked with good inner work days.
4. **D.** Diary data show association; other research supports the causal story.

sections.title: Module 7: Goals and life design
sections.summary: Turn values into direction: a short life vision, a 12-month plan with no more than three goals, WOOP for obstacles, small life-design prototypes, and a 20-minute weekly review and plan. This becomes the spine of your personal operating system.
sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

Modules 5 and 6 gave you values, strengths and a working understanding of motivation. This module turns them into a plan you will actually follow: a one-page 12-month plan that you revisit monthly, and a weekly rhythm that connects it to your calendar.

If you did the Learning Capabilities course, its [weekly learning review](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/learning-capabilities/lrn-m07) (in the Practical Learning Capabilities course) covers study-specific reviews; here the review covers your whole life, and you can merge the two into one Sunday session.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Write a best-possible-self vision grounded in your values.
- Use WOOP (mental contrasting with an if-then plan) on each goal.
- Write a 12-month plan with three goals, quarterly milestones and a "not this year" list.
- Run a 20-minute weekly review and plan, blocking big rocks first.

## Time

About 3 hours in total: 2 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: week 5, with the module project due in week 5.

## Lessons

1. PD-M07-L01: Vision and the 12-month plan (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. PD-M07-L02: The weekly plan and the weekly review (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The 12-month plan with WOOP and "not this year" list (PD-M07-L01).
- The weekly plan added to the weekly reflection (PD-M07-L02).

## Module project: your 12-month plan (version 1) and four weekly reviews

1. Finish your 12-month plan with WOOPs and milestones (PD-M07-L01).
2. Run the weekly review and plan for four consecutive Sundays (PD-M07-L02); this continues the Daily system track.
3. After four weeks, compare planned and actual hours each week and write what you learned about your realistic capacity.
4. Update the plan (version 2) if needed.

**Proof to record:** The 12-month plan, four weekly plans with planned-versus-actual numbers, and your capacity note.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- My three goals for this year: ______ (with WOOP plans).
- Every Sunday at ______: 10-minute review, 10-minute plan, big rocks first.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vision | No vision written | Vision written but vague | Vision rooted in values, across life areas |
| Goals | More than three or vague | Three goals without milestones | Three goals with WOOP and quarterly milestones |
| Weekly rhythm | Fewer than two reviews | Two or three reviews | Four consecutive reviews with plans |
| Realism | Plans far above actual | Some adjustment | Plans match actual capacity within about 20% |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Write three goals with one WOOP each.
- Do a 10-minute version of the weekly review: numbers, one lesson, three priorities.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Best possible self | Writing about a realistic best future; small to moderate wellbeing and optimism gains. |
| Positive fantasy alone | Can reduce effort; add obstacles and plans. |
| WOOP | Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan (if-then). |
| Why only three goals? | Competing goals split attention and reduce progress. |
| Life-design prototype | A small test (conversation, short trial) before a big commitment. |
| Monitoring progress | Meta-analysis: improves goal attainment, more when recorded or shared. |
| Big rocks first | Block the most important tasks in the calendar before small ones. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **A beautiful plan never looked at again.** The weekly review is what keeps it alive.
- **Rigid plans that ignore family life in Kerala.** Weddings, festivals and hospital visits happen. Plan buffer time and adjust weekly.
- **Comparing your plan with other people's.** Your plan serves your values and capacity.

sections.title: PD-M07-L01: Vision and the 12-month plan
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can write a short life vision from your values and turn it into a 12-month plan with no more than three goals and quarterly milestones. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 40 minutes of planning).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

A vision says where you are heading and why; a 12-month plan turns it into a few concrete goals with milestones, so daily choices line up with what you care about.

## The science

**Why imagine the future at all?** Two lines of research matter here.

1. **"Best possible self" writing.** Laura King and later researchers asked people to write for about 15 to 20 minutes, on several days, about their life in the future if everything went as well as it reasonably could. Studies and a 2019 meta-analysis of positive-psychology interventions found small to moderate increases in optimism and wellbeing. It is one of the better-supported positive-psychology exercises, though effects are modest and short-lived without follow-up.

2. **Mental contrasting.** Gabriele Oettingen's research found that just fantasising about a positive future can *reduce* effort, because the mind enjoys the fantasy as if it were achieved. What works better is **mental contrasting**: imagine the desired future, then imagine the main obstacle inside you or your situation, then plan for it. Combined with if-then plans (PD-M08-L03), this method is called **WOOP**: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan. Several trials found WOOP improved behaviours such as exercise, healthy eating and study effort, with small to moderate effects.

**Life design.** Stanford designers Bill Burnett and Dave Evans adapted design thinking to life choices in their course and book *Designing Your Life*: try small **prototypes** (a conversation with someone in a career, a one-week trial) before big commitments. The approach is practical rather than scientifically tested as a package, but it fits decision research: reversible small tests teach you more, more cheaply, than imagining (PD-M04-L01).

**Why only three goals?** Attention and time are limited. Goal research (PD-M06-L02) shows that competing goals reduce progress on each. For someone preparing for PSC exams, one major goal (the exam) plus one health goal plus one relationship or skill goal is plenty.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best-possible-self writing raises optimism and wellbeing | **Moderate** | Supported by several trials and meta-analyses; effects are small to moderate and fade without practice. |
| Positive fantasy alone can reduce effort | **Moderate** | Found in several studies by Oettingen and colleagues. |
| Mental contrasting with implementation intentions (WOOP) | **Moderate** | Trials show small to moderate improvements in health and study behaviours. |
| Life-design prototyping | **Practical tool** | A practical method consistent with decision research; not tested as a package. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Sreeja writes her best possible self, one year from now: "I am on the LGS rank list or at least on a short list, studying calmly with a routine. I walk every morning and sleep by 10:30. I have two close friends I meet each week, and I am teaching my neighbour's daughter English on Saturdays. I feel steady, not frantic."

Then she does WOOP for the biggest wish (rank list). **Obstacle:** "When I get anxious after a bad mock, I stop studying for days." **Plan:** "If I score badly in a mock, then the same evening I will log three errors and study one of them for 20 minutes."

Her 12-month plan has three goals: (1) PSC: a mock average of 70 by June; (2) health: walk five days a week and sleep by 10:30; (3) people: one weekly friend meeting and the Saturday class. Each gets four quarterly milestones. Ideas she cut for this year: learning guitar, starting a YouTube channel. She writes them on a "not this year" list so they stop nagging her.

## How to use it

**Build your vision and 12-month plan (about 40 minutes):**

1. **Best possible self (15 minutes):** write freely about a realistic best version of your life in 12 months, across your life-wheel areas. Use your values from PD-M05-L01.
2. **Pick three goals:** the three that matter most and fit together. One of them will usually be PSC or work.
3. **WOOP each one:** Wish, best Outcome, main inner Obstacle, if-then Plan.
4. **Quarterly milestones:** for each goal, what will be true at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months?
5. **"Not this year" list:** write the good ideas you are deliberately postponing.
6. **First prototype:** for any big uncertain goal (a career change, a business), plan one small test this month: a conversation, a one-week trial, a small paid job.

**With others:** share your three goals with one person who cares about you. Ask for support with one obstacle, not for advice on everything.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Greater Good in Action (UC Berkeley): free, research-based practices](https://ggia.berkeley.edu/) | Search for the "Best Possible Self" practice and follow its instructions | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Samuel Smiles, Self-Help (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/935) | Read chapter 1, "Self-Help: National and Individual" (a public-domain classic on effort and character; notice what is timeless and what is dated) | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [James Allen, As a Man Thinketh (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4507) | Read the short opening chapter "Thought and Character"; compare its claims with what you know about evidence | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write your best-possible-self text (15 minutes).
2. Choose three goals and write WOOP for each.
3. Write quarterly milestones for each goal and a "not this year" list.
4. Plan one prototype (a test) for your most uncertain goal and put it in your calendar this month.
5. Share the three goals with one person and note their response.

**Proof to record:** Your best-possible-self text, three WOOPs, the 12-month plan with milestones, the "not this year" list and the prototype date.

## Template: 12-month plan with WOOP

```
12-MONTH PLAN               From ______ to ______
Vision (3 lines, from my best-possible-self writing):
____________________________________________________________
GOAL 1: ______________________  Value it serves: ______
  WOOP: Wish ______ | Outcome ______ | Obstacle (inner) ______
        Plan: If ______, then I will ______.
  Milestones: 3 mo ______ 6 mo ______ 9 mo ______ 12 mo ______
GOAL 2: (same)
GOAL 3: (same)
NOT THIS YEAR: ______ ______ ______
PROTOTYPE this month: ______________________ on ______
Shared with: ______  Their support for one obstacle: ______
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Writing a fantasy and stopping.** Positive fantasy alone can lower effort. Always add the obstacle and a plan (WOOP).
- **More than three goals.** Put the rest on the "not this year" list.
- **Picking obstacles outside you.** Name the inner obstacle you can plan for ("I scroll when anxious"), not just "not enough time".
- **Treating old self-help classics as science.** Books like As a Man Thinketh inspire, but claims such as "thought alone shapes circumstance" overstate what research supports.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did Oettingen's research find about positive fantasies alone?
    - A) They can reduce effort, because the mind enjoys the fantasy
    - B) They always increase effort
    - C) They work only for athletes
    - D) They have no effect on anything
2. What does WOOP stand for?
    - A) Will, Optimism, Opportunity, Progress
    - B) Work, Order, Organise, Practise
    - C) Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan
    - D) Want, Obtain, Own, Profit
3. Why limit your 12-month plan to about three goals?
    - A) More goals are always better
    - B) Competing goals split limited time and attention
    - C) Research proves exactly three is best
    - D) Three is a lucky number
4. What is a life-design "prototype"?
    - A) A detailed five-year plan
    - B) A vision board
    - C) A personality test
    - D) A small, cheap test of an option before a big commitment

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and do the Best Possible Self practice
- **Action:** write your vision, three WOOPs and a 12-month plan with milestones, and schedule one prototype. It is done when your proof is saved: your best-possible-self text, three WOOPs, the 12-month plan with milestones, the "not this year" list and the prototype date.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Contrasting the wish with an obstacle works better than fantasy alone.
2. **C.** Mental contrasting plus an if-then plan.
3. **B.** Goal research shows competing goals reduce progress on each.
4. **D.** Small reversible tests teach you about an option quickly.
