sections.title: PD-M07-L02: The weekly plan and the weekly review
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can plan a week from your 12-month goals and run a 20-minute weekly review that keeps your plan alive. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 40 minutes of planning and review).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Plans die without a regular review; a short weekly plan and review connect your big goals to next week's calendar and let you adjust before small slips become big failures.

## The science

**Why weekly?** A year is too long to steer by, and a day is too short to see patterns. A week contains a full cycle of work, rest and family life, so it is the natural unit for planning and review.

**What the research supports:**

- **Monitoring progress helps.** A 2016 meta-analysis by Benjamin Harkin and colleagues of 138 studies found that prompting people to monitor their progress towards goals increased goal attainment, and more so when progress was recorded physically or reported to others.
- **Planning when and where** (implementation intentions) roughly doubles follow-through in many studies; the [Gollwitzer and Sheeran meta-analysis](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f) found a medium-to-large average effect (d = 0.65) across 94 tests. You will use these in PD-M08-L03; your weekly plan is where you write them.
- **Reflection improves learning from experience.** Studies of workers who spent a few minutes at the end of the day reflecting on what they learned (Di Stefano, Gino, Pisano and Staats) found better performance than those who simply worked longer. The evidence is promising but limited.

**Time blocking and the "big rocks" idea.** Putting your most important tasks in the calendar first, before smaller ones, is a practical rule from time-management writers (often illustrated with rocks, pebbles and sand in a jar). There is little direct research on it, but it follows from implementation intentions and the planning fallacy: if the important thing has no time slot, it usually loses to urgent small things.

**Your weekly reflection** (the template on the Daily system track) is already a review. This lesson adds the **planning** half and connects both to your 12-month plan.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monitoring and recording progress improves goal attainment | **Strong** | Meta-analysis of 138 studies; stronger when progress is recorded or shared. |
| Planning when and where (implementation intentions) | **Strong** | Medium-to-large average effects across many studies. |
| Brief reflection on lessons learned improves performance | **Mixed or weak** | A few promising studies; not yet widely replicated. |
| Time-blocking the most important tasks first | **Practical tool** | A practical rule consistent with planning research. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Every Sunday at 7 pm, after dinner, Ashiq spends 20 minutes on his weekly reflection and plan.

**Review (10 minutes):** habit tracker 71%; PSC study 9 hours (plan was 12); walks 3 of 5; one great conversation with his cousin about her nursing job. What went badly: Wednesday and Thursday he lost both evening blocks to helping at his uncle's shop. Lesson: weekday evenings are fragile.

**Plan (10 minutes):** he looks at his 12-month plan, then puts the big rocks in his phone calendar first: three morning study blocks of 90 minutes (6:30–8:00), Saturday mock at 10, walks at 6 am, the Sunday reflection. Only then does he add the shop help, a cousin's engagement and two errands. He writes one if-then plan for the fragile evenings: "If I'm asked to help at the shop on a study evening, then I'll offer Saturday afternoon instead."

## How to use it

**The 20-minute weekly review and plan (Sunday, same time each week):**

**Review (10 minutes):** fill in the Weekly reflection template (on the Daily system track page). Add one line: "Am I on track for this quarter's milestones? Yes / behind / ahead."

**Plan (10 minutes):**
1. Look at your 12-month plan and this quarter's milestones.
2. Choose **three priorities** for the week, one per goal if possible.
3. **Block the big rocks first** in your calendar: study blocks, workouts, the people goal.
4. Add fixed commitments and errands around them.
5. Write **one if-then plan** for the biggest risk to the week.
6. Check the total: is it realistic? Use your past weeks' numbers (the outside view).

**Monthly (first Sunday):** reread your 12-month plan and Personal Playbook; adjust milestones if life has changed.

**With others:** share your week's plan with family if their help or understanding matters ("Mornings 6:30 to 8 are my study time this week").

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), implementation intentions meta-analysis (free PDF)](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f) | Read the abstract: how big the effect of if-then planning is | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/20203) | Read the passage on Franklin's daily "Scheme of Employment" (search the text for "scheme of employment") and compare it with your plan | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Android Help: manage how you spend time with Digital Wellbeing](https://support.google.com/android/answer/9346420?hl=en) | Optional: set a weekly reminder in your phone or Loop for the Sunday review | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Choose a fixed time each Sunday for the 20-minute review and plan, and set a reminder.
2. Do the review and plan this Sunday using both halves of the routine.
3. Put your three priorities and big rocks into your phone calendar (or a paper week planner) before anything else.
4. Next Sunday, compare planned and actual hours and write one change.

**Proof to record:** Two consecutive weekly reviews and plans, with a calendar screenshot showing the big rocks, and your planned-versus-actual numbers.

## Template: Weekly plan (with the weekly reflection)

```
WEEKLY REFLECTION (Sunday, 20 minutes)      Week ___  Dates ________
1. NUMBERS  Habit tracker: ___% of boxes ticked   Study hours (PSC): ___
            Sleep average: ___ h   Screen time average: ___ h/day
            Workouts: ___   Meditation days: ___   Challenge days: ___
2. WINS     Three things that went well, and what I did to make them happen:
            ________________________________________________________
3. LESSONS  One thing that went badly. What would I tell a friend in my place?
            ________________________________________________________
4. PEOPLE   One good conversation this week, and what I learned about them:
            ________________________________________________________
5. RECORD   Speak for 1-2 minutes on your phone recorder (English one week,
            Malayalam the next): "This week I learned..." File name: ________
            Listen once. One thing to improve next time: ________________
6. NEXT     Three priorities for next week, each with a day and time:
            1. ______________ 2. ______________ 3. ______________
            One change to my system (environment, time, cue): ___________
7. MOOD     Rate the week 1-10: ___ . If below 4 for two weeks running,
            read "When to get help" (PD-M11-L01) and talk to someone.

WEEKLY PLAN (after the reflection)
Quarter milestones: Goal 1 ______ Goal 2 ______ Goal 3 ______  On track? Y / behind / ahead
Three priorities this week: 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______
Big rocks blocked first (day, time): ______________________________
Biggest risk this week: ______ -> If ______, then I will ______.
Planned study hours ___ (last 3 weeks' average ___). Realistic? Y/N
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Skipping the review when the week went badly.** Bad weeks are when the review matters most. Do the short version: numbers, one lesson, three priorities.
- **Planning more hours than you have ever done.** Use your average of the last three weeks plus a little.
- **Filling the calendar with small tasks first.** Big rocks first; errands fit around them.
- **Making the review a punishment.** Write it as you would for a friend: honest, kind, focused on the next step.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did a meta-analysis of 138 studies find about monitoring goal progress?
    - A) It only works for weight loss
    - B) It increased goal attainment, especially when recorded or shared
    - C) It had no effect
    - D) It reduced motivation
2. What does "big rocks first" mean in weekly planning?
    - A) Plan only big projects
    - B) Do the hardest physical work first
    - C) Ignore small tasks
    - D) Put the most important tasks in the calendar before smaller ones
3. How should you set this week's planned study hours?
    - A) Plan the maximum possible
    - B) Start from your recent actual average and add a little
    - C) Double last week
    - D) Do not plan hours
4. Why is a week a good unit for review?
    - A) It is not a good unit
    - B) Because research proves seven days is magic
    - C) Because months are too short
    - D) It contains a full cycle of work, rest and family life, so patterns show

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and set your review time
- **Action:** do two consecutive Sunday reviews and plans, with big rocks blocked first in your calendar. It is done when your proof is saved: two consecutive weekly reviews and plans, with a calendar screenshot showing the big rocks, and your planned-versus-actual numbers.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Harkin et al. (2016) found monitoring helps, more so when made physical or public.
2. **D.** If important tasks have no slot, urgent small things take over.
3. **B.** The outside view protects against the planning fallacy.
4. **D.** Days are too short and years too long to steer by.

sections.title: Module 8: Self-control and habits
sections.summary: The core self-control and habits toolkit: present bias, commitment devices, temptation bundling, environment design, the habit loop, if-then plans, tiny habits, identity, procrastination, and a two-week personal experiment with data. Honest notes on what failed (ego depletion, "21 days").
sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

This is the most practical module in Part B. It replaces "try harder" with design: make good behaviour easy, bad behaviour hard, and plans automatic. The best-supported tools here (if-then plans, friction, keeping temptation out of sight) work for almost everyone.

It ends with a skill you will use for life: testing a change on yourself with real numbers. The [Learning Capabilities procrastination module](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/learning-capabilities/lrn-m06) (in the Practical Learning Capabilities course) covers study-specific procrastination in more depth.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain present bias and design commitment devices and temptation bundles.
- Explain what happened to ego depletion and the marshmallow test.
- Map habit loops and redesign your environment (cues and friction).
- Write action, obstacle and restart if-then plans and grow tiny habits.
- Explain procrastination as mood repair and run a two-week personal experiment.

## Time

About 5 hours 15 minutes in total: 4 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 5–6, with the module project due in week 6.

## Lessons

1. PD-M08-L01: Present bias, commitment devices and temptation bundling (about 1 hour)
2. PD-M08-L02: Environment design and the habit loop (about 1 hour)
3. PD-M08-L03: If-then plans, tiny habits and identity-based change (about 1 hour)
4. PD-M08-L04: Procrastination, and a two-week personal experiment (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The self-control design sheet (PD-M08-L01).
- The habit loop map and redesign (PD-M08-L02).
- The if-then plan card with tiny habits and identity line (PD-M08-L03).
- The personal experiment log (PD-M08-L04).

## Module project: a two-week personal experiment with data (and the habit redesign behind it)

1. Complete the habit redesign from PD-M08-L02 and the if-then plans from PD-M08-L03.
2. Run the two-week experiment from PD-M08-L04 on one change.
3. Write a one-page report: question, method, numbers, other differences, decision.
4. Add the change you are keeping, and your best if-then plan, to your Personal Playbook.

**Proof to record:** The experiment log, the one-page report and the updated Playbook lines.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- I design, I don't rely on willpower: temptation out of sight, cues in sight, tiny starts.
- My keystone if-then plan: If ______, then I will ______. If I miss a day, I do the tiny version.
- I test changes on myself: one change, one number, two weeks.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design | No environment changes | One or two changes | Cues and friction changed for a good and a bad habit |
| Planning | No if-then plans | Vague plans | Specific action, obstacle and restart plans in use |
| Experiment | Not done | Done without a baseline or a timer | Baseline and change weeks with timer data |
| Honesty | Overclaims the result | Some caveats | Clear note on other differences and a reasoned decision |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Move one temptation out of sight and write one if-then plan.
- Do a one-week mini experiment: three days without the change, three days with it.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Present bias | Rewards now feel much bigger than the same rewards later. |
| Commitment device | Arranging things now so your future self can't easily give in. |
| Temptation bundling: honest status | Helps a little; the large replication found a smaller effect. |
| Ego depletion status | Failed large pre-registered replications (23 and 36 labs). |
| Habit loop | Cue → routine → reward; the cue alone eventually triggers the routine. |
| Habit formation time (Lally) | Median about 66 days; range 18–254. |
| If-then plan effect | Medium to large (d = 0.65) across 94 tests. |
| Procrastination is mainly… | Short-term mood repair. |
| Personal experiment rules | One change, one number, a baseline week, an honest note. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Collecting tools without testing them.** Pick two, use them for two weeks, measure.
- **Blaming your character.** Most failures are design failures: a missing cue, too much friction, too big a start.
- **Stopping a working habit once it feels easy.** Easy means it is becoming automatic: that is the goal. Keep the cue.

sections.title: PD-M08-L01: Present bias, commitment devices and temptation bundling
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain present bias, set up a commitment device, use temptation bundling, and describe honestly what happened to the "willpower as fuel" and marshmallow-test ideas. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

We overvalue rewards now compared with later, so self-control works best when you arrange things in advance (commitments, bundles, removed temptations) rather than relying on in-the-moment willpower.

## The science

**Present bias.** Offered ₹1,000 today or ₹1,100 in a week, many people take ₹1,000. Offered ₹1,000 in 52 weeks or ₹1,100 in 53 weeks, most choose to wait the extra week. The same one-week delay feels much bigger when it starts now. Economists call this **present bias** (or hyperbolic discounting). It explains why "I'll start tomorrow" feels reasonable every single day.

**Commitment devices.** If your future self will be tempted, your present self can tie its hands, like Ulysses asking to be tied to the mast so he could hear the Sirens without steering onto the rocks. In a well-known field study in the Philippines, Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan and Wesley Yin offered savings accounts that locked money until a goal date or amount; people offered them saved more on average after a year. Other commitments: paying for a weekly class in advance, promising a friend you will show up at 6 am, giving your phone to a family member during study blocks. Commitments work best when they are **small, specific and easy to set up**, and many people do not take them up when offered, so they are a tool, not a cure.

**Temptation bundling.** Katherine Milkman and colleagues gave gym members iPods loaded with audiobooks they wanted, usable only at the gym. In the 2014 study, gym visits rose noticeably at first, and the effect faded after a few weeks (and over holiday breaks). A much larger 2021 replication with members of a big US gym chain found a **smaller** but real effect. Honest summary: bundling a treat you want (a podcast, a favourite song list, the good tea) with a task you avoid helps a little, especially early on.

**Is willpower a fuel tank?** Roy Baumeister's "ego depletion" research (from 1998) claimed that self-control uses up a limited resource: resisting cookies made people give up sooner on a puzzle afterwards. It became hugely popular. But a pre-registered replication across 23 labs with about 2,100 people (2016) found no evidence of the effect, and another across 36 labs with about 3,500 people (2021) found an effect close to zero ([summary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ego_depletion)). People do get tired and lose motivation after long effort, but the strong "fuel tank" model is not supported. Studies by Veronika Job and colleagues even suggest people who *believe* willpower is limited show more depletion-like effects.

**The marshmallow test.** Walter Mischel's studies (from the late 1960s) let children wait for two treats instead of eating one now. Follow-ups linked longer waiting to better teenage outcomes. But a larger 2018 replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan found the link was about **half** as strong, and shrank further after accounting for family background. Celeste Kidd's 2013 study showed children wait much longer when the adult has been reliable, so waiting partly reflects whether waiting is likely to pay off ([summary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_marshmallow_experiment)). The useful lessons are the original ones: children waited longer when treats were out of sight, and when they distracted themselves. **Self-control is easier when temptation is out of sight.**

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Present bias (preferring now over later) | **Strong** | Found in many lab and field studies across countries. |
| Commitment devices | **Moderate** | Field studies show benefits for those who use them; many people do not take them up. |
| Temptation bundling | **Moderate** | Original effect faded; a large replication found a smaller but real effect. |
| Ego depletion (willpower as a limited fuel) | **Failed to replicate or myth** | Large pre-registered multi-lab replications found effects near zero. |
| Marshmallow test predicts life success | **Mixed or weak** | Link about half as strong in a larger study and smaller after family background. |
| Keeping temptation out of sight helps self-control | **Strong** | Shown in the original delay studies and in many later environment studies. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Anu loses her evening study block to Instagram reels nearly every day. Each night she plans "only 10 minutes", which becomes an hour (present bias: the reel's reward is now, the exam's is months away).

She sets up three things. **Commitment device:** she pays ₹200 a week in advance for a Saturday test series at a library study centre; skipping wastes the money and she has told the organiser she will be there. **Out of sight:** during the 7–8:30 pm block her phone charges in her mother's room, not hers. **Temptation bundle:** she saves her favourite film-song playlist for her evening walk only.

She stops telling herself she has "run out of willpower" by evening. Instead, she notices that she is bored and tired, and starts the block with an easy 10-minute task. Over three weeks, her evening study days go from 2 to 5 a week. The test series is the device she uses least; the phone in another room does the most.

## How to use it

**Design self-control in advance:**

1. **Name the conflict:** "When ______, I choose ______ now instead of ______ later."
2. **Choose one device:**
   - **Remove or hide the temptation** (strongest and simplest).
   - **Commit:** pay in advance, promise a specific person, set a deadline someone else checks.
   - **Bundle:** allow a treat only during the task you avoid.
3. **Make the good choice easy now:** start with a small first step.
4. **Change the story:** say "I'm tired or bored; what would make this easier?" instead of "I'm out of willpower."

**Ethics with others:** commitment devices are for yourself. Do not trap other people into commitments they would not choose (hidden auto-renewing subscriptions are exactly this, and Module 32 shows how to spot them).

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Wikipedia: Ego depletion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ego_depletion) | Read the sections on the replication attempts | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Wikipedia: Stanford marshmallow experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_marshmallow_experiment) | Read the follow-up and replication sections | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, chapter 10: Motivation and Emotion (10.1 and 10.4)](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/10-introduction) | Re-read 10.1 for the basic ideas about drives, incentives and self-regulation | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write your biggest present-bias conflict in one sentence.
2. Set up one device of each kind: a hidden or removed temptation, a commitment (money, a person or a deadline) and a temptation bundle.
3. Use them for seven days and tick each day the good choice won.
4. Write which device helped most and which you will keep.

**Proof to record:** Your conflict sentence, a photo or note of each of the three devices, and seven days of ticks with your verdict.

## Template: Self-control design sheet

```
SELF-CONTROL DESIGN                  Week of ______
Conflict: When ______________, I choose ______ now instead of ______ later.
1. Hide or remove the temptation: ______________________________
2. Commitment (money / person / deadline): ______________________
3. Temptation bundle: I only ______ (treat) while ______ (task).
4. Easy first step: ______________________________
Day:            M  T  W  T  F  S  S
Good choice won [ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ]
Most helpful device: ______  Keep? ______
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Relying on "more willpower".** Change the situation. Hiding temptation beats resisting it.
- **Commitments that are too big.** "₹5,000 to a friend if I miss one session" leads to quitting the device. Start small.
- **Telling people "willpower runs out like fuel".** The strong version failed replication. Say "effort tires us, and environment matters more".
- **Believing a child's marshmallow wait decides their future.** Larger studies show a modest link, partly explained by family background.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why does "I'll start tomorrow" feel reasonable every day?
    - A) Because of anchoring
    - B) Because plans never work
    - C) Because tomorrow you will have more willpower fuel
    - D) Present bias makes rewards now feel much bigger than the same rewards later
2. What did large multi-lab replications find about ego depletion?
    - A) That glucose drinks double willpower
    - B) That willpower increases with use
    - C) Effects close to zero
    - D) Large effects
3. What did the 2018 marshmallow replication find?
    - A) The link with later achievement was about half as strong and shrank after family background
    - B) The original results were confirmed exactly
    - C) Children cannot wait
    - D) Waiting predicts nothing at all, ever
4. Which self-control method has the strongest, simplest support?
    - A) Watching motivational videos
    - B) Keeping the temptation out of sight or out of reach
    - C) Promising yourself silently
    - D) Thinking about the temptation more

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the Wikipedia replication sections on ego depletion and the marshmallow test
- **Action:** set up a hidden temptation, a commitment and a temptation bundle and track seven days. It is done when your proof is saved: your conflict sentence, a photo or note of each of the three devices, and seven days of ticks with your verdict.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** The delay that starts now always feels largest.
2. **C.** Studies in 2016 (23 labs) and 2021 (36 labs) found little or no effect.
3. **A.** Watts, Duncan and Quan found a weaker, partly background-driven link.
4. **B.** Out of sight is easier than resisting in the moment.

sections.title: PD-M08-L02: Environment design and the habit loop
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can map a habit as cue, routine and reward, redesign your environment to make good habits easy and bad ones hard, and measure the difference. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Habits are actions triggered automatically by cues in a stable context; change the cues and the effort required, and behaviour follows with far less willpower.

## The science

**What a habit is.** In psychology, a habit is a behaviour triggered **automatically by a cue** in a familiar context, because it has been repeated and rewarded there many times. Wendy Wood's research suggests that a large share of daily actions (in diary studies, roughly 40%) are done in the same place almost every day, often while thinking about something else.

**Cue, routine, reward.** Charles Duhigg popularised the "habit loop" (cue → routine → reward) in *The Power of Habit*. It is a useful simplification of learning research: a **cue** (a time, a place, a feeling, a person, a preceding action) triggers a **routine**, which is followed by a **reward** that makes the link stronger. Over time the cue alone starts the routine, even when the reward no longer matters much. That is why you reach for your phone the moment you sit down, even when you don't want to.

**How long does it take?** In Phillippa Lally's 2009 study, 96 people chose a new daily behaviour (such as drinking water with lunch or doing sit-ups after morning coffee). It took a **median of about 66 days** to reach their peak automaticity, with a range from **18 to 254 days**, and missing a single day did not significantly derail the process ([Lally](https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/does-it-really-take-66-days-form-habit-we-asked-expert-dr-pippa-lally)). Simple behaviours became automatic faster than complex ones. The "21 days" claim is not from research.

**Friction.** Small changes in effort have big effects. Making a healthy option slightly easier (placing it first, closer, at eye level) or an unhealthy one slightly harder (further away, needing an extra step) changes behaviour in many studies of food choice, saving and screen use. Wood calls this **friction**: add it to bad habits, remove it from good ones.

**Context change is an opportunity.** Habits are tied to context. When context changes (moving house, a new job, a new term), old cues disappear and people are more open to new habits: a "habit discontinuity". This fits with the "fresh start effect" found by Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis: people are more likely to start goals at temporal landmarks such as Mondays, birthdays and new months.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Habits are cue-triggered and context-dependent | **Strong** | Supported by many lab and field studies (Wood, Neal and others). |
| Habit formation takes weeks to months, varying widely | **Moderate** | Lally (2009): median about 66 days, range 18–254; one key study plus later work. |
| Missing one day does not ruin habit formation | **Moderate** | Found in Lally's study; consistent with later work. |
| Friction (small changes in effort) changes behaviour | **Strong** | Many studies on food placement, defaults and access. |
| Fresh-start effect at temporal landmarks | **Moderate** | Found in several large datasets and studies. |
| "21 days to form a habit" | **Failed to replicate or myth** | Not from research; real times vary widely. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Ashiq maps two habits.

**Bad habit:** *cue* sitting on the bed after dinner → *routine* opening YouTube → *reward* relief from tiredness and something new. **Redesign:** the phone charges on the shelf by the door (friction: he has to get up); the Kerala PSC book is on his pillow; the YouTube app is logged out and moved off the home screen.

**Good habit he wants:** a morning walk. *Cue* the alarm at 5:50 → *routine* walk → *reward* tea with his cousin at the junction tea shop. **Redesign:** walking clothes laid out on the chair the night before; shoes by the door; a fixed meeting time with his cousin.

He measures it: before the change, YouTube after dinner took about 70 minutes on average (Digital Wellbeing); in week two, about 25. Walks went from 1 to 4 a week. He also notices that his best start was on a Monday, the first of the month: a fresh start.

## How to use it

**Habit redesign in four moves:**

1. **Map the loop:** for one habit you want and one you want to drop, write cue, routine and reward.
2. **For a good habit: make it obvious and easy.** Put the cue where you cannot miss it (the book on the pillow, shoes by the door). Remove steps. Keep the reward immediate (the tea, the tick in Loop).
3. **For a bad habit: make it invisible and hard.** Remove the cue (phone out of the bedroom) and add friction (log out, delete the app, keep snacks out of the house).
4. **Use fresh starts:** begin on a Monday, the 1st of the month, or after a context change.

**Expect weeks, not days:** keep going for at least two months. If you miss a day, don't miss twice.

**With others:** you can help family and friends by changing shared environments (fruit on the table, the TV off at study time) instead of nagging. Change the situation, not the person.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [University of Surrey (21 January 2026): does it really take 66 days to form a habit? (Dr Pippa Lally)](https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/does-it-really-take-66-days-form-habit-we-asked-expert-dr-pippa-lally) | Read the whole interview: the 66 days, the range and what helps | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Loop Habit Tracker (free, open source, GPLv3)](https://loophabits.org/) | Set up the habit with a reminder at the cue time; turn on the habit score graph | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Android Help: manage how you spend time with Digital Wellbeing](https://support.google.com/android/answer/9346420?hl=en) | Check your daily average for your top app before and after the redesign | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04; check current rules |

## Action task

1. Map one habit you want and one you want to drop (cue, routine, reward).
2. Make at least three environment changes: one cue added, one cue removed, one friction change. Photograph them.
3. Record a before number (minutes, count or days) for each habit from the last week.
4. Run the redesign for 14 days and record the after number.

**Proof to record:** Two habit maps, photos of three environment changes, and before-and-after numbers over 14 days.

## Template: Habit loop map and redesign

```
HABIT LOOP MAP
Habit I want: ______________   Habit I want to drop: ______________
Cue:     ______________                ______________
Routine: ______________                ______________
Reward:  ______________                ______________
REDESIGN
Make it obvious (cue added): ____________  Make it invisible (cue removed): ____________
Make it easy (steps removed): ___________  Make it hard (friction added): ____________
Keep it rewarding: ____________
Numbers:  before ______  after 14 days ______
Start date (a fresh start?): ______
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Relying on motivation instead of cues.** A habit needs a reliable trigger. "Sometime in the evening" is not a cue; "after dinner, at the desk" is.
- **Expecting automaticity in 21 days.** Plan for two months or more, especially for complex habits.
- **Changing everything at once.** Redesign one or two habits at a time.
- **Leaving the old cue in place.** If the phone stays by the bed, the old habit wins most nights.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. In Lally's study, how long did habits take to reach peak automaticity?
    - A) One year for everyone
    - B) Exactly 21 days
    - C) A median of about 66 days, ranging from 18 to 254
    - D) One week
2. What is "friction" in habit design?
    - A) The effort a behaviour takes; add it to bad habits, remove it from good ones
    - B) Arguments with family
    - C) A type of reward
    - D) Rubbing your hands before studying
3. Which is the best cue for a study habit?
    - A) "When I feel like it"
    - B) "After dinner, at my desk, with the book already open"
    - C) "Sometime in the evening"
    - D) "When I have free time"
4. What does the fresh-start effect suggest?
    - A) People are more likely to start goals at landmarks such as Mondays and new months
    - B) Habits only start in January
    - C) Never start on a Monday
    - D) Fresh food builds habits

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the Lally interview
- **Action:** map two habit loops, make three environment changes and compare 14 days before and after. It is done when your proof is saved: two habit maps, photos of three environment changes, and before-and-after numbers over 14 days.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** The median was about 66 days with a very wide range.
2. **A.** Small changes in effort strongly change behaviour.
3. **B.** Specific time and place cues trigger habits.
4. **A.** Temporal landmarks make new beginnings feel natural.

sections.title: PD-M08-L03: If-then plans, tiny habits and identity-based change
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can write if-then plans, start tiny habits anchored to existing routines, and use identity statements without fooling yourself. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Deciding exactly when, where and how you will act ("If X, then I will Y") roughly doubles follow-through; tiny starting versions and identity-based framing help the habit grow.

## The science

**Implementation intentions (if-then plans).** Peter Gollwitzer showed that people who form a plan of the form "If situation X arises, then I will do Y" are much more likely to act than people with the same goal and no plan. A meta-analysis of 94 tests by Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran found a **medium-to-large average effect (d = 0.65)** ([Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f)). If-then plans work because the situation becomes a cue that triggers the action automatically, so you don't need to decide in the moment. They also work for **obstacles**: "If I feel like skipping, then I will do just five minutes." They are one of the best-supported tools in this whole course.

**Tiny habits.** B. J. Fogg, a Stanford researcher, teaches starting with a behaviour so small it takes under 30 seconds (two push-ups, opening the book, one line in the journal), anchored right after an existing routine ("After I brush my teeth, I will…"), and celebrated immediately to create a good feeling. His method is popular and fits habit research (a strong cue, low friction, an immediate reward), but it has mostly been tested in his own programmes rather than in independent trials. Treat it as a practical tool.

**Habit stacking** is the same anchoring idea: "After [current habit], I will [new habit]." James Clear's *Atomic Habits* popularised it, along with the idea of **identity-based habits**: instead of "I want to run", think "I am becoming someone who moves every day". There is supporting research on identity and behaviour: in studies by Christopher Bryan and colleagues, asking people about "being a voter" rather than "voting" increased turnout in some studies (later replications were mixed), and people tend to act consistently with how they see themselves (self-perception, commitment and consistency, PD-M28-L01). Identity framing is a moderate-evidence idea; it works best when backed by small actions that give you real evidence about who you are.

**Never miss twice.** Missing once has little effect (Lally's study); what breaks habits is the slide from one miss to many. A simple rule: "If I miss a day, the next day I do at least the tiny version."

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| If-then plans (implementation intentions) | **Strong** | Meta-analysis of 94 tests: medium-to-large average effect (d = 0.65). |
| If-then plans for obstacles | **Moderate** | Supported in many studies; effects vary by task. |
| Tiny habits with anchors and celebration | **Practical tool** | Consistent with habit research; mostly tested in its creator's programmes. |
| Identity-based framing ("be a voter") | **Mixed or weak** | Some studies found effects; replications were mixed. |
| "Never miss twice" rule | **Practical tool** | Practical rule consistent with Lally's finding that single misses do little harm. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Sreeja wants three new habits. She writes them as if-then plans and starts tiny:

- "**After** I finish my morning tea, **I will** do 2 push-ups (from the knees) and say 'done!'" Within three weeks, she does 10 most days.
- "**If** it is 7 pm on a weekday, **then I will** sit at my desk with the phone in Amma's room and open the Polity book." Some evenings she only reads one page. That still counts.
- "**After** I switch off the light, **I will** think of one good thing from today."

For obstacles: "If I feel like skipping study, then I will do five minutes and decide after that." She writes an identity line in her Playbook: "I'm becoming someone who shows up every day, even for five minutes." Each tick in Loop is a small piece of evidence for that identity.

When her cousin's wedding takes three days, she misses the push-ups twice. On day four she does the tiny version: two push-ups. The chain restarts.

## How to use it

**Write three if-then plans:**

1. **Action plan:** "If/When [time + place or after current routine], then I will [specific action]."
2. **Obstacle plan:** "If [likely obstacle], then I will [response]."
3. **Restart plan:** "If I miss a day, then the next day I will do [tiny version]."

**Start tiny:** shrink each new habit to a version that takes under two minutes. Do the tiny version every day for two weeks before growing it. Celebrate immediately (a word, a tick, a small fist pump).

**Identity:** write one line: "I'm becoming someone who ______." Count each completion as a vote for it.

**With others:** if-then plans work in pairs and families too: "If Amma calls during my study block, I'll call back at 8:30." Agree on them together in advance.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), implementation intentions meta-analysis (free PDF)](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f) | Read the abstract and the summary of effect sizes | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Loop Habit Tracker (free, open source, GPLv3)](https://loophabits.org/) | Add each new habit with a reminder at its cue time | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/20203) | Read how Franklin focused on one virtue a week (search the text for "a week's strict attention") | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write one action plan, one obstacle plan and one restart plan for a habit that matters to you.
2. Choose two tiny habits anchored to existing routines and add them to Loop.
3. Do them for 14 days. Celebrate each one. Note any misses and whether you missed twice.
4. Write your identity line and three pieces of evidence for it from the 14 days.

**Proof to record:** Your three if-then plans, a 14-day Loop screenshot for two tiny habits, and your identity line with three pieces of evidence.

## Template: If-then plan card

```
IF-THEN PLANS
Action:   When ______________________ (time/place or after ______),
          then I will ______________________.
Obstacle: If ______________________, then I will ______________________.
Restart:  If I miss a day, then the next day I will ______ (tiny version).
TINY HABITS (under 2 minutes)
After I ______________, I will ______________. Celebrate: "______!"
After I ______________, I will ______________. Celebrate: "______!"
Identity: I'm becoming someone who ______________________.
Evidence this fortnight: 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Vague plans.** "I'll study in the evening" is not an if-then plan. Name the time, place and first action.
- **Starting big.** Thirty push-ups a day collapses in week one; two push-ups grows.
- **Identity statements without action.** Saying "I am a fit person" while never moving is self-deception. Identity grows from small, repeated evidence.
- **Too many if-then plans at once.** Three to five are plenty. More and they stop being memorable.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What was the average effect of if-then plans in the 94-test meta-analysis?
    - A) Zero
    - B) Tiny (d = 0.05)
    - C) Negative
    - D) Medium to large (d = 0.65)
2. Which is a good tiny habit?
    - A) "I will exercise more"
    - B) "I will be healthier this year"
    - C) "I will do 50 push-ups every morning from tomorrow"
    - D) "After I brush my teeth, I will do 2 push-ups"
3. What does "never miss twice" mean?
    - A) A single miss is fine; restart with the tiny version the next day
    - B) Never miss a day ever
    - C) Stop the habit if you miss twice
    - D) Do double the next day
4. How strong is the evidence for identity-based framing?
    - A) Proved harmful
    - B) Strong and universal
    - C) No research at all
    - D) Mixed: some studies found effects and replications were mixed

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the Gollwitzer and Sheeran abstract
- **Action:** write three if-then plans, run two tiny habits for 14 days and write your identity line with evidence. It is done when your proof is saved: your three if-then plans, a 14-day Loop screenshot for two tiny habits, and your identity line with three pieces of evidence.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Implementation intentions are among the best-supported behaviour-change tools.
2. **D.** Small, anchored to an existing routine, and specific.
3. **A.** Single misses do little harm; slides do.
4. **D.** The voter-identity studies had mixed replications.

sections.title: PD-M08-L04: Procrastination, and a two-week personal experiment
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain procrastination as mood repair, use three anti-procrastination tools, and run a two-week personal experiment on your study time with real data. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 10 minutes a day for two weeks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Procrastination is less about laziness or poor time management and more about avoiding bad feelings; the fix is to make starting feel less bad, and to test your fixes with your own data.

## The science

**Why we procrastinate.** Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl argue that procrastination is mainly **short-term mood repair**: a task makes us feel anxious, bored, confused or inadequate, and delaying it brings instant relief, at the cost of our future self ([Sirois and Pychyl, 2013](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/91793/)). That is why procrastination is common on tasks that are boring, unclear, difficult or tied to our self-worth (exam preparation is all four). It links with present bias (PD-M08-L01).

**What helps:**
1. **Make the first step tiny and clear:** "Open the book to page 112 and read one paragraph" is easier to start than "study Polity".
2. **Time-box it:** commit to 10 or 25 minutes, then decide whether to continue. Starting is the hard part.
3. **Self-forgiveness:** in a study by Michael Wohl, Pychyl and Shannon Bennett, students who forgave themselves for procrastinating on the first exam procrastinated less before the next one ([BPS summary](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself)). Harsh self-criticism makes the task feel worse, which feeds more avoidance.
4. **Expressive writing before high-stakes tasks:** writing about worries for 10 minutes before an exam improved scores for anxious students in Ramirez and Beilock's study ([University of Chicago summary](https://news.uchicago.edu/story/writing-about-worries-eases-anxiety-and-improves-test-performance)).

The Learning Capabilities course has a full module on this: [Motivation, procrastination and habits](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/learning-capabilities/lrn-m06) (in the Practical Learning Capabilities course). Here you add the most powerful tool for your whole life: **testing your own changes**.

**Personal experiments (n-of-1).** In medicine, "n-of-1 trials" test treatments on one person by switching between conditions and measuring. You can do a simple version: keep everything the same except **one change** and compare a **baseline week** with a **change week**, using one number (study minutes from a timer). It will not be perfect science: weeks differ, you know which week is which (no blinding), and two weeks is short. But it beats guessing, and it protects you from regression to the mean (PD-M02-L01) and from the confirmation bias of "I'm sure it helped". Repeating the switch (A-B-A-B) makes it stronger.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Procrastination as short-term mood repair | **Moderate** | Supported by several studies; a leading explanation, not the only one. |
| Self-forgiveness reduces later procrastination | **Mixed or weak** | One well-known study with students; consistent with self-compassion research. |
| Expressive writing about worries before exams | **Moderate** | Lab and classroom studies found benefits for anxious students; later replications varied. |
| Time-boxed starts (e.g. 10 or 25 minutes) | **Practical tool** | Widely used and consistent with mood-repair theory; little direct testing. |
| Personal A-B experiments | **Practical tool** | A sound way to test changes on yourself, with clear limits (short, unblinded). |

## Everyday Kerala example

Vinod suspects his study time is low because his books are in a cupboard in the shop's back room and his phone is always on the counter. He runs a two-week experiment.

**Question:** Does keeping a "study corner" set up (book open on the table, phone in a drawer, a timer ready) increase his study minutes?
**Week 1 (baseline):** normal routine. Study minutes measured with a phone timer each day: 35, 0, 50, 20, 45, 30, 60 → average about 34.
**Week 2 (change):** study corner set up every evening before he leaves the shop: 55, 40, 70, 60, 0 (a family function), 65, 75 → average about 52.

He writes honestly: "Week 2 had one function day; week 1 had a slow Tuesday at the shop. Both weeks were normal otherwise. The change seems to help by about 15–20 minutes a day." He keeps the study corner and plans a second experiment: does an earlier dinner help? He also notes that the timer itself may have made him study more in both weeks (people often change when they are measured), which is fine: measurement is part of the system.

## How to use it

**The two-week personal experiment:**

1. **One question, one change:** "Does ______ increase my daily study minutes?" Good changes to test: phone in another room, a fixed start time, a study corner, studying before breakfast, a Pomodoro timer, a study partner call.
2. **One number:** study minutes, measured with a timer every day.
3. **Week 1 = baseline,** with no change. **Week 2 = the change** every day. Keep everything else as similar as possible.
4. **Log unusual events** (guests, illness, festivals, power cuts).
5. **Compare averages** and write an honest note about other differences.
6. **Decide:** keep, modify or drop, and plan the next experiment.

**For procrastination moments during the experiment:** tiny first step, a 10-minute time box, and forgiveness if you slip.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sirois and Pychyl (2013), "Procrastination and the Priority of Short-Term Mood Regulation" (free author copy)](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/91793/) | Read the abstract and the introduction on mood repair | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [BPS Research Digest (4 May 2010): to cure procrastination, forgive yourself (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett)](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself) | Read the short summary of the self-forgiveness study | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [University of Chicago (2011): writing about worries eases anxiety and improves test performance (Ramirez and Beilock)](https://news.uchicago.edu/story/writing-about-worries-eases-anxiety-and-improves-test-performance) | Read the summary of the expressive-writing study | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task

1. Write your experiment question, the one change and how you will measure study minutes.
2. Week 1: record daily study minutes with a timer, with no change.
3. Week 2: make the change every day and keep recording.
4. Write averages, unusual events, an honest note about other differences, and your decision.

**Proof to record:** The completed experiment log with 14 daily numbers, both averages, notes on unusual events and your decision.

## Template: Personal experiment log

```
PERSONAL EXPERIMENT (2 weeks: one change, one number)
Question: Does ______________________ (the change) increase my study minutes?
Week 1 = normal (baseline). Week 2 = with the change. Keep everything else the same.
Day | Date | Week (1 baseline / 2 change) | Change done? (Y/N) | Study minutes (timer) | Sleep (h) | Unusual event?
Result: Week 1 average ___ min/day   Week 2 average ___ min/day   Difference ___
Honest notes: Was anything else different (exam date, guests, illness, festivals)?
Decision: keep / modify / drop the change. Next experiment: ________________
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Changing two things at once.** Then you cannot tell which one worked. One change per experiment.
- **Estimating minutes from memory.** Use a timer. Memory overestimates good days.
- **Declaring victory after a few good days.** Wait for the full week and compare averages, noting unusual days.
- **Beating yourself up for procrastinating during the experiment.** Self-criticism feeds avoidance. Note it, forgive it, restart with the tiny step.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. According to Sirois and Pychyl, procrastination is mainly:
    - A) Laziness
    - B) Poor time-management skills only
    - C) Low intelligence
    - D) Short-term mood repair: avoiding the bad feelings a task brings
2. In the Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett study, what reduced later procrastination?
    - A) Ignoring the exam
    - B) Forgiving yourself for earlier procrastination
    - C) Studying all night
    - D) Punishing yourself
3. What is the most important rule of a personal experiment?
    - A) Change everything to get quick results
    - B) Change one thing at a time and measure one number
    - C) Only do it for one day
    - D) Trust your feeling about whether it worked
4. Why compare with a baseline week?
    - A) Because baselines are traditional
    - B) It is not necessary
    - C) To make the experiment longer
    - D) Without it, natural ups and downs (and regression to the mean) can look like effects

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the three study summaries
- **Action:** run the two-week personal experiment on your study time and write the result. It is done when your proof is saved: the completed experiment log with 14 daily numbers, both averages, notes on unusual events and your decision.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Delay brings instant relief from negative feelings.
2. **B.** Self-forgiveness lowered procrastination before the next exam.
3. **B.** One change and one measure make the comparison meaningful.
4. **D.** The baseline shows what would have happened anyway.

sections.title: Module 9: Mindset and self-talk
sections.summary: Mindset and self-talk with honest evidence: what growth mindset really does (a small effect, mostly for struggling learners), how to test limiting beliefs with behavioural experiments, and how self-compassion helps you improve rather than go soft.
sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

The way you talk to yourself after a failure shapes what you do next. This module avoids the hype ("Change your mindset, change your life!") and keeps the useful core: treat your current level as temporary, change strategies, test your beliefs against reality, and be firm about standards and kind about the person.

These skills prepare you for the harder emotional work of Modules 10 and 11, and for the confidence and rejection work in Modules 13 and 14.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain growth mindset and the honest size of its effects.
- Use effort plus strategy plus help to grow a real skill, with numbers.
- Run a behavioural experiment on a limiting belief.
- Use self-compassion practices and explain why they don't make you lazy.

## Time

About 2 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 6–7, with the module project due in week 7.

## Lessons

1. PD-M09-L01: Growth mindset: what the evidence really says (about 1 hour)
2. PD-M09-L02: Limiting beliefs and self-compassion (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The skill growth card (PD-M09-L01).
- The behavioural experiment and self-compassion break (PD-M09-L02).

## Module project: a self-talk rewrite backed by evidence

1. For one week, collect five examples of your self-talk after mistakes, word for word.
2. For each, write a rewrite that is honest about the mistake, kind about the person and names one next step.
3. Run one behavioural experiment on the belief behind your harshest self-talk.
4. Write your new "default sentence" for mistakes and put it in your Playbook.

**Proof to record:** Five self-talk examples with rewrites, one behavioural experiment and your default sentence.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- After a mistake I say: "______" (honest, kind, with one next step).
- When I think "people like me can't…", I test it with a small experiment.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Honesty about mindset evidence | Repeats hype | Knows effects are mixed | Explains the small average effect and who benefits more |
| Skill growth | No measurement | Before or after only | Before and after numbers with a new strategy |
| Belief testing | No experiment | Experiment planned | Experiment done with a new belief written |
| Self-compassion | Not practised | Practised once | Practised several times with concrete next steps |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Use "yet" and the three questions (strategy, alternative, help) after one failure.
- Use the one-minute self-compassion break twice this week.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Growth mindset intervention effect (meta-analysis) | Very small on average (d = 0.08); larger for low-income and struggling students. |
| Mindset–achievement link | Weak (r = .10) across 273 samples. |
| The useful version of growth mindset | Effort + better strategies + help-seeking + learning from mistakes. |
| Behavioural experiment | Turn a belief into a prediction, test it, compare, update. |
| Self-compassion: three parts | Self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness. |
| Does self-compassion reduce motivation? | No: experiments found more motivation to improve. |
| Why affirmations can backfire | They clash with existing beliefs and can make people feel worse. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Using mindset language to blame people.** Struggles have many causes; offer strategies and support.
- **Harshness as motivation.** It increases avoidance. Be firm about standards, kind about the person.
- **Skipping the measurement.** Numbers turn a slogan into real evidence of growth.

sections.title: PD-M09-L01: Growth mindset: what the evidence really says
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain growth mindset and what the large studies really found, and use the useful part (effort plus strategy plus help) without the hype. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Believing abilities can grow is mildly helpful, mostly for struggling learners; what matters more is what you do with the belief: change strategies, seek feedback and keep practising.

## The science

**The idea.** Carol Dweck's research, from the 1990s, contrasted a **fixed mindset** (abilities are set; failure shows you lack them) with a **growth mindset** (abilities develop with effort, good strategies and help). Early studies found that students praised for being "smart" chose easier tasks and gave up sooner after failure than students praised for effort, and that growth-mindset students did better through difficult school transitions. *Mindset* (2006) became a bestseller, and schools worldwide ran mindset programmes.

**What the big studies found.** In 2018, Victoria Sisk, Alexander Burgoyne and colleagues ran two meta-analyses ([Sisk et al., 2018](https://englelab.gatech.edu/articles/2018/Sisk,%20Burgoyne%20et%20al.%20%282018%29%20-%20Mindset%20and%20Academic%20Achievement.pdf)):
- Across 273 samples (about 366,000 students), the link between holding a growth mindset and academic achievement was **weak (r = .10)**.
- Across 43 intervention studies (about 57,000 students), teaching growth mindset improved achievement by a **very small average amount (d = 0.08)**.
- Effects were larger for **students from low-income families (d = 0.34)** and somewhat larger for academically at-risk students.

A large, carefully pre-registered US national study led by David Yeager (2019) found that a short online mindset programme raised grades slightly for lower-achieving students, with bigger effects in schools whose culture supported the message. So the honest picture: **growth mindset is real but small on average**, helps most those who are struggling, and works only when the environment supports it. It is not a cure-all, and it was oversold.

**"False growth mindset."** Dweck herself warned against reducing it to "just praise effort" or "anything is possible". Effort that keeps using a failing strategy is not growth; neither is pretending. The useful version is **effort + better strategies + help-seeking + learning from mistakes**.

**Ability is not unlimited.** People differ in aptitude, and some limits are real. A growth mindset does not mean you can become anything. It means your current level is not your final level, and that the best way to find your limits is to practise well.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Growth mindset correlates with achievement | **Mixed or weak** | Weak average link (r = .10) across 273 samples. |
| Growth mindset interventions raise achievement on average | **Mixed or weak** | Very small average effect (d = 0.08) across 43 studies. |
| Benefits for low-income or struggling students | **Moderate** | Larger effects in these groups in meta-analyses and a national study. |
| Praising effort and strategy rather than "being smart" | **Moderate** | Supported by experiments; effects depend on honesty and context. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Ashiq failed the arithmetic part of his last mock badly and said, "I'm just not a maths person." His friend replied, "Have a growth mindset!" That didn't help; it felt like being told to cheer up.

What helped was the practical version. He looked at his errors and found 14 of 20 wrong answers were percentage and ratio questions. **Strategy:** he learned one method for each type from a free video and practised 10 questions a day. **Help:** he asked Joseph sir to watch him solve three problems aloud and point out where he went wrong (he was converting fractions slowly). **Effort tracked:** after three weeks, his percentage questions went from 3/10 to 7/10. His belief changed *after* the evidence did: "I'm not a maths person yet" became "I'm getting better at percentages."

He also accepted a limit: he may never be the fastest in reasoning, so he plans to collect marks in GK and language and aim for "good enough" in maths.

## How to use it

**Use the strong part, skip the hype:**

1. **When you fail at something, ask three questions:** What strategy did I use? What could I try instead? Who could show me?
2. **Track skill, not just effort:** a score on the same type of problem over weeks shows real growth and builds belief.
3. **Use "yet":** "I can't do this yet" is a small but honest reframe.
4. **Accept real limits:** choose where to invest effort; you don't have to be equally good at everything.

**With others (children, students, colleagues):**
- Praise **specific strategies and progress** ("You checked each step; that's why you caught the error"), not intelligence ("You're so smart") and not empty effort ("Good try!" when the method was wrong).
- Show your own mistakes and how you fixed them.
- Change the environment: a teacher or parent who punishes every mistake undermines any mindset talk.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sisk, Burgoyne et al. (2018), "To What Extent and Under Which Circumstances Are Growth Mind-Sets Important to Academic Achievement?" (PDF)](https://englelab.gatech.edu/articles/2018/Sisk,%20Burgoyne%20et%20al.%20%282018%29%20-%20Mindset%20and%20Academic%20Achievement.pdf) | Read the abstract and the discussion section: where effects were found and where not | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, chapter 10: Motivation and Emotion (10.1 and 10.4)](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/10-introduction) | Re-read the self-efficacy part of 10.1 (it connects to Module 13) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [William James, Talks to Teachers on Psychology; and to Students on Some of Life's Ideals (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/16287) | Read the chapter "The Laws of Habits" (in Talks to Teachers): James on how practice shapes ability, written in 1899 | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Pick one skill where you say "I'm not a ______ person".
2. Write your current level with a number (a score on 10 questions, a time, a count).
3. Choose one new strategy and one person or resource to learn from. Practise for 10 to 20 minutes on at least five days.
4. Measure the same way again and write the change, plus one honest limit you accept.

**Proof to record:** Your before and after numbers for one skill, the strategy and help used, and one accepted limit.

## Template: Strategy, not slogans

```
SKILL GROWTH CARD                  Skill: ______________________
"I'm not a ______ person" -> "I'm not good at ______ YET."
Before: ______ (score / time / count) on ______ (date)
What strategy was I using? ____________________________
New strategy to try: ____________________________
Who or what can show me? ____________________________
Practice log: Day | Minutes | Score
After: ______ on ______ (date)   Change: ______
A limit I accept, and where I'll invest instead: ______________
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Treating growth mindset as positive thinking.** It is about strategy, practice and help, not feeling good.
- **Praising effort when the method is wrong.** Praise effective strategies and progress; help change ineffective ones.
- **Believing mindset is the main cause of success.** Average effects are small; ability, teaching, resources and practice matter more.
- **Blaming people for a "fixed mindset".** Context matters. Change the environment and offer better strategies first.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did the 2018 meta-analysis find about growth-mindset interventions on average?
    - A) They made students worse
    - B) A very small effect (d = 0.08)
    - C) No studies existed
    - D) A huge effect
2. For whom did growth-mindset interventions seem to help most?
    - A) Nobody
    - B) Only adults
    - C) Students from low-income families and struggling students
    - D) Top students
3. What is the most useful response when you fail at a skill?
    - A) Give up on that skill forever
    - B) Ask what strategy you used, what to try instead and who could show you
    - C) Tell yourself to have a growth mindset
    - D) Work harder with the same method
4. Which praise fits the research best?
    - A) "You're a natural"
    - B) "You're so smart"
    - C) "Good try" when the method was wrong
    - D) "You checked each step, which is why you caught the error"

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the Sisk et al. abstract and discussion
- **Action:** measure one "I'm not a ___ person" skill, practise a new strategy with help for five days, and measure again. It is done when your proof is saved: your before and after numbers for one skill, the strategy and help used, and one accepted limit.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Sisk et al. found small average effects, larger for low-income students.
2. **C.** Effects were larger for low-SES (d = 0.34) and at-risk students.
3. **B.** Effort plus better strategy plus help is the real "growth" recipe.
4. **D.** Specific praise of strategies and progress supports learning.

sections.title: PD-M09-L02: Limiting beliefs and self-compassion
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can find and test a limiting belief, and use self-compassion practices to handle mistakes without beating yourself up or letting yourself off the hook. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes of practice).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Beliefs like "people like me can't…" are predictions you can test; and treating yourself with the kindness you would show a friend helps you recover and improve, not go soft.

## The science

**Limiting beliefs.** A limiting belief is a general rule about yourself or the world that stops you trying: "People from villages can't speak good English", "I'm too old to start exercising at 30", "Rich people are all cheats, so I'll never earn well". In CBT terms (PD-M03-L02), these are often **core beliefs** or **rules** built from early experiences. CBT's main way of changing them is the **behavioural experiment**: turn the belief into a prediction, test it in real life, and see what happens. This is better supported than repeating positive affirmations. In one study by Joanne Wood and colleagues (2009), people with low self-esteem who repeated "I am a lovable person" felt *worse*, apparently because the statement clashed with what they believed.

**Self-compassion.** Kristin Neff defines self-compassion as three parts:
1. **Self-kindness** instead of harsh self-judgement.
2. **Common humanity:** seeing your struggles as part of being human ("many people fail interviews"), not proof that you are uniquely broken.
3. **Mindfulness:** noticing painful feelings clearly, without exaggerating or suppressing them.

Research finds self-compassion is linked to lower anxiety and depression and greater resilience, and meta-analyses of self-compassion training (such as Mindful Self-Compassion programmes) report moderate improvements. Many studies are correlational or small, so effects may be smaller than claimed.

**Does it make you lazy?** The common fear is that being kind to yourself removes the drive to improve. Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012) found the opposite in several experiments: people who wrote self-compassionately about a failure or weakness were **more** motivated to improve, studied longer for a retest and were more willing to make amends for a wrong. Self-compassion is not self-pity or excuses; it is honest about the mistake and kind about the person. The self-forgiveness and procrastination study (PD-M08-L04) fits the same pattern.

**Kerala context.** Many of us grew up with harsh correction ("Why only 92? Who got 98?"). Harsh self-talk can feel normal, even virtuous. It is worth knowing that the research favours being firm about standards and kind about the person.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Behavioural experiments for changing beliefs (CBT) | **Moderate** | Core CBT method with good support as part of therapy; fewer studies of it alone. |
| Positive self-statements can backfire for low self-esteem | **Mixed or weak** | One well-known study; replications are limited. |
| Self-compassion is linked to lower anxiety and depression | **Moderate** | Many studies, largely correlational; training trials show moderate gains. |
| Self-compassion increases motivation to improve after failure | **Moderate** | Several experiments (Breines and Chen, 2012); consistent with later work. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Anu believes, "People from Malayalam-medium schools can't speak English confidently in front of others." It stops her from speaking up in her study group's English sessions.

She turns it into a **behavioural experiment**. *Prediction:* "If I speak for two minutes in English in the group, people will laugh, and I'll freeze." *Test:* she prepares two minutes on a current-affairs topic and speaks on Sunday. *Result:* she stumbled twice; nobody laughed; one friend said her points were clear; she did not freeze. *New belief:* "I can speak English in a friendly group. My grammar slips when I'm nervous, and I can practise that."

That night she notices harsh self-talk about the stumbles: "You sounded stupid." She uses the **self-compassion break**: "This is a moment of embarrassment (mindfulness). Lots of people feel this when speaking a second language (common humanity). May I be patient with myself while I learn (kindness)." Then she writes one specific improvement: "Practise past-tense verbs with shadowing for 10 minutes a day."

## How to use it

**Test a limiting belief (behavioural experiment):**

1. Write the belief: "People like me can't ______."
2. Turn it into a prediction about a specific situation: "If I ______, then ______ will happen."
3. Design a small, safe test and do it.
4. Record what actually happened, compared with the prediction.
5. Write a new, more accurate belief.

**Self-compassion break (1 minute, when you're upset with yourself):**
- "This is hard / painful right now." (mindfulness)
- "Others go through this too." (common humanity)
- "May I be kind to myself and learn from this." (kindness; use words that feel natural, in Malayalam if you prefer)
- Then: "What would help now?" (one concrete step)

**"How would I treat a friend?" (5 minutes):** write how you'd respond to a friend in your situation; compare it with how you talk to yourself; write a response to yourself in the friend version.

**With others:** offer common humanity rather than comparisons ("Lots of people struggle with this") and avoid "At least…" responses that dismiss feelings.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kristin Neff, self-compassion.org: free practices (How would you treat a friend?, Self-Compassion Break)](https://self-compassion.org/self-compassion-practices/) | Do Exercise 1 ("How would you treat a friend?") and Exercise 2 ("Self-Compassion Break") | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Greater Good in Action (UC Berkeley): free, research-based practices](https://ggia.berkeley.edu/) | Search for "Self-Compassionate Letter" and read the practice | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Epictetus, The Enchiridion, Higginson translation (Project Gutenberg)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45109) | Read sections 1 to 5 (what is and isn't in our control; it is not things but our judgements about them that disturb us) | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write one limiting belief and turn it into a testable prediction.
2. Design and carry out a small, safe test this week.
3. Record the result versus the prediction and write a new belief.
4. Use the self-compassion break at least three times this week, and do the "treat a friend" exercise once. Note what you did next each time.

**Proof to record:** Your behavioural experiment (belief, prediction, test, result, new belief) and notes on three self-compassion breaks plus one friend exercise.

## Template: Behavioural experiment and self-compassion break

```
BEHAVIOURAL EXPERIMENT                    Date ______
Belief: "People like me can't ________________________."
How much I believe it (0-100%): ___
Prediction: If I ________________, then ________________ will happen.
Test (small and safe): ________________ on ______
What actually happened: ________________________________
New belief: ____________________________  Belief in old one now: ___%

SELF-COMPASSION BREAK (1 minute)
1. "This is hard right now."
2. "Others go through this too."
3. "May I be kind to myself and learn from this."
4. One concrete step now: ______________
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Repeating affirmations you don't believe.** They can backfire. Test beliefs with experiments instead.
- **Confusing self-compassion with excuses.** Be honest about the mistake and kind about the person; then take a concrete step.
- **Designing tests that are too big.** A test should be small and safe enough to actually do this week.
- **Expecting one experiment to erase a belief.** Beliefs weaken with repeated evidence. Run several small tests.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the main CBT way of changing a limiting belief?
    - A) Ignoring it
    - B) Arguing with others about it
    - C) A behavioural experiment: test the belief as a prediction in real life
    - D) Repeating positive affirmations
2. What are Neff's three parts of self-compassion?
    - A) Self-kindness, common humanity and mindfulness
    - B) Positive thinking, optimism and hope
    - C) Forgiveness, forgetting and moving on
    - D) Self-esteem, confidence and pride
3. What did Breines and Chen find about self-compassion after failure?
    - A) It made people lazy
    - B) It increased self-pity
    - C) It increased motivation to improve
    - D) It had no effect
4. Why might "I am a lovable person" backfire for some people?
    - A) It never backfires
    - B) It can clash with what people with low self-esteem believe and make them feel worse
    - C) It is not in Malayalam
    - D) It is too short

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and do Neff's two exercises
- **Action:** run one behavioural experiment on a limiting belief and use the self-compassion break three times. It is done when your proof is saved: your behavioural experiment (belief, prediction, test, result, new belief) and notes on three self-compassion breaks plus one friend exercise.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Real evidence changes beliefs better than slogans.
2. **A.** Neff's model has these three components.
3. **C.** Self-compassionate people studied longer and were more willing to make amends.
4. **B.** Wood and colleagues found it made low self-esteem participants feel worse.
