sections.title: PD-M12-L02: Journaling and gratitude
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can use three journaling methods (three good things, expressive writing and a daily log) and run a 30-day journaling challenge with honest expectations. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 5 minutes a day for 30 days).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Writing a few lines a day about what went well and what you learned helps many people modestly; writing about difficult experiences can help too, but gratitude is not a cure and forcing it can backfire.

## The science

**Gratitude practices.** In a study by Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough (2003), people who wrote weekly lists of things they were grateful for reported feeling better about their lives than people who listed hassles or neutral events. Martin Seligman and colleagues (2005) tested the **Three Good Things** exercise (each night, write three things that went well and why) and found improvements in happiness and depressive symptoms that lasted months in some participants ([Greater Good in Action: Three Good Things](https://ggia.berkeley.edu/practice/three-good-things)). A 2016 meta-analysis by Davis and colleagues found that gratitude interventions had **small** effects on wellbeing compared with neutral activities, and smaller still compared with other positive activities. Sonja Lyubomirsky found in one study that counting blessings once a week worked better than three times a week, perhaps because daily practice became routine. So: helpful for many, modest in size, and best kept fresh.

**Expressive writing.** James Pennebaker's research from the 1980s found that writing about stressful or traumatic experiences for 15 to 20 minutes on three or four days led to fewer doctor visits and better mood weeks later in many studies. Meta-analyses find **small** average benefits, with large variation between studies. People often feel worse immediately after writing and better later. This is different from rumination: the writing makes sense of the experience rather than replaying it. If writing about a trauma overwhelms you, stop and seek professional support.

**Daily logs and reflection.** Short daily notes (what I did, what I learned, one win) support memory, progress awareness (the progress principle, PD-M06-L02) and the weekly review. The evening review in PD-M11-L03 is one version.

**Kerala note.** Many people already practise gratitude through prayer or thanking elders. Journaling adds two things: **specific** details ("my mother made pathiri even though she was tired") and **why** it happened, which seems to be part of what makes the exercise work.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gratitude interventions improve wellbeing | **Moderate** | Many trials, but a meta-analysis found small effects versus neutral activities. |
| Three Good Things | **Moderate** | Positive results in trials, including follow-ups of months; effects modest. |
| Expressive writing about stressful events | **Moderate** | Small average benefits across many studies, with wide variation. |
| Daily practice always beats weekly practice | **Mixed or weak** | One study found weekly gratitude worked better; findings vary. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Sreeja keeps a small notebook by her bed for the 30-day challenge. Each night she writes:

**Three good things (and why):** "1. Solved 8/10 percentage questions: because I practised the method daily. 2. Amma laughed at my imitation of the bus conductor: because I made time to talk with her after dinner. 3. Rain stopped just as I walked home: luck!"

**One line of the day:** "Studied 3 h; walk done; argued with my brother, then apologised."

On day 9, after a bad mock, she does **expressive writing** instead: 15 minutes about her fear of failing again and what her family expects. She feels worse that night and better the next morning, with a clearer plan. By day 20 the three good things feel repetitive, so she varies them: one day "three people I'm grateful for", another "three small pleasures". Her day-30 review: "Small lift in mood, more noticing of good moments, best for my sleep routine. Keep it, but four nights a week."

## How to use it

**Three methods (choose one or rotate):**

1. **Three good things (3–5 minutes, at night):** write three things that went well today and, for each, why it happened. Be specific. Include small things.
2. **Expressive writing (15 minutes, when something is weighing on you):** write your deepest thoughts and feelings about it, without worrying about grammar. Do it for 3–4 days. Stop if it overwhelms you.
3. **Daily log (2 minutes):** one line on what you did, one on what you learned, one win.

**The 30-day journaling challenge:** 5 minutes a night, anchored to your evening routine (after brushing teeth, in bed). Rotate prompts when it gets stale. Never miss twice. Day-30 honest review.

**With others:** a **gratitude letter** or message to someone who helped you (a teacher, a relative) is one of the stronger short-term mood boosters in studies, for you and for them. Make it specific: what they did, how it affected you.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Greater Good in Action: Three Good Things](https://ggia.berkeley.edu/practice/three-good-things) | Read the practice: how to do it, why it works and the evidence | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Greater Good in Action (UC Berkeley): free, research-based practices](https://ggia.berkeley.edu/) | Search for "Gratitude Letter" and read the practice | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley: free articles, quizzes and podcasts](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/) | Take the free Gratitude quiz (under Quizzes) now and again on day 30 | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Choose your journal (a small notebook or a Joplin note) and add "Journal (5 minutes)" to Loop.
2. Write every night for 30 days, mainly Three Good Things with why, plus a one-line log.
3. Do one expressive-writing session (15 minutes on 3 days) if something is weighing on you during the 30 days.
4. Send one specific gratitude message or letter to someone who helped you.
5. On day 30, retake the Gratitude quiz and write a five-line review.

**Proof to record:** Photos or screenshots of journal entries across the 30 days, your gratitude message (or a note of it), quiz scores at start and day 30, and your review.

## Template: Journal prompts

```
NIGHTLY JOURNAL (5 minutes)
Three good things today, and why:
1. ______________________ because ______________________
2. ______________________ because ______________________
3. ______________________ because ______________________
Log: Did ______  Learned ______  Win ______
ROTATING PROMPTS (when it gets stale)
- Three people I'm grateful for, and one thing each did
- Three small pleasures today (food, weather, music)
- One thing I'm looking forward to tomorrow
- One mistake and what it taught me
- One thing about my body I'm thankful for
EXPRESSIVE WRITING (15 minutes, 3-4 days): my deepest thoughts and feelings about ______
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Writing the same three things every night.** Vary prompts and be specific; routine dulls the effect.
- **Forcing gratitude to cover real problems.** Gratitude is not denial. Write about problems too (expressive writing) and act on them.
- **Expecting a big transformation.** Effects are modest. Judge by your day-30 review.
- **Continuing expressive writing that overwhelms you.** Stop, and talk to a professional if a past event keeps causing distress.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does the Three Good Things exercise ask you to write?
    - A) Three people who annoyed you
    - B) Three problems to solve
    - C) Three goals for tomorrow
    - D) Three things that went well today and why each happened
2. What did a 2016 meta-analysis find about gratitude interventions?
    - A) No studies existed
    - B) Huge effects for everyone
    - C) They make people worse
    - D) Small effects on wellbeing compared with neutral activities
3. How do people often feel right after expressive writing about a stressful event?
    - A) Nothing at all
    - B) Always better at once
    - C) Immediately cured
    - D) Worse at first, and often better later
4. Which is a strong short-term mood booster in studies?
    - A) A specific gratitude letter to someone who helped you
    - B) Complaining to friends
    - C) Scrolling social media
    - D) Writing a to-do list

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the Three Good Things practice
- **Action:** complete the 30-day journaling challenge, send one gratitude message and write the day-30 review. It is done when your proof is saved: photos or screenshots of journal entries across the 30 days, your gratitude message (or a note of it), quiz scores at start and day 30, and your review.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Specific good events plus their causes.
2. **D.** Davis et al. found modest effects.
3. **D.** Short-term distress, later benefit, in many studies.
4. **A.** Gratitude letters and visits showed strong short-term effects.

sections.title: Module 13: Confidence and courage
sections.summary: Confidence and courage built the way research says it grows: self-efficacy through mastery experiences, the spotlight effect, honest handling of impostor feelings (and why power posing doesn't do the job), and a fear ladder climbed with exposure principles.
sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

Confidence is not a personality trait you have or lack. It is a set of task-specific beliefs that grow when you succeed at slightly harder steps. This module gives you the method; Module 14 applies it to the fear of rejection, and Module 27 applies it to public speaking.

If you have severe anxiety (panic attacks, avoiding normal life), use these ideas only with a professional's guidance.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy and design mastery steps.
- Use the spotlight effect to reduce fear of being judged.
- Handle impostor feelings with an evidence file.
- Explain why power posing is not a confidence tool.
- Build and climb a fear ladder without safety behaviours.

## Time

About 2 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: week 9, with the module project due in week 9.

## Lessons

1. PD-M13-L01: Self-efficacy, the spotlight effect and impostor feelings (about 1 hour)
2. PD-M13-L02: Fear ladders: exposure step by step (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The self-efficacy builder, spotlight check and evidence file (PD-M13-L01).
- The fear ladder and exposure record (PD-M13-L02).

## Module project: your personal fear ladder, climbed halfway

1. Build a 10-step fear ladder for the fear that holds you back most (PD-M13-L02).
2. Over two to three weeks, climb at least the first five steps, with an exposure record for each attempt.
3. Keep your evidence file going (PD-M13-L01).
4. Write a half-page review: SUDS changes, predictions that were wrong, safety behaviours dropped, next three steps.

**Proof to record:** Your ladder, at least five exposure records and the half-page review.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- Confidence comes after action: I design small mastery steps.
- When I fear being judged: "People notice about half as much as I think."
- My fear ladder: next step is ______. I drop the safety behaviour ______.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ladder quality | Vague or too few steps | Ten steps but uneven | Ten specific, realistic steps with SUDS |
| Practice | Fewer than three attempts | Three or four attempts | Five or more attempts with repeats |
| Learning | No predictions recorded | Predictions without results | Predictions, results and lessons for each step |
| Safety behaviours | Not identified | Identified, still used | Identified and dropped step by step |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Write a five-step ladder and do step 1 twice.
- Add one item to your evidence file each week.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Self-efficacy | Belief you can do a specific task (Bandura). |
| Four sources of self-efficacy | Mastery, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion, physical/emotional states. |
| Spotlight effect | People notice us about half as much as we think (T-shirt study). |
| Impostor phenomenon | Capable people feeling like frauds; common, not a diagnosis. |
| Power posing status | Hormone and behaviour claims failed replication. |
| SUDS | Subjective Units of Distress, 0–100. |
| Safety behaviour | Something done to feel safe that keeps fear alive (scripts, avoiding eye contact). |
| Inhibitory learning | Exposure works by testing predictions and creating new learning. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Collecting confidence quotes instead of doing steps.** Small successful actions build confidence; quotes don't.
- **Comparing your step 2 with someone else's step 10.** Compare with your own last attempt.
- **Pushing someone else up their ladder.** Exposure must be chosen, not forced.

sections.title: PD-M13-L01: Self-efficacy, the spotlight effect and impostor feelings
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain where confidence comes from (self-efficacy), use the spotlight effect to worry less about being judged, and handle impostor feelings, without relying on power poses. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes of tasks).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Confidence grows mainly from doing things successfully, step by step; other people notice us far less than we think; and feeling like a fraud is common and says little about your real ability.

## The science

**Self-efficacy.** Albert Bandura (1977) defined **self-efficacy** as your belief that you can carry out a specific task, such as giving a talk, solving percentage problems or asking for a discount. It is specific, not general: you can have high self-efficacy for cooking and low for public speaking. Bandura identified four sources, in order of strength:
1. **Mastery experiences:** succeeding at the task, especially after effort. The strongest source.
2. **Vicarious experiences:** seeing someone similar to you succeed ("If Anu from my village can, so can I").
3. **Verbal persuasion:** encouragement from people you trust (weaker on its own; it works when followed by success).
4. **Physical and emotional states:** how you read your racing heart (as fear, or as readiness).

Self-efficacy is one of the best-supported ideas in psychology: it predicts effort, persistence and performance across education, health and work. The practical lesson: **build confidence by designing small successes**, not by waiting to feel confident first.

**The spotlight effect.** In a study by Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky (2000), students were asked to wear an embarrassing T-shirt (with a picture of the singer Barry Manilow) into a room of peers. Wearers estimated that about **half** the room would notice; in fact, about **a quarter** did, roughly half as many as they expected ([summary of the figures](https://atticusli.com/replication-crisis/spotlight-effect/); [background](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotlight_effect)). Later studies found the same direction for bad hair days, mistakes in a group discussion and even for good performances. Most people are too busy thinking about themselves to watch you closely.

**Impostor feelings.** Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes (1978) described the "impostor phenomenon": capable people who feel like frauds and fear being found out. It is **not a mental illness** or a formal diagnosis. A 2020 review by Dena Bravata and colleagues found it reported very widely, though estimates vary enormously depending on how it is measured. It often comes with perfectionism and with being the first in a family to enter a field (common for first-generation government employees or graduates). Useful responses: talk about it (you will find others feel it too), keep a record of evidence of competence, and redefine mistakes as part of learning.

**What about power posing?** As you saw in PD-M02-L02, the claim that two minutes of a "power pose" changes hormones and risk-taking failed larger replications. A small effect on *feeling* powerful may exist, and the authors still disagree about it. Standing upright and breathing slowly before a talk does no harm; just don't expect it to transform you. Mastery experiences do the real work.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-efficacy predicts effort and performance | **Strong** | Decades of research across education, health and work. |
| Mastery experiences are the strongest source of self-efficacy | **Strong** | Consistent with many studies and meta-analyses. |
| Spotlight effect: people overestimate how much they are noticed | **Moderate** | The direction replicates across studies; the size varies. |
| Impostor feelings are common, especially among high achievers and newcomers to a field | **Moderate** | Widely reported; prevalence estimates vary greatly with measurement. |
| Power posing changes hormones or behaviour | **Failed to replicate or myth** | Not supported by larger replications. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Ashiq has been asked to explain the new bus timetable at the residents' association meeting. He feels sure everyone will notice his shaking hands and his "village English" mixed with Malayalam.

He uses **mastery experiences** in small steps: he explains the timetable to his mother, then to two neighbours, then records himself on his phone. Each success raises his rating of "I can explain this clearly" from 3/10 to 7/10. He watches a video of a friend from his school speaking at a panchayat meeting (**vicarious experience**). On the day, his heart races; he tells himself "my body is getting ready" (**physical state**). He speaks for four minutes, mostly in Malayalam with some English terms.

Afterwards he asks two people, "Did you notice I was nervous?" Both say no; one only remembers that the 7:40 bus had moved to 7:55 (**spotlight effect**). When his brother calls him "the new president", Ashiq feels like an impostor. He writes down three pieces of evidence that he explained the timetable well, and smiles.

## How to use it

**Build self-efficacy deliberately:**
1. Pick one skill you want confidence in (speaking, maths, talking to strangers).
2. Rate your confidence 0–10 for a specific task: "explain the timetable for 3 minutes".
3. Design three small mastery steps, from easy to harder. Do them.
4. Find a similar person who has done it (a video, a friend) and watch them.
5. Re-rate after each step.

**Use the spotlight effect:** before something embarrassing, say "Most people will notice half as much as I fear, and forget it sooner." Afterwards, check by asking one person.

**Impostor feelings:** keep an **evidence file**: a note with every compliment, good result and solved problem. Read it when you feel like a fraud. Say the feeling aloud to a friend; you will often hear "Me too".

**With others:** give **specific** encouragement *after* a success ("You explained that clearly; the example helped"), and share your own nervous moments. That builds others' self-efficacy far more than "You'll be fine!"

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, chapter 10: Motivation and Emotion (10.1 and 10.4)](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/10-introduction) | Re-read the section on self-efficacy in 10.1 | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Wikipedia: Spotlight effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotlight_effect) | Read the article | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Wikipedia: Power posing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_posing) | Re-read the replication section so you can explain it to others | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Choose one confidence skill and one specific task. Rate your confidence 0–10.
2. Design and do three mastery steps this week, re-rating after each.
3. After one mildly embarrassing moment, ask one person whether they noticed. Write what they said.
4. Start an evidence file with at least five entries.

**Proof to record:** Your confidence ratings before and after three mastery steps, one spotlight check, and an evidence file with five entries.

## Template: Confidence builder

```
SELF-EFFICACY BUILDER          Skill: ______________________
Task: ______________________   Confidence now (0-10): ___
Mastery steps (easy -> harder):          Done   Confidence after
1. ______________________________        [ ]    ___
2. ______________________________        [ ]    ___
3. ______________________________        [ ]    ___
Someone like me who has done it: ______________
SPOTLIGHT CHECK: I feared ___% would notice ______. I asked ______; they said ______.
EVIDENCE FILE (add whenever it happens)
Date | Evidence of competence (result, compliment, problem solved)
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Waiting to feel confident before acting.** Confidence follows successful action. Start with a step small enough to succeed.
- **Steps that are too big.** If a step fails badly, make the next one smaller.
- **Relying on power poses or affirmations.** They do little on their own. Mastery experiences do the work.
- **Telling impostor feelings to go away.** Name them, check the evidence file, carry on. They usually fade with experience.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. According to Bandura, what is the strongest source of self-efficacy?
    - A) Encouragement from others
    - B) Mastery experiences: succeeding at the task
    - C) Power poses
    - D) Watching motivational videos
2. In the T-shirt study, how many people noticed compared with what wearers predicted?
    - A) Roughly half as many
    - B) Exactly as many
    - C) Twice as many
    - D) Nobody noticed at all
3. Which statement about impostor feelings is accurate?
    - A) They are common, not a diagnosis, and often fade with experience and evidence
    - B) Only beginners feel them
    - C) They are a mental illness
    - D) They mean you really are a fraud
4. What is the honest status of power posing?
    - A) Proven harmful
    - B) Never studied
    - C) Hormone and behaviour effects failed replication; a small effect on feeling powerful is debated
    - D) Proven to raise testosterone

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the spotlight-effect article
- **Action:** do three mastery steps for one skill with ratings, one spotlight check and start an evidence file. It is done when your proof is saved: your confidence ratings before and after three mastery steps, one spotlight check, and an evidence file with five entries.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Doing it successfully builds belief most strongly.
2. **A.** About a quarter noticed versus about half predicted.
3. **A.** Common among capable people and newcomers to a field.
4. **C.** Larger studies did not support the original claims.

sections.title: PD-M13-L02: Fear ladders: exposure step by step
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can build a personal fear ladder of 10 steps and climb the first steps using exposure principles, without safety behaviours. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes of planning plus practice).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Fears shrink when you face them step by step, staying with the discomfort long enough to learn that the feared outcome doesn't happen or is bearable; avoidance keeps fears alive.

## The science

**Exposure.** Exposure therapy is one of the best-supported treatments in psychology, especially for phobias, social anxiety, panic and obsessive-compulsive disorder. The idea is simple: avoiding what you fear brings short-term relief but teaches your brain that the situation is dangerous and that you couldn't have coped. **Facing it, gradually and repeatedly,** teaches the opposite.

**How it works.** Two explanations are used:
- **Habituation:** the fear response weakens with repeated, prolonged contact (like getting used to cold water).
- **Inhibitory learning:** Michelle Craske and colleagues argue that exposure works mainly by creating **new learning** ("I spoke and nobody laughed"; "I felt anxious and it passed") that competes with the old fear memory. On this view, what matters most is **testing your feared prediction**, not just waiting until the fear goes down.

**The fear ladder (exposure hierarchy).** You list feared situations from easiest to hardest and rate each with **SUDS** (Subjective Units of Distress, 0–100). Start with a step that causes some anxiety (around 30–40), repeat it until it feels manageable, then move up.

**Safety behaviours.** These are small things people do to feel safer that secretly keep the fear alive: avoiding eye contact, rehearsing every word, holding a phone as a shield, speaking very fast to finish, always taking a friend. Research by Paul Salkovskis and David Clark on social anxiety found that dropping safety behaviours during exposure made it work better. Some researchers find that limited, early use of safety aids does little harm, but the general advice is to reduce them.

**Kerala-friendly ladders** can cover speaking (in class, at a function, in English), social situations (talking to strangers, going alone to a hotel), assertiveness (refusing a relative, returning a product) and performance (singing at a family event). **This module is for everyday fears.** If fear is severe (panic attacks, avoiding leaving home, avoiding all social contact) or linked to trauma, work with a professional; Tele-MANAS (14416) can guide you.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exposure therapy for phobias, social anxiety and panic | **Strong** | Many trials and reviews; a core part of CBT for anxiety. |
| Inhibitory learning (testing predictions) as a mechanism | **Moderate** | Supported by lab and clinical research; still being refined. |
| Dropping safety behaviours improves exposure | **Moderate** | Supported in social anxiety studies; some debate about limited early use. |
| Self-directed graded exposure for everyday fears | **Moderate** | Guided self-help shows benefits; severe fears need professional support. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Anu fears speaking English in front of others. She builds a fear ladder:

| Step | Situation | SUDS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Record a 1-minute English voice note for myself | 20 |
| 2 | Send a 1-minute English voice note to a friend | 35 |
| 3 | Ask a question in English at the bank counter | 40 |
| 4 | Speak 2 minutes in English in my study group | 50 |
| 5 | Order food in English at a restaurant in Kozhikode city | 55 |
| 6 | Make an English phone call to a company helpline | 60 |
| 7 | Introduce myself in English to a stranger at a library event | 70 |
| 8 | Record and post a 1-minute English video on my status | 75 |
| 9 | Give a 3-minute English talk at a Toastmasters guest visit | 85 |
| 10 | Give a 5-minute English talk to a real audience | 95 |

She starts at step 2, repeats it three times in a week until it drops to 15, then moves to step 3. Her safety behaviour is writing out every sentence first; she drops it from step 4. Her prediction before step 4: "I'll freeze and people will look away." Result: she paused twice, one person nodded, nobody looked away. She writes: "Pauses feel long to me, not to them."

## How to use it

**Build your fear ladder (30 minutes):**
1. Choose one fear area (speaking, strangers, saying no, being seen).
2. List 10 situations from easy (SUDS 10–20) to very hard (SUDS 90–100). Make them specific and realistic in your life.
3. Name your safety behaviours for this fear.

**Climb it:**
1. Before each step, write your **feared prediction** ("I will…", "They will…") and rate SUDS.
2. Do the step **without safety behaviours**, and stay in the situation until you've tested the prediction (don't escape early).
3. Afterwards, write what actually happened and rate SUDS again.
4. Repeat a step until SUDS drops by about half or it feels manageable, then move up.
5. Two or three steps a week is a good pace. A setback means: go back one step, not to zero.

**Connection to the next module:** rejection therapy (Module 14) is a fear ladder for the fear of hearing "no".

**With others:** you can support a friend's ladder by being there, but don't do the step for them and don't reassure them over and over (reassurance can become a safety behaviour). Ask, "What did you predict, and what happened?"

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 14.4 Regulation of Stress](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/14-4-regulation-of-stress) | Re-read the section on coping and control (why avoidance maintains stress) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Noba Project: free psychology modules and textbooks (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://nobaproject.com/) | Search for the module "Anxiety and Related Disorders" and read the treatment section on exposure | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Gummere translation (Standard Ebooks; free in the USA, check your local law)](https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/seneca/moral-letters-to-lucilius/richard-m-gummere) | Read Letter 13 ("On Groundless Fears"): "we suffer more often in imagination than in reality" | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write a 10-step fear ladder for one fear area, with SUDS ratings and your safety behaviours.
2. Do the first two or three steps this week, each with a written prediction, the result and SUDS before and after.
3. Repeat at least one step until its SUDS drops by about half.
4. Write one sentence about what you learned that your fear did not tell you.

**Proof to record:** Your 10-step ladder with SUDS and safety behaviours, at least three exposure records (prediction, result, SUDS before and after) and your learning sentence.

## Template: Fear ladder and exposure record

```
FEAR LADDER                  Fear area: ______________________
Step | Situation (specific) | SUDS (0-100) | Done (dates)
1  | ______________________________ | __ | ______
...
10 | ______________________________ | __ | ______
My safety behaviours (drop them): ______  ______  ______
EXPOSURE RECORD
Date | Step | Feared prediction | SUDS before | What actually happened | SUDS after | Learned
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Starting too high.** Begin with a step around SUDS 30–40. Too hard too soon leads to escape and stronger fear.
- **Escaping as soon as anxiety rises.** Stay long enough to test the prediction.
- **Keeping hidden safety behaviours.** Scripts, avoiding eye contact, rushing: drop them step by step.
- **Treating severe fears alone.** Panic attacks, trauma-related fear or avoiding daily life need professional support.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why does avoiding a feared situation keep the fear alive?
    - A) Relief teaches the brain the situation is dangerous and you couldn't have coped
    - B) Fear has nothing to do with avoidance
    - C) Avoidance cures fear
    - D) Because you forget the situation
2. According to the inhibitory-learning view, what matters most in exposure?
    - A) Doing the hardest step first
    - B) Testing your feared prediction and learning it doesn't happen or is bearable
    - C) Reassurance from others
    - D) Feeling no anxiety at all
3. Which is a safety behaviour in public speaking?
    - A) Breathing slowly
    - B) Making eye contact
    - C) Practising beforehand
    - D) Reading a fully written script so you never look up
4. When should you move up the ladder?
    - A) Only when you feel no fear at all
    - B) When the current step's distress has dropped by about half or feels manageable
    - C) After a month on each step
    - D) Immediately after the first try

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and Seneca's Letter 13
- **Action:** build a 10-step fear ladder and climb the first steps with prediction records. It is done when your proof is saved: your 10-step ladder with SUDS and safety behaviours, at least three exposure records (prediction, result, SUDS before and after) and your learning sentence.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Avoidance blocks the new learning that exposure provides.
2. **B.** New learning competes with the old fear memory.
3. **D.** It feels safer but stops you learning you can cope without it.
4. **B.** Repeat until manageable, then climb.

sections.title: Module 14: Rejection therapy
sections.summary: A full rejection-therapy programme: the idea and the psychology (exposure and desensitisation), Jason Comely's original game and Jia Jiang's 100 days, strict safety and respect rules, a 33-step ladder realistic for Kerala, a 30-day challenge with a daily log, five comfort-zone challenges, and how the courage transfers to sales, networking and public speaking.
sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

Fear of rejection quietly decides a lot: the tuition you never offered, the expert you never messaged, the raise you never asked for, the question you never asked in class. This module turns that fear into a skill you practise daily for a month.

It is built on exposure, one of the best-supported methods in psychology, but rejection therapy itself has not been tested in trials, so you will measure your own results. **The rules are part of the method:** every request must be legal, safe, respectful and low-stakes; every no is accepted at once; nothing romantic or personal; local culture respected.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain rejection therapy, its origins and the honest evidence behind it.
- Apply the safety and respect rules to every request.
- Choose and adapt requests from a 33-step ladder.
- Complete a 30-day rejection challenge with a daily log and numbers.
- Complete five comfort-zone challenges and connect the skill to sales, networking and speaking.

## Time

About 4 hours 15 minutes in total: 3 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 9–10, with the module project due in week 10.

## Lessons

1. PD-M14-L01: The idea and the psychology behind it (about 1 hour)
2. PD-M14-L02: The rules and the 30-step ladder (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. PD-M14-L03: The 30-day challenge, comfort-zone challenges and where it pays off (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The rejection history and feared prediction (PD-M14-L01).
- The rules, the 33-step ladder and the request planner (PD-M14-L02).
- The 30-day rejection log with comfort-zone challenges (PD-M14-L03).

## Module project: the 30-day rejection challenge

1. Plan with the rules and the ladder (PD-M14-L02).
2. Run the 30-day challenge and the five comfort-zone challenges (PD-M14-L03).
3. Make at least three requests linked to a real goal (income, networking, speaking).
4. Write a one-page report: numbers, the most surprising yes, the most useful no, and how you will keep asking.

**Proof to record:** Your 30-day log, the comfort-zone entries and the one-page report.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- I ask. A no is information: not now, not this, not me. I accept it politely and once.
- Every request is legal, safe, respectful, low-stakes and easy to refuse.
- I make one real, goal-linked ask every week.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Consistency | Fewer than 15 requests | 15 to 24 requests | 25 to 30 requests over the month |
| Climbing | Stayed at Level 1 | Reached Level 3 | Reached Level 4 or 5 with goal-linked requests |
| Respect | Any rule broken | Rules followed but some awkward choices | Every request passed the rules check |
| Learning | No numbers | Some numbers | Fear before and after, yes-rate and lessons over four weeks |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Do 10 requests over 30 days (one every three days), still logged.
- Do two of the five comfort-zone challenges.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Who created Rejection Therapy? | Jason Comely; Jia Jiang made it famous with 100 days of rejection. |
| Psychological principle | Exposure: facing small rejections gradually so the fear shrinks. |
| Evidence status | No trials of the method itself; indirect support from exposure and asking research. |
| Core rule after a no | "No problem, thank you!" and leave. Never ask twice. |
| Requests never allowed | Illegal, unsafe, deceptive, pressuring, romantic or personal-space requests. |
| Daily log fields | Request, fear before (0–10), result, fear after, lesson. |
| Why aim for a no? | Asking becomes the success, so you keep practising. |
| Five comfort-zone challenges | New person daily, speak up in a group, post a video, eat alone, digital-detox day. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Turning it into social-media content.** Filming people without consent breaks the rules and their trust.
- **Pushing for yes.** That is pressure, not practice.
- **Never connecting it to real goals.** Make some requests count: a pitch, an expert, a talk.

sections.title: PD-M14-L01: The idea and the psychology behind it
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can explain what rejection therapy is, where it came from, why it may work (exposure and desensitisation), and what the evidence does and does not show. **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes including the TED talk).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Fear of rejection shrinks when you deliberately collect small, safe "no"s; each one teaches your brain that rejection is survivable and often not about you.

## The science

**The original game.** Rejection Therapy was created by **Jason Comely**, a Canadian who, after a painful break-up, found himself avoiding people. He set himself a rule: get rejected by someone every day. He turned it into a self-help game, with optional suggestion cards, in which the "win" is being rejected, not getting a yes ([background](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rejection_therapy)).

**Jia Jiang's 100 days.** In 2012, Jia Jiang, a Chinese-born entrepreneur in the United States, discovered the game after an investor rejected his startup and he realised how much fear of rejection controlled him. He set himself **100 days of rejection** and filmed them: asking a stranger to lend him $100, asking for a "burger refill", asking to play football in a stranger's back garden, and, most famously, asking a Krispy Kreme doughnut shop to make doughnuts linked like the Olympic rings, which the employee did. His TEDx talk (2015) describes what he learned: people say yes far more often than we fear; asking "Why?" after a no often opens a conversation; and rejection says as much about the other person's situation as about you. He later bought the Rejection Therapy brand (2016) ([TED talk](https://www.ted.com/talks/jia_jiang_what_i_learned_from_100_days_of_rejection)).

**The psychology: exposure and desensitisation.** Rejection therapy is a **fear ladder for rejection** (PD-M13-L02). Fear of rejection makes us avoid asking; avoidance keeps the fear strong. Deliberately seeking small rejections:
1. **Tests the feared prediction** ("If they say no, I'll be humiliated") and shows it is wrong or bearable (inhibitory learning).
2. **Reduces the fear response** through repeated contact (habituation).
3. **Builds self-efficacy** for asking (mastery experiences, PD-M13-L01).
4. **Corrects the spotlight effect:** most people forget your request within minutes.

**What the evidence shows, honestly.** There are **no controlled clinical trials of rejection therapy itself.** Its support is **indirect**: exposure therapy has strong evidence for social anxiety, and studies of asking show people underestimate how often others will say yes. In experiments by Francis Flynn and Vanessa Lake (2008), people asking strangers for favours (filling in a questionnaire, borrowing a phone) predicted they would need to ask about twice as many people as they actually did to get the yeses they needed. So treat rejection therapy as a **practical tool built on strong principles**, not a proven treatment.

**What it is not.** It is not about pushing people until they give in, tricking them, or collecting stunts for social media. Done that way, it becomes harassment. The rules in PD-M14-L02 are part of the method.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exposure reduces social fears | **Strong** | Well-established for social anxiety as part of CBT. |
| People underestimate how often others say yes to requests | **Moderate** | Several experiments by Flynn, Lake, Bohns and colleagues. |
| Rejection therapy as a specific method | **Practical tool** | No controlled trials; a practical application of exposure principles. |
| Jia Jiang's experience as evidence | **Mixed or weak** | One person's story: inspiring, but not research. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Ashiq watches Jia Jiang's talk and laughs at the doughnut story, then feels the fear in his own stomach: he has wanted to offer tuition to students in his ward for a year, but cannot bring himself to ask parents. "What if they say no? What if they tell others I'm desperate?"

He writes his feared prediction: "If I ask and they say no, I'll feel humiliated for days, and people will gossip." Then he notices that he has been rejected many times already (by PSC short lists, by a girl in college, by a job interview) and survived each time. He also realises his fear is not of asking a shopkeeper for the time; it is of **asking for something that matters to him**. That tells him where his ladder should end.

He decides to start the challenge the following Monday (a fresh start), with simple requests at shops, and to aim, by day 30, at asking three parents about tuition.

## How to use it

**Why "aim for a no" works:** if your goal is a yes, every no is a failure and you will avoid asking. If your goal is to **ask**, every request, yes or no, is a success. This takes the pressure off and keeps you practising.

**Three things to try after a no** (from Jiang's experience, used politely and only once):
1. **Thank them** sincerely.
2. If it feels right, **ask "Could I ask why?"** with curiosity, not argument. You often learn something useful ("We can't show the kitchen during lunch rush; come at 4").
3. **Accept and leave.** No second ask.

**Rejection is information, not a verdict.** A no can mean: not now, not this way, not me (the person can't), or not interested. Only rarely does it mean "not you as a person".

**With others:** notice how you say no. A kind, clear no ("I can't, but thanks for asking") is a gift to people practising courage. You will learn to say no well in PD-M26-L02.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [TED: Jia Jiang, "What I learned from 100 days of rejection" (about 15 minutes)](https://www.ted.com/talks/jia_jiang_what_i_learned_from_100_days_of_rejection) | Watch the whole talk; write down his three lessons | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Wikipedia: Rejection therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rejection_therapy) | Read the article: origin, Jiang's project and how it is described | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, chapter 12: Social Psychology (12.1 to 12.7)](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-introduction) | Read 12.4 Conformity, Compliance, and Obedience, the part on compliance (why people say yes to requests) | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Watch Jia Jiang's talk and write his three main lessons in your own words.
2. Write your rejection history: five times you were rejected, how you felt then, and how you feel about each now.
3. Write your main feared prediction about rejection and the request you most avoid making.
4. Do one Level 1 request from the ladder in PD-M14-L02 (for example, ask a shopkeeper which brand they recommend). Write what happened.

**Proof to record:** Jiang's three lessons, your five-item rejection history, your feared prediction, and one Level 1 request with its result.

## Template: Rejection history and prediction

```
REJECTION HISTORY
When | What I asked or wanted | How I felt then (0-10) | How I feel now (0-10) | What I learned
1. ______ | ______ | __ | __ | ______
...
MY FEARED PREDICTION: "If I ask ______ and they say no, then ______."
The request I most avoid making: ______________________
Jiang's three lessons (my words): 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Treating it as a prank or content stunt.** The aim is your courage, not their discomfort or your followers.
- **Thinking it is proven therapy.** It is a practical tool built on exposure principles; there are no trials of it as such.
- **Starting with the request that matters most.** Start at Level 1 and climb.
- **Taking every no personally.** Most no's are about timing, rules or the other person's situation.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Who created the Rejection Therapy game?
    - A) Albert Bandura
    - B) Dale Carnegie
    - C) Jason Comely
    - D) Jia Jiang
2. What is the main psychological principle behind rejection therapy?
    - A) Positive affirmations
    - B) Ego depletion
    - C) Exposure: facing a feared situation gradually so the fear shrinks
    - D) Hypnosis
3. What did Flynn and Lake find about asking strangers for favours?
    - A) People predicted needing about twice as many asks as they actually did to get yeses
    - B) Asking makes people angry
    - C) People overestimate how often others say yes
    - D) Strangers almost never help
4. What is the honest evidence status of rejection therapy?
    - A) Proven by many clinical trials
    - B) No controlled trials; indirect support from exposure and asking research
    - C) Evidence comes only from animals
    - D) Shown to be harmful

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and watch Jia Jiang's TED talk
- **Action:** write your rejection history and feared prediction, and make one Level 1 request. It is done when your proof is saved: jiang's three lessons, your five-item rejection history, your feared prediction, and one Level 1 request with its result.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Comely created it; Jiang made it famous with 100 days of rejection.
2. **C.** It is a fear ladder for rejection.
3. **A.** We underestimate others' willingness to help.
4. **B.** It is a practical tool, not a tested treatment.

sections.title: PD-M14-L02: The rules and the 30-step ladder
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can apply the safety and respect rules to every request and choose requests from a 33-step ladder realistic for Kerala. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes of planning).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Courage practice is only good if it is good for the other person too: every request must be legal, safe, respectful and low-stakes, and every "no" must be accepted at once.

## The science

**Why the rules are part of the method.** Exposure works when the feared situation is faced **in a way that is safe**. For rejection, that means two kinds of safety:

1. **Safety for the other person.** A request that makes someone feel pressured, tricked, watched or unsafe is not courage practice; it is harassment. Research on compliance shows that people often find it **hard to say no** to direct requests. Vanessa Bohns's studies found that people agreed to unethical or uncomfortable requests (such as vandalising a library book) far more often than the askers predicted, because refusing feels awkward. That means the asker holds more power than they feel, and must use it carefully: **make it easy to say no.**
2. **Safety for you.** Requests that could lead to conflict, legal trouble or danger (asking to enter private property, approaching people at night in isolated places, anything with money transfers or personal data) teach the wrong lesson and can hurt you.

**Low-stakes means:** saying no costs them nothing, saying yes costs them very little, and nothing bad happens to either of you whatever the answer.

**Culture.** What is a normal request differs by place. In Kerala, bargaining is normal in markets and many small shops but not in supermarkets, pharmacies or hospitals; asking strangers for directions is normal; approaching women you don't know with unusual requests can cause real fear; religious places have their own norms; and gossip travels fast in small towns. Choose settings where requests are expected (shops, counters, offices, events) and behave as a polite customer or visitor would.

**The rules (all must be true for every request):**
- Every request must be **legal, safe, respectful and low-stakes**.
- **Accept "no" immediately and politely.** Say "No problem, thank you!" and leave. Never ask twice, argue or bargain after a no.
- **Never pressure, deceive or harass anyone.** No fake stories, no pretending to be someone else, no filming people without their permission.
- **Never make requests that could make someone feel unsafe,** including **romantic or personal-space requests** (no asking for numbers, dates, hugs, touching, following someone, or approaching people who are alone in isolated places).
- **Respect local culture:** dress, time of day, religious places and customs, and who you approach (in many places in Kerala, approaching women you don't know with unusual requests can cause real discomfort; choose shops, counters, offices and public settings where requests are normal).
- **Low-stakes for them:** saying no must cost them nothing and saying yes must cost them very little (a minute, a small favour, a small discount they can refuse).
- **Stop if someone seems uncomfortable,** even if they said yes.

**Before every request, run the rules check** in the rejection log (PD-M14-L03). If any box is not ticked, choose another request.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| People find it hard to refuse direct requests | **Moderate** | Studies by Bohns and others show askers underestimate compliance. |
| Exposure should be safe and chosen | **Strong** | A basic principle of exposure therapy. |
| A graded ladder from easy to hard | **Strong** | Graded exposure is standard practice for anxiety. |
| The specific 33-step ladder | **Practical tool** | Written for this course; adjust it to your town. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Sreeja plans her first week. She crosses out "ask a stranger for their phone to make a call": it could worry people about theft or scams. She keeps "ask the bakery to taste a new snack before buying" and "ask the librarian for a recommendation".

Her cousin suggests a "funny" request: asking a girl at the bus stop to dance. Sreeja says no: it is a personal and romantic-type request, it could make the girl feel unsafe, and it would break two rules. Instead, she adds "ask an older man at the bus stop where to find a good tailor", which is normal, public and easy to refuse.

On day 3, she asks a textile shop for a discount on a churidar set. The owner says no, fixed price. She says, "No problem, thank you!" and leaves. Her fear before was 6/10; after, 3/10. Lesson: "A fixed-price shop isn't rejecting me; it's their rule."

## How to use it

**The 33-step ladder (Level 1 easiest, Level 5 hardest).** Use it as a menu. Swap in requests that fit your town, as long as they pass the rules check.

| Level | Request | Where | Builds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Ask a stranger for the time or directions, even if you know | Bus stand, junction | The easiest first contact |
| 1 | Ask a shopkeeper which brand of a product they recommend and why | Grocery or hardware shop | Asking for opinions |
| 1 | Ask a tea-shop owner for a recommendation of the best local snack | Tea shop | Starting small talk |
| 1 | Ask a librarian to recommend a book on a topic you like | Public or panchayat library | Asking experts |
| 2 | Ask for a small discount on a purchase ("Can you do a little better on the price?") | Textile or vegetable shop | Price conversations |
| 2 | Ask a stranger at a bus stop for a recommendation (a good tailor, a mechanic) | Bus stop | Talking to strangers |
| 2 | Ask a restaurant if you can have a dish that is not on the menu, or a half portion | Hotel or restaurant | Unusual but reasonable requests |
| 2 | Ask a shop for a free sample or to taste before buying | Bakery, spice or sweet shop | Asking for something free |
| 2 | Return or exchange an item politely, with your reason | Any shop | Standing up for yourself |
| 3 | Ask a restaurant if you can see the kitchen | Restaurant (quiet hours) | A bolder request |
| 3 | Ask a bank or post office clerk to explain a scheme in detail | Bank, post office | Taking up people's time politely |
| 3 | Ask a stranger to take a photo of you at a public place | Beach, park, tourist spot | Asking help from strangers |
| 3 | Ask a shop to give you a carry bag free or a little extra | Market | Small favours |
| 3 | Ask a bookshop if you can sit and read for 15 minutes | Bookshop | Testing flexible rules |
| 3 | Ask for a "loyal customer" price at a shop you use often | Regular shop | Negotiation through relationship |
| 3 | Ask a senior aspirant or ex-PSC rank holder for one study tip | Library, coaching centre, online group | Asking for advice |
| 4 | Ask an autorickshaw driver for a lower fare on a regular route (before getting in) | Auto stand | Negotiating in public |
| 4 | Ask a local business owner what their biggest problem is (research, no pitch) | Small shop | Customer discovery |
| 4 | Ask an expert (doctor, teacher, officer, engineer) for 10 minutes of career advice | By message or in person, by appointment | Networking |
| 4 | Ask three people for honest feedback on your English or Malayalam speaking | Friends, relatives, study group | Asking for feedback |
| 4 | Ask a stranger at an event what they do and how they got into it | Library event, seminar, wedding | Networking conversations |
| 4 | Ask a hotel if you could use their wifi or a table to study for an hour for the price of a tea | Hotel, cafe | Creative requests |
| 4 | Ask a school or college if you can attend one free public lecture or seminar | College office | Getting access |
| 5 | Ask a shop owner if you can put up a small notice for your tuition or service | Shop, library notice board | Selling yourself |
| 5 | Pitch a service to a local business (posters, social media posts, accounts help, tuition for their child) | Small business | Real sales |
| 5 | Ask your employer or a client for a raise, a better rate or a better shift | Workplace | High-value asks |
| 5 | Ask a local club or library if you can give a 5-minute talk | Club, library, residents' association | Public speaking |
| 5 | Ask a respected local person to mentor you for one hour a month | By appointment | Mentorship |
| 5 | Ask a newspaper, local channel or community page if they would feature a community event you help with | Office or message | Media and outreach |
| 5 | Ask a stranger to join you in a small good act (picking up litter, donating blood together) | Public place | Leading others |
| 5 | Ask five people in a row for something unusual but harmless (e.g. to recommend a book, write it on paper and sign it) | Market or event | Volume and resilience |
| 5 | Ask a business for a paid trial task or a small contract | Small business, startup, office | Turning rejection skills into income |
| 5 | Ask an audience for questions at the end of your talk | Your talk | Inviting judgement |

**How to choose each day:**
- Week 1: Levels 1–2. Week 2: Levels 2–3. Week 3: Levels 3–4. Week 4: Levels 4–5.
- Repeat a level until fear before a request is about 3/10 or less, then move up.
- Mix in requests linked to your goals: speaking (Level 5 talk), networking (expert advice), income (pitching a service).

**Phrasing that keeps it easy to say no:**
- "Would it be possible to…? It's completely fine if not."
- "I'm practising asking for things; would you mind if…?" (honest, and people often warm to it).
- "Can you do a little better on the price? If not, that's fine."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, chapter 12: Social Psychology (12.1 to 12.7)](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-introduction) | Re-read 12.4 on compliance techniques (foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face) so you can recognise them and not misuse them | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [TED: Jia Jiang, "What I learned from 100 days of rejection" (about 15 minutes)](https://www.ted.com/talks/jia_jiang_what_i_learned_from_100_days_of_rejection) | Re-watch the section on asking "why" after a no | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Copy the rules into your rejection log note.
2. Go through the 33-step ladder: cross out any request that doesn't fit your town or culture and add at least three of your own that pass the rules check.
3. Plan your first seven requests (Levels 1–2), with day, place and exact words.
4. Show your plan to one trusted person and ask: "Would any of these make someone uncomfortable?" Adjust.

**Proof to record:** Your rules note, your edited ladder (with three of your own requests), the seven-day plan with exact words, and the trusted person's comment.

## Template: Request planner

```
REQUEST PLANNER (week ___)
Day | Level | Request (exact words) | Where | Rules check (legal / safe / respectful / low-stakes / easy no / not romantic or personal / fits culture) | Fear prediction (0-10)
1 | __ | "______________________" | ______ | [ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ] | __
...
Easy-no phrases: "It's completely fine if not." "If not, no problem."
After a no: "No problem, thank you!" -> leave. Never ask twice.
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Choosing requests that embarrass the other person.** The discomfort should be yours (asking), not theirs (being put on the spot).
- **Asking again after a no, or arguing.** That turns practice into pressure. One ask, accept, leave.
- **Requests involving money transfers, phones or personal data.** They trigger scam fears and can harm both of you. Avoid them.
- **Ignoring local norms.** Bargaining in a pharmacy or making requests at a place of worship can offend. Choose normal settings.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which request breaks the rules?
    - A) Asking a shopkeeper for a small discount
    - B) Asking a woman you don't know at a bus stop for her phone number
    - C) Asking a librarian for a recommendation
    - D) Asking a restaurant for a half portion
2. What should you do after a "no"?
    - A) Say "No problem, thank you!" and leave
    - B) Ask their manager
    - C) Ask again more firmly
    - D) Explain why they are wrong
3. Why must requests be easy to refuse?
    - A) It doesn't matter
    - B) Because the law says so
    - C) People often find it hard to say no, so the asker must make refusal easy
    - D) To get more yeses
4. When should you move up a level?
    - A) Only after 30 days
    - B) After every request
    - C) When someone says yes
    - D) When your fear before a request is about 3/10 or less

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the rules, and edit the ladder for your town
- **Action:** write your rules note, edit the ladder, and plan seven requests with exact words, checked by a trusted person. It is done when your proof is saved: your rules note, your edited ladder (with three of your own requests), the seven-day plan with exact words, and the trusted person's comment.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Romantic or personal requests can make people feel unsafe.
2. **A.** Accept every no immediately and politely.
3. **C.** Askers hold more power than they feel (Bohns).
4. **D.** Graded exposure: repeat until manageable, then climb.

sections.title: PD-M14-L03: The 30-day challenge, comfort-zone challenges and where it pays off
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can run a 30-day rejection challenge with a daily log, add five comfort-zone challenges, and use the skill in sales, networking and public speaking. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 5 to 15 minutes a day for 30 days).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Thirty days of small, safe requests turn asking into a habit; the same courage then transfers to selling, networking and speaking in public.

## The science

**Why 30 days?** Thirty days is not a magic number; it is long enough to climb a ladder from easy to hard requests, to see your fear ratings fall, and to make asking feel normal. Habit research suggests automaticity takes longer (a median of about 66 days, PD-M08-L02), so treat day 30 as the end of the training phase, not the end of asking.

**What to measure.** The daily log records five things: **the request, fear before (0–10), the result, fear after (0–10) and the lesson.** Over 30 days you should see (a) fear before falling, (b) the gap between fear before and after (anticipation is usually worse than the event), and (c) your yes-rate: often **higher** than you expected, consistent with the research on underestimating compliance (PD-M14-L01).

**Transfer to real life:**
- **Sales:** most sales involve hearing no many times. Salespeople who treat a no as information ("not now", "not this", "not me") keep going and learn. The [Entrepreneurship course sales module](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/entrepreneurship/ent-m07) (in the Practical Entrepreneurship course) teaches the process; rejection practice gives you the nerve.
- **Networking:** asking an expert for 10 minutes, introducing yourself at an event, following up after a meeting (Module 31).
- **Public speaking:** the core fear is being judged (Module 27). Requests in front of others are a stepping stone.

**Comfort-zone challenges.** Five extra challenges, done at least once each during the 30 days:
1. **Talk to one new person a day** for a week (a neighbour you've never spoken to, a shopkeeper, a person at the library).
2. **Speak up in a group** (study group, family meeting, residents' association): one question or one idea.
3. **Post a short video of yourself** (on your WhatsApp status or a private group first), talking for 30–60 seconds about something you learned.
4. **Eat alone at a restaurant** without your phone for the first 10 minutes.
5. **A digital-detox day:** a whole day with your phone off except for calls (prepared in Module 16).

These are exposures to being **seen**, **judged** or **alone with yourself**, the cousins of rejection.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anticipated distress is usually higher than actual distress in feared social situations | **Moderate** | Common finding in exposure and social anxiety research. |
| People underestimate others' willingness to say yes | **Moderate** | Several experiments on help-seeking. |
| Courage transfers from practice requests to sales and networking | **Practical tool** | Plausible from exposure and self-efficacy research; not directly tested. |
| Comfort-zone challenges | **Practical tool** | Practical exposures to being seen and judged. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Ashiq's 30-day log, selected days:

| Day | Request | Fear before | Result | Fear after | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Ask the tea-shop owner for his best snack | 3 | Yes, chatted 5 min | 1 | People like being asked for advice |
| 5 | Ask for ₹50 off a ₹650 shirt | 6 | No, fixed price | 3 | No about the rule, not me |
| 11 | Ask a hotel to show the kitchen | 7 | Yes, at 4 pm | 3 | Timing matters |
| 17 | Ask a retired headmaster for 10 minutes of career advice | 8 | Yes, gave 40 minutes | 2 | Experts enjoy helping |
| 23 | Ask a stationery shop to display my tuition notice | 7 | Yes | 3 | Locals support locals |
| 28 | Ask three parents about tuition for their children | 9 | 1 yes, 2 "next term" | 4 | "Not now" is not "no" |

His averages: fear before fell from about 6 in week 1 to about 4 in week 4; his yes-rate was about 55%. By day 30 he has one tuition student, earning ₹1,500 a month, and three parents who said "next term".

## How to use it

**The 30-day rejection challenge:**
1. **One request a day,** from your edited ladder, passing the rules check.
2. **Log it the same day:** request, fear before, result, fear after, lesson.
3. **Climb weekly:** Levels 1–2 → 2–3 → 3–4 → 4–5.
4. **Weekly numbers** (Sunday reflection): average fear before and after, yes-rate.
5. **Comfort-zone challenges:** do each of the five at least once during the 30 days, logged in the same note.
6. **Day 30:** compare week 1 and week 4, and write how you will use asking in sales, networking or speaking.

**Bad days:** a Level 1 request counts. Never miss twice.

**With others:** if a friend wants to join, do it together but make separate requests; never gang up on one person, and never film people without consent.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [TED: Jia Jiang, "What I learned from 100 days of rejection" (about 15 minutes)](https://www.ted.com/talks/jia_jiang_what_i_learned_from_100_days_of_rejection) | Re-watch the last five minutes (what he learned about himself) | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Loop Habit Tracker (free, open source, GPLv3)](https://loophabits.org/) | Add "Rejection request (one a day)" with a reminder | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task

1. Add the challenge to Loop and start on a fresh-start day.
2. Make and log one request a day for 30 days.
3. Complete each of the five comfort-zone challenges at least once and log them.
4. On day 30, write your numbers (fear before and after, yes-rate, week 1 versus week 4) and a paragraph on using this in sales, networking or speaking.

**Proof to record:** Your 30-day rejection log, five comfort-zone entries, your day-30 numbers and the transfer paragraph.

## Template: 30-day rejection log

```
30-DAY REJECTION LOG (one request a day)
Day | Date | Request (exact words) | Who / where | Fear before (0-10) | Result (yes / no / partial / counter-offer) | Fear after (0-10) | Lesson
1 | ____ | "_____________________" | ________ | __ | ________ | __ | ________
Rules check before every request (all must be YES):
[ ] Legal  [ ] Safe for both of us  [ ] Respectful  [ ] Low-stakes for them
[ ] Easy for them to say no  [ ] Not romantic, not about personal space or the body
[ ] Fits local culture (place, time, dress, language)
After a "no": say "No problem, thank you!" and leave. Never ask twice.
Weekly: average fear before ___ -> after ___ ; yes-rate ___% (expect 20-60%).

COMFORT-ZONE CHALLENGES (each at least once)
[ ] New person a day for a week   [ ] Speak up in a group   [ ] Post a 30-60 s video of myself
[ ] Eat alone at a restaurant (no phone for 10 min)   [ ] Digital-detox day
Date | Challenge | Fear before | What happened | Fear after | Lesson
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Collecting only yeses.** If everything is a yes, your requests are too easy. Aim for some no's.
- **Skipping the log.** The numbers show progress your feelings miss.
- **Breaking the rules for a bigger thrill.** The challenge only works if it is respectful and safe.
- **Stopping completely after day 30.** Keep one real ask a week tied to your goals.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What five things does the daily rejection log record?
    - A) Names and phone numbers
    - B) Only yes or no
    - C) Time, place, weather, mood, food
    - D) Request, fear before, result, fear after, lesson
2. What do people usually find about fear before and after a request?
    - A) Fear disappears on day 1
    - B) Fear before is usually higher than fear after
    - C) They are always the same
    - D) Fear after is always higher
3. How does rejection practice help in sales?
    - A) It guarantees sales
    - B) It teaches you to pressure customers
    - C) It helps you treat "no" as information and keep asking
    - D) It has no connection
4. Which is a comfort-zone challenge from this lesson?
    - A) Eating alone at a restaurant without your phone for 10 minutes
    - B) Asking strangers for money
    - C) Following people home
    - D) Arguing with a shopkeeper

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and set up the 30-day log
- **Action:** complete the 30-day rejection challenge and the five comfort-zone challenges, and write your day-30 numbers. It is done when your proof is saved: your 30-day rejection log, five comfort-zone entries, your day-30 numbers and the transfer paragraph.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** These show fear falling and lessons building.
2. **B.** Anticipation is usually worse than the event.
3. **C.** Sales involves many no's; courage keeps you learning.
4. **A.** It is an exposure to being seen alone.

sections.title: Module 15: Happiness science
sections.summary: Happiness science without the fluff: hedonic adaptation and the impact bias, social comparison, what the 2023 money-and-happiness collaboration found, experiences and spending on others, flow, meaning and relationships. You test one happiness change on yourself with data.
sections.content:
*Part B: Master yourself.*

## Overview

Most people chase happiness through the things that adapt fastest: purchases, status and comparison wins. Research points elsewhere: absorbing challenge, meaning, relationships, and enough money to be secure. This module gives you the evidence and lets you check it against your own life.

Yale's free course [The Science of Well-Being](https://www.coursera.org/learn/the-science-of-well-being) covers these topics in more depth if you want to go further.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain hedonic adaptation, the impact bias and social comparison.
- Summarise the current evidence on money and happiness honestly.
- Use savouring, experiences and spending on others.
- Describe the conditions for flow and design tasks for it.
- Run a two-week happiness experiment.

## Time

About 2 hours 45 minutes in total: 2 hours of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 10–11, with the module project due in week 11.

## Lessons

1. PD-M15-L01: Hedonic adaptation, social comparison, and money (about 1 hour)
2. PD-M15-L02: Meaning and flow (about 1 hour)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The happiness experiment sheet: impact-bias check, savouring, spending test, comparison audit (PD-M15-L01).
- The flow and meaning log with a two-week experiment (PD-M15-L02).

## Module project: a two-week happiness experiment

1. Use your flow and meaning log (PD-M15-L02) to choose one change.
2. Run the experiment: one baseline week and one change week with daily mood ratings.
3. Add one savouring practice and one act of spending on others during the change week.
4. Write a half-page report and add your keeper change to the Playbook.

**Proof to record:** The flow and meaning log, two weeks of mood ratings and your half-page report.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- Before big purchases: "How happy will this make me in 3 months?" I prefer experiences and giving.
- I compare with my own past, not others' highlights.
- My best flow activity: ______. My most meaningful weekly act: ______.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Understanding | Repeats "money can't buy happiness" | Knows some findings | Explains adaptation, comparison and the 2023 income finding accurately |
| Self-data | No log | Partial log | Full one-week log with ratings |
| Experiment | Not done | Done without a baseline | Baseline and change weeks compared |
| Application | No change kept | Vague plan | A specific change kept and added to the Playbook |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Savour one good moment a day for a week.
- Mute three accounts that make you feel worse.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Hedonic adaptation | We get used to most good and bad changes; incomplete for some. |
| Impact bias | Overestimating how strongly and how long events will affect us. |
| Money and happiness (2023) | Rises with income on average; plateau only for the least happy (US data). |
| Happiest spending | Experiences, spending on others, buying time. |
| Upward comparison | Comparing with people doing better: often lowers mood. |
| Flow conditions | High, balanced challenge and skill; clear goals; quick feedback. |
| PERMA | Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment. |
| Strongest everyday happiness predictor | Quality of close relationships. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Expecting one purchase or event to change your life.** Impact bias. Predict, then check.
- **Using happiness research to judge others' choices.** Apply it to your own life.
- **Ignoring the boring basics.** Sleep, exercise, relationships and financial security do much of the work.
