sections.title: PD-M17-L03: Cardio, mobility and the 30-day fitness challenge
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can plan safe cardio and mobility work, combine them with strength into a weekly plan, and complete a 30-day fitness challenge with a retest. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 20 to 30 minutes on five days a week for 30 days).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

A balanced week mixes brisk walking or walk-running for the heart, strength twice or three times, and a few minutes of mobility daily; consistency over 30 days matters more than any single hard session.

## The science

**Cardio (aerobic exercise).** Activities that raise your heart rate and breathing for several minutes strengthen the heart and lungs. **Moderate intensity** means you can talk but not sing (brisk walking, easy cycling). **Vigorous** means you can say only a few words (running, fast cycling, skipping). The WHO target is 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, or half that of vigorous. Walking is underrated: brisk walking is linked to substantial health benefits, and in a large 2023 meta-analysis, risk of early death kept falling as daily steps rose, starting from around 4,000 a day and levelling off around 8,000 to 10,000 for many adults. (The "10,000 steps" number started as a 1960s marketing slogan in Japan, though it happens to sit in a reasonable range.)

**Starting to run.** The free [NHS Couch to 5K](https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/get-active/get-running-with-couch-to-5k/) plan takes beginners from walking to running 5 km in nine weeks, with three sessions a week of alternating walking and running. It is a good structure if you want to run; if not, brisk walking with some uphill stretches is excellent.

**Interval training.** Short bursts of harder effort with recovery (for example, 1 minute fast, 2 minutes easy) improve fitness efficiently; high-intensity interval training (HIIT) can match longer moderate exercise for some outcomes. For beginners, keep intervals moderate and build up.

**Mobility and flexibility.** Gentle range-of-motion work and stretching improve or maintain flexibility, and many people find it reduces stiffness from long sitting. Evidence for stretching preventing injury is weak; its main value is comfort and range of motion. Five to ten minutes a day (or yoga, Module 18) is enough.

**Why a 30-day challenge?** Thirty days of 5 sessions a week builds the routine and lets you see early strength gains; it is a training phase, not a finish line. Expect noticeable changes in your push-up and plank numbers within a month, mainly from your nervous system learning the movements.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brisk walking improves health | **Strong** | Large observational studies and trials. |
| More daily steps linked to lower mortality, levelling off | **Moderate** | Large meta-analyses; observational, so causation is partly inferred. |
| "10,000 steps" as a scientific threshold | **Failed to replicate or myth** | Started as a marketing slogan; benefits begin well below it. |
| Interval training improves fitness efficiently | **Moderate** | Many trials; effects similar to longer moderate exercise for some outcomes. |
| Stretching prevents injury | **Mixed or weak** | Weak evidence; main benefit is range of motion and comfort. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Ashiq's weekly plan for the 30-day challenge:

| Day | Session | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday | Strength A + 5 min mobility | 35 min |
| Tuesday | Brisk walk with two hill stretches | 30 min |
| Wednesday | Strength B + 5 min mobility | 35 min |
| Thursday | Walk-run intervals (1 min jog, 2 min walk × 6) | 25 min |
| Friday | Strength A + 5 min mobility | 35 min |
| Saturday | Long walk with his cousin, or a football game | 45 min |
| Sunday | Rest, or yoga (Module 18) | 20 min |

He counts five "challenge sessions" a week. Monsoon rain cancels two walks, so he does 20 minutes of brisk marching and step-ups inside instead. On day 30 he retests: push-ups (knees) from 7 to 16, plank from 35 to 70 seconds, 1 km from 11:40 to 9:55. His resting heart rate is 78 (from 82). Sit and reach is −6 cm (from −9). He writes: "Strength up a lot, heart a bit, flexibility a bit. Keep going: next goal is full push-ups."

## How to use it

**Plan your week (choose five challenge sessions):**
- **Strength:** 2 or 3 sessions (A and B, PD-M17-L02).
- **Cardio:** 2 or 3 sessions of brisk walking, walk-run intervals or Couch to 5K, 20 to 45 minutes each.
- **Mobility:** 5 minutes after every session (the cool-down stretches) or the yoga routine.
- **Rest:** at least one full rest day.

**Talk test for intensity:** moderate = can talk, not sing; vigorous = only a few words.

**The 30-day fitness challenge:**
1. Five sessions a week for 30 days (about 20 to 22 sessions), logged.
2. Warm up every time; follow the progression rule.
3. On bad-weather or busy days, do a 10-minute indoor version (squats, push-ups, marching), which still counts.
4. Day 30: retest push-ups and plank (and ideally all five tests) and compare with your baseline.

**With others:** walk-run with a friend, join a local football or volleyball game, or start a 6 am walking group in your ward. Group exercise is linked to better adherence.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NHS Couch to 5K: free 9-week running plan (app, website and PDF)](https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/get-active/get-running-with-couch-to-5k/) | Read how the 9-week plan works; download the app if you want to run | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [NHS Fitness Studio: aerobic exercise videos](https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/aerobic-exercises/) | Do one aerobic video on a rainy day | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [NHS: flexibility exercises](https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/flexibility-exercises/) | Use the flexibility exercises as your 5-minute mobility routine | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Write your weekly plan with five challenge sessions and a rest day.
2. Add "Fitness challenge session" to Loop for 30 days.
3. Complete and log the sessions for 30 days, using indoor versions when needed.
4. On day 30, retest push-ups and plank (and ideally all five tests) and write the changes.

**Proof to record:** Your weekly plan, a 30-day Loop screenshot or workout log, and day-30 retest numbers compared with your baseline.

## Template: 30-day fitness plan

```
30-DAY FITNESS CHALLENGE        Start ______  End ______
Weekly plan:
Mon ______ Tue ______ Wed ______ Thu ______ Fri ______ Sat ______ Sun rest/yoga
Intensity: moderate = can talk, not sing; vigorous = a few words only
Indoor backup (10 min): 3 rounds of 10 squats, 5-10 push-ups (any level),
  30 s marching, 20 s plank
Sessions done: week 1 ___ week 2 ___ week 3 ___ week 4 ___
RETEST (day 30)      Baseline   Day 30   Change
Push-ups             ___        ___      ___
Plank (s)            ___        ___      ___
1 km                 ___        ___      ___
Resting HR           ___        ___      ___
Sit and reach (cm)   ___        ___      ___
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Doing hard sessions every day.** Rest and easy days let your body adapt. Hard every day leads to injury or quitting.
- **Skipping because of rain or a busy day.** Do the 10-minute indoor version; it keeps the habit.
- **Running too much too soon.** Use walk-run intervals or Couch to 5K; increase gradually.
- **Exercising hard in the midday heat.** Train early or late, drink water, slow down on hot days.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does "moderate intensity" feel like, by the talk test?
    - A) You can sing easily
    - B) You can talk but not sing
    - C) You feel nothing
    - D) You can't say a word
2. Where did the "10,000 steps a day" figure come from?
    - A) An Indian government rule
    - B) A 1960s marketing slogan in Japan
    - C) A WHO study
    - D) The Olympic committee
3. What is the NHS Couch to 5K plan?
    - A) A diet plan
    - B) A free 9-week walk-run plan with three sessions a week
    - C) A paid gym membership
    - D) A 5-day fast
4. What is the main proven benefit of stretching?
    - A) Guaranteed injury prevention
    - B) Bigger muscles
    - C) Better range of motion and comfort
    - D) Weight loss

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the Couch to 5K page
- **Action:** complete the 30-day fitness challenge with five sessions a week and retest on day 30. It is done when your proof is saved: your weekly plan, a 30-day Loop screenshot or workout log, and day-30 retest numbers compared with your baseline.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** The talk test is a simple intensity guide.
2. **B.** Benefits start well below 10,000 steps.
3. **B.** It builds from walking to running 5 km.
4. **C.** Evidence for injury prevention is weak.

sections.title: Module 18: Yoga basics
sections.summary: Yoga basics using the free Ministry of Ayush Common Yoga Protocol: the sequence, the general guidelines, the cautions for each practice, honest evidence, and your own 20-minute routine three times a week.
sections.content:
*Part C: Strengthen your body.*

## Overview

Yoga fits easily into a Kerala home routine: it needs a mat or a bedsheet, can be done by the whole family and complements the strength programme in Module 17 (it can replace the Sunday session). Its proven benefits are modest but real: flexibility, balance, back comfort and calm.

Check the cautions before you start. If you have high blood pressure, heart problems, hernia, a recent surgery, or are pregnant, some practices are not suitable; ask a doctor or a qualified yoga teacher.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Follow the Common Yoga Protocol sequence.
- Apply the general guidelines and the cautions for each practice.
- Explain what yoga research supports and what it does not.
- Run your own 20-minute routine three times a week.

## Time

About 1 hour 45 minutes in total: 1 hour 15 minutes of lessons and 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 12–13, with the module project due in week 13.

## Lessons

1. PD-M18-L01: The Common Yoga Protocol, safely (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Copy-ready tools in this module

- The CYP sequence table and your 20-minute routine with log (PD-M18-L01).

## Module project: a safe 20-minute yoga routine, practised for two weeks

1. Do one full CYP session.
2. Write your 20-minute routine, leaving out any practices your health rules out.
3. Practise it three times a week for two weeks, logged.
4. Retest sit and reach and stiffness; decide whether yoga replaces or adds to one weekly session in your fitness plan.

**Proof to record:** Your routine, six logged sessions and before-and-after measures.

## Add to your Personal Playbook

Copy these lines into the Playbook note in Joplin (set up in Week 0). By the end of the course they become your one-page Personal Playbook.

- Yoga: my 20-minute routine ___ times a week; practices I skip: ______.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Safety | Cautions not read | Cautions read but not applied | Cautions applied to your own health |
| Practice | Fewer than three sessions | Three to five sessions | Six or more sessions |
| Form | Forcing postures | Mostly gentle | Slow, within capacity, breathing steadily |
| Evaluation | No measures | Feelings only | Before-and-after measures and a decision |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Do 10 minutes of loosening practices and Shavasana three times a week.
- Learn one pranayama (Bhramari or Nadi shodhana) for stressful moments.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Put the ones you miss on your phone's flashcard app (AnkiDroid, if you did the Learning Capabilities course).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Common Yoga Protocol | A free, 45-minute standard sequence from the Ministry of Ayush (MDNIY). |
| CYP order | Prayer, loosening, standing, sitting, prone, supine, Kapalabhati, pranayama, dhyana, sankalpa. |
| Meals and yoga | Practise on an empty or light stomach. |
| Kapalabhati cautions | Avoid with heart problems, high BP, vertigo, epilepsy, migraine, stroke, hernia, ulcer, pregnancy, menstruation. |
| Best-supported yoga benefits | Flexibility, balance, lower-back pain; modest mental-health benefits. |
| Golden rule | Practise within your own capacity: stretch, never pain. |

## Top mistakes and misuses in this module

- **Copying advanced poses from social media.** Stay with the beginner protocol.
- **Treating yoga as medicine.** Use it alongside, not instead of, medical care.
- **Skipping the cautions.** Read them for every practice you choose.

sections.title: PD-M18-L01: The Common Yoga Protocol, safely
sections.summary: **Outcome:** You can follow the Ministry of Ayush Common Yoga Protocol safely, know its cautions, and run a 20-minute routine of your own three times a week. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 45 minutes for one full session).
sections.content:
## The principle in one line

Yoga combines postures, breathing and meditation; it improves flexibility, balance and wellbeing modestly and safely for most people, when practised gently and within your own capacity.

## The science

**What yoga is.** Yoga is an Indian tradition of physical postures (**asanas**), breath regulation (**pranayama**), concentration and meditation (**dharana**, **dhyana**), with ethical and philosophical roots described in texts such as Patanjali's *Yoga Sutras*. Modern practice usually emphasises the physical and breathing parts. The **International Day of Yoga** (21 June) is observed worldwide, and the Government of India publishes a free **Common Yoga Protocol (CYP)** for it.

**The Common Yoga Protocol.** The protocol, prepared by the Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga under the Ministry of Ayush, is a standard sequence of about **45 minutes** for beginners. The 4th revised edition (2019) lists the sequence below and detailed instructions with cautions for each practice ([Common Yoga Protocol, 2019 PDF](https://www.mea.gov.in/images/pdf/common-yoga-protocol-english.pdf); a 5th revised edition was published in 2022 with a slightly shorter list: [2022 PDF](https://www.sanskrit.nic.in/uploads/CYP_2022/English.pdf)).

**What the research shows.** Reviews of yoga trials find **moderate** evidence that yoga improves **flexibility, balance and lower-back pain**, and **small to moderate** improvements in **anxiety, depression and stress**, often similar to other forms of exercise. Benefits for blood pressure and blood sugar have been found in some trials, but many studies are small, short or of mixed quality. Claims that particular asanas "cure" diseases, detoxify organs or balance chakras are not supported by good evidence. Yoga is generally safe; injuries are uncommon and mostly come from forcing advanced postures.

**General guidance from the protocol (paraphrased):**
- Practise in a calm, clean place, on an empty or light stomach (many teachers suggest waiting 2 to 3 hours after a full meal), with the bladder and bowels empty, in light cotton clothes.
- Don't practise when exhausted, ill, in a hurry or under acute stress.
- **Consult a doctor or yoga expert first** if you have a chronic illness, pain, heart problems, or are pregnant.
- Move slowly, with awareness of body and breath. Breathe through the nose unless told otherwise. Don't hold the breath unless the practice asks for it. **Practise within your own capacity**; no jerks or forcing.
- After practice, wait 20 to 30 minutes before bathing or eating.

**Key cautions in the protocol** include: avoid **Kapalabhati** with heart problems, high blood pressure, vertigo, epilepsy, migraine, a history of stroke, hernia, gastric ulcer, during pregnancy or menstruation; avoid **Pada-hastasana** with heart problems, disc problems, hernia, ulcers, glaucoma, high myopia or vertigo; avoid **Ushtrasana** with heart disease or hernia; avoid **Bhujangasana** for 2 to 3 months after abdominal surgery, and with hernia or ulcers; avoid **Shalabhasana** with high blood pressure, peptic ulcer or hernia; avoid **Pavanamuktasana** with abdominal injury, hernia, sciatica, severe back pain or pregnancy. Read the PDF for the full list.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Principle or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yoga improves flexibility and balance | **Moderate** | Several reviews of trials. |
| Yoga helps chronic lower-back pain | **Moderate** | Reviews find benefits similar to other exercise therapies. |
| Yoga reduces anxiety, depression and stress | **Moderate** | Small to moderate effects; study quality mixed. |
| Specific asanas cure diseases or "detoxify" organs | **Failed to replicate or myth** | Not supported by good evidence. |
| Yoga is generally safe when practised gently | **Moderate** | Injury rates are low; most injuries come from forcing postures. |

## Everyday Kerala example

Anu's mother, 56, has knee pain and mild high blood pressure; Anu, 29, has stiff shoulders from studying. They decide to practise together three mornings a week.

Before starting, her mother's doctor at the Family Health Centre approves gentle yoga but advises avoiding Kapalabhati because of her blood pressure. They follow the CYP from a phone video, skipping Kapalabhati and doing Bhadrasana and Vajrasana with a folded towel under the knees. Anu's mother cannot do Trikonasana fully, so she bends only a little, holding a chair.

After six weeks, Anu can reach 4 cm further in the sit-and-reach test and her shoulders feel looser. Her mother says she sleeps better and enjoys the morning routine with her daughter. Neither notices dramatic change in anything else, which matches the research: modest, real benefits, especially when it becomes a shared routine.

## How to use it

**The Common Yoga Protocol sequence (about 45 minutes):**

| Step | Practice | What it includes | About |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Prayer (opening) | A short prayer or a calm, prayerful mood | 1 min |
| 2 | Loosening practices (chalana kriya / sukshma vyayama) | Neck bending, shoulder movement, trunk movement, knee movement | 4 min |
| 3 | Standing asanas | Tadasana, Vrikshasana, Pada-hastasana, Ardha chakrasana, Trikonasana | 7 min |
| 4 | Sitting asanas | Bhadrasana, Vajrasana, Ardha ushtrasana, Ushtrasana, Shashankasana, Uttana mandukasana, Vakrasana | 7 min |
| 5 | Prone asanas (lying on the front) | Makarasana, Bhujangasana, Shalabhasana | 4 min |
| 6 | Supine asanas (lying on the back) | Setubandhasana, Uttanapadasana, Ardha halasana, Pavanamuktasana, Shavasana | 7 min |
| 7 | Kapalabhati | Forceful exhalation, passive inhalation (see cautions) | 2 min |
| 8 | Pranayama | Nadi shodhana (alternate nostril), Sheetali, Bhramari | 6 min |
| 9 | Dhyana | Meditation | 5 min |
| 10 | Sankalpa and Shanti patha | A resolution, and a closing peace chant | 2 min |

(The timings in the last column are a rough guide for planning; the protocol describes the practices rather than a minute-by-minute schedule.)

**Your 20-minute routine (three times a week):** choose from the protocol, for example: loosening practices (4 min), Tadasana, Vrikshasana and Trikonasana (5 min), Vajrasana and Shashankasana (3 min), Bhujangasana and Makarasana (3 min), Setubandhasana and Shavasana (3 min), Nadi shodhana or Bhramari (2 min). Skip anything your health conditions rule out.

**Practising safely:** follow one clear video or the PDF pictures; enter and leave each posture slowly; stop at the point of stretch, never pain; use a wall or chair for balance postures; keep breathing.

**With others:** yoga is easy to share with family members of any age, with adjustments. A family or ward yoga session on Sundays (or on International Day of Yoga) builds connection as well as flexibility.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Ministry of AYUSH and MDNIY, Common Yoga Protocol, 4th revised edition, 2019 (PDF, MEA copy)](https://www.mea.gov.in/images/pdf/common-yoga-protocol-english.pdf) | Read the general guidelines and the instructions and cautions for each practice | 40 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [Ministry of Ayush, Common Yoga Protocol, 5th revised edition, 2022 (PDF)](https://www.sanskrit.nic.in/uploads/CYP_2022/English.pdf) | Skim the 2022 edition to compare the sequence | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |
| [NHS Fitness Studio: Pilates and yoga videos](https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/exercise/pilates-and-yoga/) | Optional: try one beginner yoga video | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-04 |

## Action task

1. Read the CYP general guidelines and cautions; list any practices you should skip and why.
2. Do one full CYP session (about 45 minutes) following the PDF or a clear video.
3. Design your own 20-minute routine and do it three times a week for two weeks.
4. Before and after the two weeks, measure sit and reach and rate how stiff you feel (0–10).

**Proof to record:** Your list of practices to skip, a note on the full session, your 20-minute routine, six logged sessions and before-and-after sit-and-reach and stiffness ratings.

## Template: Yoga routine and log

```
MY YOGA ROUTINE (20 minutes)           Practices I skip, and why: ______
1. Loosening practices ............ 4 min
2. Standing: ______________ ........ 5 min
3. Sitting: _______________ ........ 3 min
4. Prone: ________________ ......... 3 min
5. Supine + Shavasana ............. 3 min
6. Pranayama: ________________ ..... 2 min
LOG: Date | Routine (full CYP / 20 min) | Minutes | Felt (stiff / ok / loose) | Any pain? (stop)
Before: sit and reach ___ cm, stiffness ___/10   After 2 weeks: ___ cm, ___/10
```

## Common mistakes and misuses

- **Forcing a posture to look like the picture.** Stop at a stretch, never pain. Use a wall or chair.
- **Doing Kapalabhati with health conditions.** Check the cautions; skip it if you have blood-pressure, heart or other listed conditions.
- **Practising after a heavy meal.** Practise on an empty or light stomach.
- **Believing cure claims.** Yoga's benefits are real but modest; it does not replace medical treatment.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first; that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. About how long is the Common Yoga Protocol?
    - A) It has no set length
    - B) 5 minutes
    - C) 3 hours
    - D) About 45 minutes
2. Who should avoid Kapalabhati, according to the protocol?
    - A) Nobody
    - B) People with heart problems, high blood pressure, vertigo, epilepsy, hernia, during pregnancy and others listed
    - C) Only children
    - D) Everyone over 20
3. What does research show yoga reliably improves?
    - A) Flexibility, balance and lower-back pain, with modest mental-health benefits
    - B) It cures diabetes
    - C) It replaces all medicine
    - D) It removes toxins from the liver
4. When should you practise, relative to meals?
    - A) Only after eating sweets
    - B) Straight after a big meal
    - C) On an empty or light stomach (many teachers suggest 2 to 3 hours after a full meal)
    - D) Meals make no difference

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** read the lesson and the CYP general guidelines and cautions
- **Action:** do one full CYP session, then your own 20-minute routine three times a week for two weeks. It is done when your proof is saved: your list of practices to skip, a note on the full session, your 20-minute routine, six logged sessions and before-and-after sit-and-reach and stiffness ratings.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It is a 45-minute standard sequence.
2. **B.** The protocol lists several cautions.
3. **A.** Moderate evidence for these outcomes; cure claims are unsupported.
4. **C.** The protocol advises an empty or light stomach.

sections.title: Final retest and checklist
sections.summary: Repeat every baseline test (form B of the quiz), compare start and end, tick the final checklist of your personal operating system and write a one-page reflection.
sections.content:
Take every test again, the same way as in week 0, then compare. Use **form B** of the thinking-traps quiz (form A's answers would be remembered). Use the same push-up version, route and time of day as at the start.

## How to read your results honestly

- **Small changes are real changes.** One or two points on a 25-point scale, or a few more push-ups, matter when they come from habits you will keep.
- **Personality barely moves in months.** If your Big Five scores hardly changed, that is normal. Habits and skills change faster than traits.
- **Some numbers get worse for good reasons.** Your screen time may rise in an exam month; your rejection fears may feel bigger because you finally notice them. Write the reason next to the number.
- **The quiz is not an IQ test.** It measures whether you now slow down on trap questions. Knowing the traps helps less than you would hope (PD-M03-L03): the habit of checking is what counts.

Take every test now, in week 30, on a normal week, and write the results in a note called **Baseline B** in your Playbook notebook (00 Baseline). Be honest; nobody else sees these numbers. The point is to measure change, not to score high.

## 1. Life wheel (5 minutes)

Score each area of your life from 1 (very unhappy with it) to 10 (couldn't be better). Draw it as a wheel with eight spokes if you like; low spokes show where the wheel is "flat".

| Area | What it includes | Score 1–10 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Health and fitness | energy, strength, sleep, food |  |
| Mind and emotions | calm, mood, handling stress |  |
| Learning and career | PSC preparation, skills, work |  |
| Money | income, savings, control over spending |  |
| Family | relationships at home |  |
| Friends and social life | people you can call, new connections |  |
| Fun and rest | hobbies, play, real breaks |  |
| Purpose and contribution | meaning, helping others, community |  |

## 2. Big Five personality (10 minutes)

Take the free [IPIP Big Five Factor Markers test](https://openpsychometrics.org/tests/IPIP-BFFM/) (50 statements, 3 to 8 minutes; educational use only). Write down your five percentile scores: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional stability, Openness (Intellect/Imagination). Traits change slowly; at the end of the course expect small shifts at most, mainly in conscientiousness and emotional stability. Lesson PD-M05-L02 explains what the scores mean and don't mean.

## 3. VIA character strengths (15 minutes)

Take the free [VIA character strengths survey](https://www.viacharacter.org/) (about 12 minutes). Write down your top five strengths in order. (The site offers paid reports; you don't need them.)

## 4. Fitness tests (30 minutes, plus heart rate on 3 mornings)

Read the safety box on **Start here** first. Warm up for 5 minutes (march on the spot, arm circles, gentle squats). Rest 3 to 5 minutes between tests. Stop if anything hurts sharply.

| Test | How to do it safely | Unit | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Push-ups | Full push-ups on the floor, or from the knees if you cannot do 5 full ones. Body straight from head to knees or heels, chest to a fist's height from the floor, arms fully straight at the top. Count clean reps until form breaks. Write which version you did and use the same version at the end. | reps |  |
| Plank hold | Forearms under shoulders, body in a straight line, squeeze your seat. Time it until your hips sag or lift. Stop at 3 minutes at most. | seconds |  |
| 1 km walk or walk-run | A flat, safe 1 km route (a marked km stone, a school ground, or measured with a maps app). Brisk walk, or walk-run if you already run. Time it. | minutes:seconds |  |
| Resting heart rate | In the morning before tea or coffee, sit quietly for 5 minutes, find the pulse at your wrist or neck and count for 30 seconds, then double it. Do it on 3 mornings and take the average. | beats per minute |  |
| Sit and reach | Sit on the floor, legs straight, feet against a wall or step. Reach forward slowly with both hands, no bouncing. Measure with a ruler or tape from fingertips to toes: minus if short of the toes, plus if past them. | centimetres |  |

## 5. One-week sleep log (1 minute each morning for 7 days)

Use this log every morning for 7 days. Write the averages at the bottom.

```
7-DAY SLEEP LOG (fill in each morning, takes 1 minute)
Day | Into bed | Lights out | Minutes to fall asleep (guess) | Times awake | Got up | Total sleep (h) | Quality (1-5) | Caffeine after 2 pm? | Screen in last 30 min? | Daytime nap?
Average total sleep: ___ h  Average quality: ___  Latest lights-out: ___
```

## 6. Screen time (2 minutes, after 7 days)

In Digital Wellbeing, write down your **daily average screen time** for the last 7 days, the **number of unlocks** per day, and your **top 3 apps** by time.

## 7. Self-ratings (5 minutes)

Rate each statement 1 to 5. Add up each scale (5 to 25).

| Scale | Statement (rate 1 = not at all like me, 5 = very like me) | Start | End |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Confidence | When I set myself a hard task, I believe I can do it if I keep working. |  |  |
|  | I try new things even when I might fail at first. |  |  |
|  | I can say what I think in a group without rehearsing it many times. |  |  |
|  | A setback or a "no" does not ruin my week. |  |  |
|  | I feel comfortable being seen by others (on video, on a stage, in a shop). |  |  |
| Social confidence | I can start a conversation with a stranger (a shopkeeper, a person at a bus stop). |  |  |
|  | I can keep a conversation going for five minutes with someone new. |  |  |
|  | I can ask for help, advice or a discount without much fear. |  |  |
|  | I can say no to a friend or relative politely and clearly. |  |  |
|  | I have at least three people I could call if I needed help. |  |  |
| Listening | I let people finish their sentences before I reply. |  |  |
|  | I ask follow-up questions about what people tell me. |  |  |
|  | I can sum up what someone said to their satisfaction. |  |  |
|  | I remember the names of people I meet. |  |  |
|  | People tell me things they do not tell others. |  |  |

## 8. Thinking-traps quiz, form B (10 minutes)

Answer quickly, the way you normally would; don't look anything up. Score 1 per correct answer, out of 10. The answers are under the questions: cover them first.

1. A bat and a ball (for gully cricket) cost Rs 220 together. The bat costs Rs 200 more than the ball. How much is the ball?
    - A) Rs 22
    - B) Rs 2
    - C) Rs 10
    - D) Rs 20
2. Salma from Vadakara is shy, precise and loves numbers. Which is she more likely to work as?
    - A) A professional statistician
    - B) There is no way to reason about it
    - C) A shop or office worker
    - D) Equally likely
3. Arun loves cricket and coaches children on weekends. Which is more probable?
    - A) The second, because the details fit
    - B) Arun is a teacher
    - C) Both are equally probable
    - D) Arun is a teacher and plays in a local cricket club
4. You have spent eight months and Rs 6,000 on a coaching class that you now find much worse than free material. What matters most in deciding whether to continue?
    - A) That you have already spent eight months
    - B) Which option will help you most from now on, counting only future time and money
    - C) What the class teacher will think
    - D) The Rs 6,000 already paid
5. Your friend says he will finish building his YouTube channel "in a month". Projects like his usually take three to four months. What is the best estimate?
    - A) Three to four months, unless he has a specific reason to be faster
    - B) One month: he is very motivated
    - C) It will never happen
    - D) Two weeks
6. A student scores 98% in one mock test after months of 70s. In the next mock he scores 78%. What is the likeliest explanation?
    - A) The second test was rigged
    - B) He forgot everything in one week
    - C) He became lazy after the high score
    - D) Part of the 98% was luck, and scores tend to drift back towards the usual level
7. Students who use a certain study app score higher in exams. What can we conclude?
    - A) Users score higher; without an experiment we don't know if the app causes it
    - B) Apps never help
    - C) Good students avoid the app
    - D) The app raises scores
8. In a lottery, the number 7 has not come up as the first digit for 20 draws. What is the chance it comes up next time?
    - A) Certain within two more draws
    - B) Higher, because it is overdue
    - C) Lower, because it is unlucky
    - D) The same as any other digit
9. After a friend's phone was hacked, you feel that most phones in your town are being hacked. What would tell you if that is true?
    - A) How many forwards about hacking you received
    - B) Figures on how often phones are hacked, compared with how many phones there are
    - C) Your feeling, because it is strong
    - D) How upset your friend was
10. A salesman first shows you a Rs 45,000 phone and then a Rs 22,000 one, which suddenly feels cheap. What is happening?
    - A) The second phone is objectively good value
    - B) The salesman made a mistake
    - C) Phones are always cheaper the second time
    - D) The first price is acting as an anchor for the second

### Answers, form B

1. **C.** Rs 10 (the bat is Rs 210). The quick answer, Rs 20, would make the total Rs 240. Same trap as before: fast thinking unchecked (PD-M01-L01).
2. **C.** Shop and office workers vastly outnumber statisticians, so the base rate wins even though the description "sounds like" a statistician (representativeness, PD-M01-L02).
3. **B.** Adding a detail can only make a story less probable, even when it makes it more convincing (conjunction fallacy, PD-M01-L02).
4. **B.** Money and time already spent cannot be recovered either way. Judge only the future (sunk cost, PD-M03-L01).
5. **A.** The typical time for similar projects (the outside view, or reference class) beats an inside-view guess (planning fallacy, PD-M03-L01).
6. **D.** An extreme score is usually partly luck, so the next one is closer to average: regression to the mean (PD-M02-L01).
7. **A.** Keen students may both download apps and score well. Only a fair comparison (ideally random assignment) shows cause (PD-M02-L01).
8. **D.** Each draw is independent: past draws do not change the odds (gambler's fallacy, PD-M01-L02).
9. **B.** One vivid case feels like many. Rates and base numbers decide (availability, PD-M03-L01).
10. **D.** The first number you see pulls your judgement towards it. Compare with your own budget and with other shops instead (anchoring, PD-M03-L01, PD-M29-L01).

## Compare start and end

| Measure | Start | End | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Life wheel: total of 8 areas (out of 80) |  |  |  |
| Life wheel: lowest area |  |  |  |
| Big Five: conscientiousness / emotional stability percentiles |  |  |  |
| VIA top five (same or different?) |  |  |  |
| Average sleep (hours) and quality (1–5) |  |  |  |
| Screen time per day and unlocks |  |  |  |
| Confidence scale (5–25) |  |  |  |
| Social-confidence scale (5–25) |  |  |  |
| Listening scale (5–25) |  |  |  |
| Thinking-traps quiz (out of 10; A at start, B at end) |  |  |  |

### Fitness

| Test | Start | End | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Push-ups |  |  |  |
| Plank hold |  |  |  |
| 1 km walk or walk-run |  |  |  |
| Resting heart rate |  |  |  |
| Sit and reach |  |  |  |

## Final checklist: your personal operating system

Tick each item under **Your tasks**. Each line shows where it was built.

| Item | Built in |
| --- | --- |
| Habit tracker in use for the whole course, with at least 5 habits above 80% in the last month | Week 0 onwards |
| At least 20 weekly reflections and recordings | Daily system track |
| Two weeks of bias journal, and your top three traps named | PD-M03-L03 |
| A decision sheet used for a real decision | PD-M04-L02 |
| A 12-month plan and a weekly planning routine | Module 7 |
| A two-week personal experiment with data and a decision | PD-M08-L04 |
| Two weeks of thought records | PD-M11-L02 |
| The 30-day meditation, journaling, rejection and fitness challenges completed (or restarted and completed) | Modules 12, 14 and 17 |
| A training plan, a sleep window and a plate you actually follow | Part C |
| 14 days of conversation challenges logged | PD-M25-L02 |
| One real piece of constructive feedback given with the script | PD-M26-L03 |
| A 5-minute talk given to a real audience, recorded | Module 27 |
| The persuasion lab and a real negotiation, with results | Modules 28 and 29 |
| A manipulation-spotting file with at least 10 real examples analysed | Module 32 |
| Capstone: 30-day behaviour-change project and social-skills project, with data | Module 36 |
| Your one-page Personal Playbook, morning and evening routines, and 12-month growth plan | PD-M36-L03 |

## Your final reflection (one page)

1. The three biggest changes, with the numbers that show them.
2. The three habits you will keep for the next 12 months, with their cues.
3. One thing that did not work for you, and why.
4. Who helped, and how you will thank them.
5. Read your Personal Playbook aloud and record it (2 to 3 minutes). Listen to it on the 1st of each month.

sections.title: What next: your 12-month roadmap
sections.summary: How to keep the system running for a year, free resources to go deeper, other courses in the app, and when to get professional help.
sections.content:
## The next 12 months

| When | Focus | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every day | Keep the 3 to 6 habits that earned a place in your Playbook | Loop Habit Tracker; never miss twice |
| Every Sunday | Weekly reflection and recording | The same template; it is your steering wheel |
| 1st of each month | Re-read your Personal Playbook and pick one monthly focus | One module's project, repeated at a harder level |
| Every 3 months | Retest fitness and the three self-rating scales | The baseline page; write the change in your Playbook |
| Every 6 months | Life wheel and 12-month plan review | PD-M07-L01 and PD-M07-L02 |
| Once a year | A new 30-day challenge (rejection, speaking, fitness or a new one) | The challenge templates on the Toolkit page |

## Go deeper (all free)

- **Psychology:** read [OpenStax Psychology 2e](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/preface) chapters 2, 7, 10, 12 and 14 in full (about 2 hours each), then work through the [MIT OCW Introduction to Psychology](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/9-00sc-introduction-to-psychology-fall-2011/) lectures (about 1 hour each) and the [Noba modules](https://nobaproject.com/) on topics you liked.
- **Wellbeing:** audit [The Science of Well-Being](https://www.coursera.org/learn/the-science-of-well-being) (about 13 hours over 6 weeks) and try one new [Greater Good in Action](https://ggia.berkeley.edu/) practice a month.
- **Stoicism and character:** one letter of [Seneca](https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/seneca/moral-letters-to-lucilius/richard-m-gummere) a week, and a book of [Meditations](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2680) a month.
- **Speaking:** visit [Calicut Toastmasters](https://www.toastmasters.org/Find-a-Club/03984104-calicut-toastmasters) as a guest (check meeting details and any fees with the club first), or start a speaking circle with friends using the PD-M27 practice plan.
- **Other courses in this app:** [Practical Learning Capabilities](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/learning-capabilities/lrn-start) (in the Practical Learning Capabilities course) for study skills and PSC exam mastery; [Practical Personal Finance](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/personal-finance/fin-m01) (in the Practical Personal Finance for India course) for money habits; [Practical Entrepreneurship](https://naipunyam.github.io/vidhyarambham/#/course/entrepreneurship/ent-m03) (in the Practical Entrepreneurship course) to turn people skills into customer conversations and sales.

## Signs you need more than a course

If a problem keeps returning despite your best effort for several weeks (sleep, mood, anxiety, anger, a habit you cannot control), that is a reason to see a professional, not a personal failure. Tele-MANAS (**14416**) is free and confidential to call; a doctor at your local Family Health Centre can refer you.

sections.title: Glossary with Malayalam meanings
sections.summary: 86 key terms in English and Malayalam, with simple meanings.
sections.content:
Key words from the course, roughly in the order you meet them. Some English terms (CBT, BATNA, MLM) are used as they are in Malayalam conversation; the Malayalam is a plain-language rendering so you can explain the idea to family and friends. Malayalam psychology terms vary between textbooks; if your PSC material uses a different word, use that one.

| English | മലയാളം (Malayalam) | Simple meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **System 1 / System 2** | വേഗ ചിന്ത / മന്ദ ചിന്ത | Fast, automatic thinking versus slow, effortful thinking |
| **Heuristic** | ചിന്താ കുറുക്കുവഴി | A mental shortcut that is usually good enough but sometimes wrong |
| **Cognitive bias** | ചിന്താ പക്ഷപാതം | A predictable error in thinking |
| **Confirmation bias** | സ്ഥിരീകരണ പക്ഷപാതം | Looking only for evidence that agrees with what you already believe |
| **Sunk cost** | മുടക്കിപ്പോയ ചെലവ് | Money or time already spent that cannot be recovered |
| **Overconfidence** | അമിത ആത്മവിശ്വാസം | Being more sure than your accuracy justifies |
| **Planning fallacy** | ആസൂത്രണ പിഴവ് | Underestimating how long tasks will take |
| **Loss aversion** | നഷ്ടഭയം | Losses feel bigger than equal gains |
| **Anchoring** | നങ്കൂരമിടൽ (ആദ്യ സംഖ്യയുടെ സ്വാധീനം) | The first number you hear pulls your judgement |
| **Availability heuristic** | ഓർമ്മയിൽ എളുപ്പം വരുന്നതിനെ ആശ്രയിക്കൽ | Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind |
| **Base rate** | അടിസ്ഥാന നിരക്ക് | How common something is in general, before details |
| **Correlation** | പരസ്പര ബന്ധം | Two things that tend to go together, without proof that one causes the other |
| **Causation** | കാര്യകാരണ ബന്ധം | One thing actually making another happen |
| **Experiment** | പരീക്ഷണം | A study where researchers change one thing and compare groups |
| **Sample size** | സാമ്പിൾ വലിപ്പം | How many people a study included |
| **Replication** | ആവർത്തന പഠനം | Repeating a study to see if the result holds |
| **Replication crisis** | ആവർത്തന പ്രതിസന്ധി | The discovery that many famous findings did not repeat |
| **Effect size** | ഫലത്തിന്റെ വലിപ്പം | How big a difference is, not just whether it exists |
| **Cognitive distortion** | ചിന്താ വൈകല്യം | An unhelpful thinking pattern named in CBT |
| **CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy)** | കോഗ്നിറ്റീവ് ബിഹേവിയറൽ തെറാപ്പി | A well-tested therapy that works on thoughts and actions |
| **Pre-mortem** | മുൻകൂർ പരാജയ വിശകലനം | Imagining a plan has failed in order to find its weak points |
| **Choice overload** | തിരഞ്ഞെടുപ്പ് ബാഹുല്യം | Feeling stuck when there are too many options |
| **Values** | മൂല്യങ്ങൾ | What matters most to you, guiding how you want to act |
| **Big Five** | അഞ്ച് പ്രധാന വ്യക്തിത്വ ഗുണങ്ങൾ | Five broad personality traits measured on a scale |
| **Character strengths** | സ്വഭാവ ശക്തികൾ | Positive traits such as kindness, curiosity and honesty |
| **Intrinsic motivation** | ആന്തരിക പ്രചോദനം | Doing something because it is interesting or meaningful in itself |
| **Extrinsic motivation** | ബാഹ്യ പ്രചോദനം | Doing something for a reward or to avoid punishment |
| **Autonomy** | സ്വയംഭരണം | Feeling that your actions are your own choice |
| **Present bias** | വർത്തമാന പക്ഷപാതം | Valuing rewards now far more than bigger rewards later |
| **Commitment device** | പ്രതിജ്ഞാ ഉപാധി | An arrangement that makes it harder to break a promise to yourself |
| **Temptation bundling** | ഇഷ്ടവും കടമയും ചേർക്കൽ | Allowing a treat only while doing a task you avoid |
| **Habit loop (cue, routine, reward)** | ശീല ചക്രം (സൂചന, പ്രവൃത്തി, പ്രതിഫലം) | The trigger, the action and the payoff that build a habit |
| **Implementation intention (if-then plan)** | എങ്കിൽ-അപ്പോൾ പദ്ധതി | A plan of the form "If X happens, then I will do Y" |
| **Procrastination** | നീട്ടിവയ്ക്കൽ | Delaying a task even though delay will make things worse |
| **Growth mindset** | വളർച്ചാ മനോഭാവം | The belief that abilities can be developed with effort and good strategies |
| **Self-compassion** | സ്വയം കരുണ | Treating yourself with the kindness you would show a friend |
| **Emotional intelligence** | വൈകാരിക ബുദ്ധി | Noticing, understanding and managing emotions in yourself and others |
| **Affect labelling** | വികാരത്തിന് പേര് നൽകൽ | Putting a feeling into words, which can calm it |
| **Reappraisal** | പുനർ വിലയിരുത്തൽ | Changing how you interpret a situation to change how you feel |
| **Empathy** | സഹാനുഭൂതി | Understanding and sharing another person's feelings |
| **Negativity bias** | നിഷേധാത്മക പക്ഷപാതം | Bad events weigh more in the mind than good ones |
| **Stress response** | സമ്മർദ്ദ പ്രതികരണം | The body's fight-or-flight reaction to a demand or threat |
| **Resilience** | അതിജീവന ശേഷി | Bouncing back from difficulty |
| **Thought record** | ചിന്താ രേഖ | A CBT worksheet for examining an upsetting thought |
| **Stoicism** | സ്റ്റോയിക് ചിന്ത | An ancient philosophy of focusing on what you can control |
| **Mindfulness** | സൂക്ഷ്മ ബോധം | Paying attention to the present moment without judging it |
| **Self-efficacy** | സ്വയം കാര്യക്ഷമതാ വിശ്വാസം | Belief in your ability to do a specific task |
| **Spotlight effect** | ശ്രദ്ധാകേന്ദ്ര മിഥ്യ | Overestimating how much others notice you |
| **Impostor feelings** | കപടനാണെന്ന തോന്നൽ | Feeling like a fraud despite evidence of ability |
| **Exposure (fear ladder)** | ഭയ ഗോവണി | Facing fears step by step, from easy to hard, until they shrink |
| **Rejection therapy** | നിരസന ചികിത്സ (നിരസനം ശീലിക്കൽ) | Seeking small, safe "no"s on purpose to lose the fear of rejection |
| **Hedonic adaptation** | സുഖാനുകൂലനം | Getting used to good and bad changes so they stop affecting mood |
| **Social comparison** | സാമൂഹിക താരതമ്യം | Judging yourself against others |
| **Flow** | ലയാവസ്ഥ | Being fully absorbed in a challenging task |
| **Dark pattern** | വഞ്ചനാത്മക ഡിസൈൻ | An app or website design that tricks you into choices |
| **Warm-up** | ശരീരം ചൂടാക്കൽ | Light movement that prepares the body for exercise |
| **Progressive overload** | ക്രമാനുഗത ഭാരവർധന | Making exercise slightly harder over time |
| **Resting heart rate** | വിശ്രമ ഹൃദയമിടിപ്പ് | Heartbeats per minute when sitting still |
| **Asana / pranayama** | ആസനം / പ്രാണായാമം | Yoga postures / yoga breathing practices |
| **Circadian rhythm** | ശരീര ഘടികാരം | The body's roughly 24-hour clock |
| **Protein** | മാംസ്യം (പ്രോട്ടീൻ) | The nutrient the body uses to build and repair |
| **Ergonomics** | ശരീരസൗഹൃദ ക്രമീകരണം | Arranging your space to fit your body |
| **Halo effect** | പ്രഭാവലയ പ്രഭാവം | One good trait making us rate everything about a person higher |
| **Fundamental attribution error** | അടിസ്ഥാന ആരോപണ പിഴവ് | Blaming people's character and ignoring their situation |
| **Stereotype** | മുൻധാരണ | A fixed, oversimplified idea about a group |
| **Rapport** | ആത്മബന്ധം | A feeling of connection and understanding between people |
| **Active listening** | സജീവ ശ്രവണം | Listening to understand, and showing it |
| **Assertiveness** | ദൃഢനിശ്ചയത്തോടെയുള്ള ആശയവിനിമയം | Saying what you need clearly and respectfully |
| **Non-violent communication** | അക്രമരഹിത ആശയവിനിമയം | Observations, feelings, needs and requests instead of blame |
| **Face-saving** | മാനം കാക്കൽ | Letting someone keep their dignity in a disagreement |
| **Reciprocity** | പ്രത്യുപകാരം | The urge to return favours |
| **Social proof** | സാമൂഹിക തെളിവ് | Doing what others like us are doing |
| **Scarcity** | ദൗർലഭ്യം | Things seem more valuable when they are rare or running out |
| **Framing** | അവതരണ രീതി | How the same facts are presented changes choices |
| **BATNA** | ഒത്തുതീർപ്പിലെത്തിയില്ലെങ്കിലുള്ള മികച്ച ബദൽ | Your best option if the negotiation fails |
| **Conformity** | അനുരൂപപ്പെടൽ | Changing behaviour to match a group |
| **Obedience** | അനുസരണ | Following orders from an authority |
| **Groupthink** | സംഘ ചിന്ത | A group agreeing too quickly and ignoring doubts |
| **Social loafing** | കൂട്ടത്തിലെ ഉഴപ്പ് | Putting in less effort when working in a group |
| **Bystander effect** | കാഴ്ചക്കാരന്റെ നിഷ്ക്രിയത്വം | Being less likely to help when others are present |
| **Gaslighting** | ഗ്യാസ്‌ലൈറ്റിംഗ് (ഓർമ്മയെ സംശയിപ്പിക്കൽ) | Making someone doubt their own memory or sanity |
| **Emotional blackmail** | വൈകാരിക ഭീഷണി | Using fear, obligation or guilt to control someone |
| **MLM (multi-level marketing)** | ബഹുതല വിപണനം | Selling schemes where income depends on recruiting others |
| **Integrity** | സത്യസന്ധത / ധർമ്മനിഷ്ഠ | Acting by your values even when no one is watching |
| **Humility** | വിനയം | An accurate, modest view of yourself and openness to learning |
| **Personal operating system** | വ്യക്തിഗത ജീവിതക്രമം | Your routines, reviews and rules working together |

sections.content:
Every link in this course is listed here with the date it was checked. Links were opened and read for this course (most on 2026-11-04, some on 2026-11-03); nothing was copied from memory. If a link stops working, search for its title on the same website.

- **verified [date]:** the page was opened on that date and its content matched what the course says.
- **verified; check current rules:** as above, but it describes something that changes (an app, a price, free access, a meeting time, a law). Check before you rely on it.
- **headline figures checked; secondary summary:** the numbers were checked on a summary page, not the original paper. Treat them as approximate.
- **found in a web search; page not opened:** the address came from a search result but the page itself could not be opened for checking. Marked unverified.
- **unverified:** the site blocks automated checks. The address is the official one; type it yourself and check that it is the real site.

Open-licensed and official sources are preferred: OpenStax and Noba (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), MIT OpenCourseWare, public-domain classics on Project Gutenberg and Standard Ebooks, government and health bodies (WHO, NHS, ICMR-NIN, the Ministry of Ayush), university centres (Greater Good, Harvard), and open-source apps (Loop, Medito, Joplin). Wikipedia is used for the history and criticism of classic experiments, because its articles on them cite the replication studies.

**Studies named without a link** (for example "Iyengar and Lepper, 2000") are well-known published papers described through the linked review or summary in the same lesson. The course gives numbers only where they were checked against a linked source.
